title: Asthma – Severe Attack Criteria in Children
content: A severe asthma attack in children is indicated by SpO2 < 92%, PEF 33-50% of best or predicted, being too breathless to talk or feed, heart rate >125 bpm (>5 years) or >140 bpm (1-5 years), respiratory rate >30 breaths/min (>5 years) or >40 breaths/min (1-5 years), and use of accessory neck muscles.

title: Asthma – Life-Threatening Attack Criteria in Children
content: A life-threatening asthma attack in children is indicated by SpO2 < 92%, PEF < 33% of best or predicted, silent chest, poor respiratory effort, agitation, altered consciousness, or cyanosis.

title: Asthma – Management of Moderate Attack in Children (2-5 years)
content: In children aged 2-5 years with a moderate asthma attack (SpO2 > 92% and no clinical features of severe asthma), management involves bronchodilator therapy with a beta-2 agonist via a spacer (1 puff every 30-60 seconds up to 10 puffs) and steroid therapy (prednisolone for 3-5 days).

title: Asthma – Management of Severe Attack in Children (2-5 years)
content: Children aged 2-5 years with a severe asthma attack (SpO2 < 92%, too breathless to talk or feed, heart rate > 140/min, respiratory rate > 40/min, use of accessory neck muscles) should be transferred immediately to hospital.

title: Asthma – Management of Life-Threatening Attack in Children (2-5 years)
content: Children aged 2-5 years with a life-threatening asthma attack (SpO2 < 92%, silent chest, poor respiratory effort, agitation, altered consciousness, cyanosis) require immediate hospital transfer.

title: Asthma – Management of Moderate Attack in Children (>5 years)
content: In children over 5 years with a moderate asthma attack (SpO2 > 92%, PEF > 50% best or predicted, no clinical features of severe asthma), management involves bronchodilator therapy and steroid therapy.

title: Asthma – 2024 NICE/BTS/SIGN Guideline Changes
content: In 2024, joint guidelines from NICE, the British Thoracic Society, and SIGN advocated for using combined inhalers (ICS + long-acting beta-2 agonist) as either reliever therapy or for regular use, a change from the previous standard of starting with a short-acting beta-2 agonist (SABA) inhaler.

title: Asthma – Maintenance and Reliever Therapy (MART)
content: Maintenance and reliever therapy (MART) involves using a single inhaled corticosteroid (ICS)/formoterol combination inhaler for both daily maintenance therapy and for the relief of symptoms as needed.

title: Asthma – Initial Management in Children (5-11 years)
content: The first step in managing asthma in children aged 5 to 11 is a twice-daily paediatric low-dose inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) plus a short-acting beta2 agonist (SABA) as needed.

title: Biliary atresia – Pathophysiology
content: Biliary atresia is a condition in children involving the obliteration or discontinuity of the extrahepatic biliary system, leading to an obstruction in bile flow and resulting in neonatal cholestasis.

title: Biliary atresia – Epidemiology
content: Biliary atresia is more common in females and occurs in 1 in every 10,000-15,000 live births. The perinatal form presents in the first two weeks of life, and the postnatal form presents within the first 2-8 weeks.

title: Biliary atresia – Classification
content: Biliary atresia is classified into three types. Type 1: common duct is obliterated. Type 2: atresia of the cystic duct. Type 3: atresia of the left and right ducts to the level of the porta hepatis, accounting for over 90% of cases.

title: Biliary atresia – Clinical Features
content: Patients with biliary atresia typically present in the first few weeks of life with jaundice extending beyond two weeks, dark urine, pale stools, and potentially appetite and growth disturbance.

title: Biliary atresia – Signs
content: Signs of biliary atresia include jaundice, hepatomegaly with splenomegaly, abnormal growth, and cardiac murmurs if associated cardiac abnormalities are present.

title: Biliary atresia – Investigations
content: Investigations for biliary atresia include serum bilirubin (conjugated will be high), LFTs, serum alpha 1-antitrypsin, sweat chloride test, ultrasound of the biliary tree, and a percutaneous liver biopsy with intraoperative cholangioscopy.

title: Biliary atresia – Management
content: The only definitive treatment for biliary atresia is surgical intervention, such as a Kasai procedure. Medical management includes post-operative antibiotics and bile acid enhancers.

title: Biliary atresia – Complications and Prognosis
content: Complications of biliary atresia include unsuccessful anastomosis, progressive liver disease, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma. The prognosis is good if surgery is successful; otherwise, a liver transplant may be required within the first two years of life.

title: Bronchiolitis – Pathophysiology
content: Bronchiolitis is an acute inflammation of the bronchioles, most commonly caused by Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) in 75-80% of cases.

title: Bronchiolitis – Epidemiology
content: Bronchiolitis is the most common cause of serious lower respiratory tract infection in children under 1 year old, with a peak incidence between 3-6 months. It is more common in winter.

title: Bronchiolitis – Aetiology and Risk Factors
content: The most common cause of bronchiolitis is Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV). Other causes include mycoplasma and adenoviruses. The condition is more serious in children with bronchopulmonary dysplasia, congenital heart disease, or cystic fibrosis.

title: Bronchiolitis – Clinical Features
content: Bronchiolitis typically presents with coryzal symptoms followed by a dry cough, increasing breathlessness, wheezing, and fine inspiratory crackles. Feeding difficulties due to dyspnoea are a common reason for hospital admission.

title: Bronchiolitis – Indications for Immediate Hospital Referral
content: Immediate hospital referral for a child with bronchiolitis is recommended for apnoea, appearing seriously unwell, severe respiratory distress (grunting, marked chest recession, RR > 70), central cyanosis, or persistent oxygen saturation < 92%.

title: Bronchiolitis – Indications for Considering Hospital Referral
content: Consider hospital referral for a child with bronchiolitis if they have a respiratory rate over 60 breaths/minute, difficulty with breastfeeding or inadequate oral fluid intake (50-75% of usual volume), or clinical dehydration.

title: Bronchiolitis – Investigations
content: Diagnosis of bronchiolitis is primarily clinical. Immunofluorescence of nasopharyngeal secretions may be used to detect RSV.

title: Bronchiolitis – Management
content: Management of bronchiolitis is largely supportive, including humidified oxygen via a head box if saturations are persistently < 92%, nasogastric feeding if oral intake is inadequate, and suction for excessive upper airway secretions.

title: Croup – Pathophysiology
content: Croup is an upper respiratory tract infection in infants and toddlers, characterized by stridor from laryngeal oedema and secretions. Parainfluenza viruses are the most common cause.

title: Croup – Epidemiology
content: Croup has a peak incidence between 6 months and 3 years of age and is more common in the autumn.

title: Croup – Clinical Features
content: The clinical features of croup include stridor, a barking cough that is worse at night, fever, and coryzal symptoms.

title: Croup – Admission Criteria
content: Admission for a child with croup should be considered if they are under 6 months of age, have known upper airway abnormalities (e.g., Laryngomalacia, Down's syndrome), or if there is uncertainty about the diagnosis.

title: Croup – Management
content: All children with croup, regardless of severity, should receive a single dose of oral dexamethasone (0.15mg/kg). Prednisolone is an alternative if dexamethasone is unavailable.

title: Croup – Emergency Management
content: Emergency treatment for severe croup includes high-flow oxygen and nebulised adrenaline.

title: Cystic fibrosis – Pathophysiology
content: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a defect in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene, leading to increased viscosity of secretions.

title: Cystic fibrosis – Genetics and Epidemiology
content: In the UK, 80% of cystic fibrosis cases are due to the delta F508 mutation on chromosome 7. The condition affects 1 in 2,500 births, with a carrier rate of approximately 1 in 25.

title: Cystic fibrosis – Common Colonising Organisms
content: Organisms that commonly colonise the respiratory tract of patients with cystic fibrosis include Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Burkholderia cepacia, and Aspergillus.

title: Cystic fibrosis – Diagnosis (Sweat Test)
content: The sweat test is used to diagnose cystic fibrosis. A sweat chloride level greater than 60 mEq/l is indicative of the condition. False positives can occur due to malnutrition, adrenal insufficiency, and other conditions.

title: Cystic fibrosis – Presenting Features
content: Cystic fibrosis can present in the neonatal period with meconium ileus or prolonged jaundice (20%), with recurrent chest infections (40%), or with malabsorption and failure to thrive (30%).

title: Cystic fibrosis – Other Clinical Features
content: Other features of cystic fibrosis include short stature, diabetes mellitus, delayed puberty, rectal prolapse, nasal polyps, male infertility, and female subfertility.

title: Cystic fibrosis – Management
content: Management of cystic fibrosis involves regular chest physiotherapy, a high-calorie diet, vitamin supplementation, and pancreatic enzyme supplements. Lung transplantation may be considered in severe cases.

title: Cystic fibrosis – Lumacaftor/Ivacaftor (Orkambi)
content: Lumacaftor/ivacaftor (Orkambi) is a combination therapy used to treat cystic fibrosis patients who are homozygous for the delta F508 mutation. Lumacaftor increases the number of CFTR proteins transported to the cell surface, while ivacaftor potentiates the function of the defective channel.

title: Epiglottitis – Pathophysiology
content: Acute epiglottitis is a serious infection caused by Haemophilus influenzae type B, which can lead to life-threatening airway obstruction. Its incidence has decreased due to the Hib immunisation programme.

title: Epiglottitis – Clinical Features
content: Clinical features of acute epiglottitis include a rapid onset, high temperature, stridor, drooling of saliva, and the patient adopting a 'tripod' position (leaning forward, neck extended).

title: Epiglottitis – Diagnosis
content: Diagnosis of acute epiglottitis is made by direct visualisation of a swollen epiglottis, which should only be performed by senior staff able to intubate. A lateral neck X-ray may show the 'thumb sign'.

title: Epiglottitis – Management
content: Management of acute epiglottitis requires immediate senior involvement (anaesthetics, ENT). Endotracheal intubation may be necessary to protect the airway. Intravenous antibiotics and oxygen should be administered.

title: Epiglottitis – Contraindicated Action
content: If acute epiglottitis is suspected, the throat must NOT be examined due to the high risk of precipitating acute airway obstruction.

title: Febrile convulsion – Definition
content: Febrile convulsions are seizures provoked by fever in otherwise normal children, typically occurring between the ages of 6 months and 5 years. They are seen in approximately 3% of children.

title: Febrile convulsion – Clinical Features
content: Febrile convulsions usually occur early in a viral infection as the temperature rises rapidly. The seizures are typically brief, lasting less than 5 minutes, and are most commonly tonic-clonic.

title: Febrile convulsion – Simple vs. Complex
content: A simple febrile convulsion lasts less than 15 minutes, is generalized, and does not recur within 24 hours. A complex febrile convulsion lasts 15-30 minutes, is focal, and may have repeat seizures within 24 hours.

title: Febrile convulsion – Febrile Status Epilepticus
content: Febrile status epilepticus is defined as a febrile convulsion lasting longer than 30 minutes.

title: Febrile convulsion – Management
content: Children who have had a first febrile seizure or any features of a complex seizure should be admitted to a paediatrics ward for further assessment.

title: Kawasaki disease – Definition
content: Kawasaki disease is a vasculitis that predominantly affects children and can lead to serious complications, including coronary artery aneurysms.

title: Kawasaki disease – Clinical Features
content: Kawasaki disease is characterized by a high-grade fever lasting more than 5 days, conjunctival injection, bright red cracked lips, a 'strawberry' tongue, cervical lymphadenopathy, and red palms and soles that later peel.

title: Kawasaki disease – Diagnosis
content: The diagnosis of Kawasaki disease is clinical, as there is no specific diagnostic test.

title: Kawasaki disease – Management
content: Management of Kawasaki disease includes high-dose aspirin and intravenous immunoglobulin. An echocardiogram is used as the initial screening test for coronary artery aneurysms.

title: Kawasaki disease – Complications
content: The main complication of Kawasaki disease is the development of coronary artery aneurysms.

title: Meningitis – Causative Organisms (Neonatal to 3 months)
content: In neonates up to 3 months old, the common causative organisms for meningitis are Group B Streptococcus (usually acquired from the mother), E. coli and other Gram-negative organisms, and Listeria monocytogenes.

title: Meningitis – Causative Organisms (1 month to 6 years)
content: In children aged 1 month to 6 years, the common causative organisms for meningitis are Neisseria meningitidis (meningococcus), Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus), and Haemophilus influenzae.

title: Meningitis – Causative Organisms (>6 years)
content: In children older than 6 years, the common causative organisms for meningitis are Neisseria meningitidis (meningococcus) and Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus).

title: Meningitis – Contraindications to Lumbar Puncture
content: Contraindications to performing a lumbar puncture in a child with suspected meningitis include signs of raised intracranial pressure such as focal neurological signs, papilloedema, significant bulging of the fontanelle, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), and signs of cerebral herniation.

title: Meningitis – Management (<3 months)
content: The antibiotic management for meningitis in children under 3 months of age is intravenous amoxicillin plus intravenous cefotaxime.

title: Meningitis – Management (>3 months)
content: The antibiotic management for meningitis in children over 3 months of age is intravenous cefotaxime.

title: Acute kidney injury – Definition
content: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is characterized by a reversible increase in the blood concentration of creatinine and nitrogenous waste products and by the inability of the kidney to regulate fluid and electrolyte homeostasis appropriately.

title: Acute kidney injury – Aetiology
content: The etiology of AKI in children has shifted from primary renal disease to multifactorial causes, including pre-renal injury (decreased intravascular volume), intrinsic renal disease (e.g., acute tubular necrosis, glomerulonephritis, vascular lesions), and obstructive uropathy.

title: Acute kidney injury – Pathophysiology of Hypoxic/Ischemic Injury
content: The pathophysiology of hypoxia/ischemia-induced AKI is complex and involves cellular, biochemical, and molecular events that are not yet fully understood.

title: Acute kidney injury – Diagnosis
content: The diagnosis of AKI is established through history, physical examination, and laboratory studies, including urinalysis and radiographic studies. The serum creatinine level is an insensitive and delayed measure of decreased kidney function.

title: Acute kidney injury – Management
content: Many interventions, such as ‘renal-dose dopamine’ and diuretic therapy, have not been shown to alter the course of AKI. Management is largely supportive and focused on the underlying cause.

title: Acute kidney injury – Prognosis and Long-Term Risks
content: The prognosis of AKI is highly dependent on the underlying etiology. Children who have had AKI are at risk for the late development of chronic kidney disease several years after the initial insult.

title: Muscular dystrophies – Definition
content: Muscular dystrophy (MD) is a group of more than 30 genetic diseases that cause progressive weakness and degeneration of skeletal muscles. All forms of MD worsen over time as muscles progressively degenerate and weaken.

title: Muscular dystrophies – Pathophysiology
content: In muscular dystrophy, defects in the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex in the muscle fiber membrane lead to muscle fiber damage, leakage of creatine kinase, and excess calcium entry, ultimately causing muscle fiber death and progressive degeneration.

title: Muscular dystrophies – Inheritance Patterns
content: Muscular dystrophies can be inherited in three ways: autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, and X-linked recessive.

title: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD) – Clinical Features
content: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), the most common childhood form, primarily affects boys and becomes apparent in the toddler years. It presents with progressive weakness and muscle wasting, a waddling gait, frequent falls, and difficulty rising from a sitting position.

title: Becker Muscular Dystrophy – Clinical Features
content: Becker muscular dystrophy is less severe than DMD and usually appears around age 11. It is characterized by muscle weakness in the upper arms, shoulders, upper legs, and pelvis, with toe-walking and frequent falls as early symptoms.

title: Congenital Muscular Dystrophy – Clinical Features
content: Congenital muscular dystrophy is present at birth or evident before age 2. Most children with this type are unable to sit or stand without support, and some may never learn to walk. It can also cause contractures, scoliosis, and breathing difficulties.

title: Non-accidental injury – Definition
content: Non-accidental injury (NAI) or physical abuse is any bodily injury that is deliberately inflicted on a vulnerable person. It can include hitting, kicking, burning, biting, or choking.

title: Non-accidental injury – Suspicious History
content: Suspicion of non-accidental injury should be raised by factors such as a delay in seeking medical attention, an implausible or changing history of the injury, a lack of concern from the caregiver, or abnormal behaviour from the child.

title: Non-accidental injury – Bruising Patterns
content: In non-accidental injury, bruises are often multiple, in different stages of healing, and located on soft tissues like the thighs, abdomen, buttocks, and cheeks. They may also have a pattern indicative of the object used, such as a handprint or belt buckle.

title: Non-accidental injury – Burn Patterns
content: Cigarette burns often appear as rounded ulcers or erosions. Immersion burns from scalding water have a sharp demarcation in a 'glove and stocking' distribution. Branding injuries may represent the shape of the heated object used.

title: Non-accidental injury – Bite Marks
content: Human bites tend to cause a crush injury. If the distance between the canine marks is greater than 3 cm, the perpetrator is likely an adult. Animal bites have narrower puncture marks and different spacing.

title: Non-accidental injury – Signs of Neglect
content: Physical neglect can present with poor hygiene, malnutrition, and untreated illnesses such as dermatitis, scabies, or head lice. A lack of immunizations may also be a sign.

title: Obesity in children – Definition and Assessment
content: Defining obesity in children is complex as BMI varies with age. UK 1990 BMI percentile charts are used for accurate assessment. A BMI at or above the 91st centile suggests a need for tailored clinical intervention.

title: Obesity in children – Comorbidity Assessment
content: NICE recommends considering an assessment for comorbidities in children with a BMI at or above the 98th centile.

title: Obesity in children – Causes and Associations
content: The most common cause of childhood obesity is lifestyle factors. Other associations include being of Asian ethnicity, female, and taller than average. Medical causes include growth hormone deficiency, hypothyroidism, Down's syndrome, and Cushing's syndrome.

title: Pneumothorax – Definition
content: Pneumothorax is the accumulation of air in the pleural space, the area between the lungs and the chest wall. It can occur spontaneously or be associated with trauma or pre-existing pulmonary conditions.

title: Pneumothorax – Clinical Features
content: The symptoms of a pneumothorax develop suddenly and include sharp chest pain and shortness of breath. On examination, there may be decreased breath sounds on the affected side.

title: Tension Pneumothorax – Clinical Features
content: A tension pneumothorax is a life-threatening emergency that presents with more severe symptoms and respiratory distress than a simple pneumothorax. Prompt diagnosis and intervention are crucial.

title: Pneumothorax – Diagnosis
content: A pneumothorax is confirmed with an upright inspiratory chest radiograph. A CT scan may be recommended for unusual cases or to evaluate for recurrence.

title: Pneumothorax – Management
content: Many spontaneous pneumothoraces resolve with conservative therapy, such as the administration of high-concentration oxygen. Large, complicated, or tension pneumothoraces require decompression and chest tube placement.

title: Septic arthritis in children – Epidemiology
content: Septic arthritis has an incidence of around 4-5 per 100,000 children and is more common in boys (M:F ratio = 2:1). The most commonly affected joints are the hip, knee, and ankle.

title: Septic arthritis in children – Clinical Features
content: Septic arthritis in children presents with joint pain, limp, fever, and systemic signs of illness such as lethargy. The affected joint is typically swollen and red, with minimal movement possible.

title: Tuberculosis in children – Definition
content: Tuberculosis (TB) is a chronic bacterial infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It usually affects the lungs but can also affect other parts of the body like the brain, kidneys, or spine.

title: Tuberculosis in children – Latent vs. Active Disease
content: Children can have latent TB infection, where they have TB germs but are not sick and cannot spread them, or active TB disease, where the germs are multiplying, causing illness, and can be spread to others.

title: Tuberculosis in children – Clinical Features
content: Symptoms of active TB disease in children include cough, weakness, lethargy, weight loss or failure to thrive, fever, and night sweats. TB meningitis can cause sleepiness, headache, irritability, and seizures.

title: Tuberculosis in children – Risk Factors
content: Children are at higher risk for TB if they live with adults with TB risk factors, were born in or travel to high-prevalence countries, live in congregate settings, have been exposed to someone with active TB, or have a weakened immune system.

title: Tuberculosis in children – Diagnosis
content: Diagnosis of TB in children involves a medical history, physical exam, TB test (skin or blood), chest x-ray, and laboratory tests on sputum or other samples. Diagnosis can be challenging as it is often difficult to collect sputum from children.

title: Tuberculosis in children – Treatment
content: Treatment is recommended for children with latent TB to prevent active disease. Active TB disease requires a multi-drug regimen for 4, 6, or more months. Directly Observed Therapy (DOT) is the best way to ensure adherence.

title: Anaemia – Definition
content: Anaemia in paediatrics is defined as a haemoglobin concentration below the age-specific lower limit: for children aged 6 months to 5 years, Hb < 110 g/L; for 5 to 12 years, Hb < 115 g/L; and for 12 to 15 years, Hb < 120 g/L.

title: Anaemia – Epidemiology
content: Anaemia affects approximately 25% of children worldwide, with higher prevalence in low-income settings; in the UK, iron deficiency anaemia is the most common cause in paediatric populations.

title: Anaemia – Aetiology/Risk factors: Iron deficiency
content: Iron deficiency is the leading cause of anaemia in UK children, commonly due to inadequate dietary intake, increased requirements during growth, or chronic blood loss; risk factors include prematurity, exclusive breastfeeding beyond 6 months without supplementation, and poor weaning practices.

title: Anaemia – Aetiology/Risk factors: Haemolytic anaemia
content: Haemolytic anaemia in children can be caused by hereditary conditions such as sickle cell disease or thalassaemia, or acquired causes like autoimmune haemolytic anaemia; these conditions lead to premature red blood cell destruction.

title: Anaemia – Pathophysiology
content: Anaemia results from decreased red blood cell production, increased destruction, or blood loss, leading to reduced oxygen-carrying capacity and tissue hypoxia; compensatory mechanisms include increased cardiac output and erythropoietin production.

title: Anaemia – Clinical features: Pallor
content: Pallor, especially of the conjunctivae, palms, and nail beds, is a common clinical feature of anaemia in children and may be the earliest visible sign.

title: Anaemia – Clinical features: Breathlessness
content: Children with moderate to severe anaemia may present with breathlessness on exertion due to reduced oxygen delivery to tissues.

title: Anaemia – Clinical features: Fatigue and irritability
content: Fatigue and irritability are common non-specific symptoms in paediatric anaemia due to decreased oxygen delivery and resultant tissue hypoxia.

title: Anaemia – Investigations: Full blood count
content: Full blood count (FBC) is essential for diagnosis, showing low haemoglobin, haematocrit, and red cell indices; microcytic hypochromic anaemia suggests iron deficiency, while macrocytic anaemia suggests B12 or folate deficiency.

title: Anaemia – Investigations: Iron studies
content: Serum ferritin is the most specific test for iron deficiency anaemia; ferritin < 12 µg/L in children indicates depleted iron stores; serum iron, total iron-binding capacity, and transferrin saturation assist in diagnosis.

title: Anaemia – Management: Iron supplementation
content: First-line treatment for iron deficiency anaemia in children is oral ferrous sulphate at 3 mg/kg elemental iron twice daily for at least 3 months; vitamin C enhances absorption and should be given with iron supplements.

title: Anaemia – Management: Blood transfusion
content: Blood transfusion is indicated in paediatric anaemia when haemoglobin is < 70 g/L with symptoms or < 50 g/L regardless of symptoms; transfuse 10-15 mL/kg of packed red cells slowly with monitoring for transfusion reactions.

title: Anaemia – Complications
content: Severe or chronic anaemia in children can lead to cardiac complications such as left ventricular hypertrophy and heart failure, developmental delay, and increased susceptibility to infections.

title: Anaemia – Prognosis
content: With timely diagnosis and appropriate management, prognosis of paediatric anaemia is excellent; iron deficiency anaemia typically resolves with supplementation, though untreated cases may cause long-term developmental impairment.

title: Anaphylaxis – Definition
content: Anaphylaxis is a severe, potentially life-threatening systemic hypersensitivity reaction characterised by rapid onset and involving multiple organ systems, typically mediated by IgE antibodies.

title: Anaphylaxis – Epidemiology
content: In the UK, the incidence of anaphylaxis in children is approximately 1-3 per 10,000 per year, with food allergies being the most common trigger in paediatric populations.

title: Anaphylaxis – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Common triggers of paediatric anaphylaxis in the UK include foods (peanuts, tree nuts, milk, eggs), insect stings, medications (e.g. penicillin), and latex; risk factors include previous anaphylaxis, asthma, and atopy.

title: Anaphylaxis – Pathophysiology
content: Anaphylaxis results from IgE-mediated mast cell and basophil degranulation releasing histamine, tryptase, leukotrienes, and prostaglandins causing vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, bronchospasm, and mucous secretion.

title: Anaphylaxis – Clinical features: Skin and mucosal signs
content: In paediatric anaphylaxis, skin signs such as urticaria, flushing, and angioedema occur in over 80% of cases and are often the earliest manifestations.

title: Anaphylaxis – Clinical features: Respiratory symptoms
content: Respiratory involvement in paediatric anaphylaxis includes stridor, wheeze, cough, and breathlessness, occurring in approximately 70% of cases and may rapidly progress to airway obstruction.

title: Anaphylaxis – Clinical features: Cardiovascular symptoms
content: Cardiovascular signs in paediatric anaphylaxis include hypotension, tachycardia, dizziness, and shock; hypotension is defined as systolic BP <70 + (2 × age in years) mmHg in children.

title: Anaphylaxis – Clinical features: Gastrointestinal symptoms
content: Gastrointestinal manifestations in paediatric anaphylaxis include abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhoea, present in up to 45% of cases.

title: Anaphylaxis – Investigations
content: Serum tryptase measurement within 1-3 hours of symptom onset can support diagnosis but is not required for acute management; baseline tryptase may be elevated in mastocytosis.

title: Anaphylaxis – Management: First-line treatment
content: Intramuscular adrenaline (epinephrine) is the first-line treatment for paediatric anaphylaxis; dose is 0.01 mg/kg (max 0.5 mg) administered into the mid-anterolateral thigh, repeat every 5-15 minutes as needed.

title: Anaphylaxis – Management: Adjunctive treatments
content: Adjunctive treatments include high-flow oxygen, intravenous fluids (20 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid bolus), antihistamines (chlorphenamine 0.1 mg/kg IV max 10 mg), and corticosteroids (hydrocortisone 4 mg/kg IV max 100 mg), although steroids have no immediate effect.

title: Anaphylaxis – Management: Observation and referral
content: Children treated for anaphylaxis should be observed for at least 4-6 hours due to risk of biphasic reactions; referral to allergy services for assessment and provision of adrenaline auto-injectors is essential.

title: Anaphylaxis – Complications
content: Complications of paediatric anaphylaxis include biphasic reactions occurring in up to 20% of cases, airway obstruction, hypoxic brain injury, and rarely death if untreated.

title: Anaphylaxis – Prognosis
content: With prompt recognition and treatment, paediatric anaphylaxis has an excellent prognosis; however, risk of recurrence exists, necessitating education and avoidance strategies.

title: Appendicitis – Definition
content: Appendicitis is inflammation of the vermiform appendix, typically caused by obstruction of the appendiceal lumen leading to bacterial infection and inflammation.

title: Appendicitis – Epidemiology
content: Appendicitis is the most common surgical emergency in children, with peak incidence between 10 and 19 years of age. It affects approximately 70,000 children annually in the UK.

title: Appendicitis – Aetiology and Risk Factors
content: Common causes include luminal obstruction by faecoliths, lymphoid hyperplasia (especially post-viral), foreign bodies, or rarely tumours. Risk factors include male sex, age 10-19 years, and family history.

title: Appendicitis – Pathophysiology
content: Obstruction of the appendiceal lumen leads to increased intraluminal pressure, venous congestion, bacterial overgrowth, ischemia, and eventual inflammation and necrosis of the appendix wall.

title: Appendicitis – Clinical features: Abdominal pain
content: Initial periumbilical pain that later localises to the right lower quadrant (McBurney’s point) is characteristic in paediatric appendicitis.

title: Appendicitis – Clinical features: Fever
content: Low-grade fever (37.5-38.5°C) is common in paediatric appendicitis, with higher temperatures suggesting perforation or abscess formation.

title: Appendicitis – Clinical features: Nausea and vomiting
content: Nausea and vomiting typically follow the onset of abdominal pain in paediatric appendicitis and are present in approximately 80% of cases.

title: Appendicitis – Clinical features: Tenderness and signs
content: Tenderness at McBurney’s point, rebound tenderness, guarding, and Rovsing’s sign are common physical examination findings in paediatric appendicitis.

title: Appendicitis – Investigations: Blood tests
content: Blood tests often show leukocytosis with neutrophilia (white cell count >12 x10^9/L) and elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) in paediatric appendicitis.

title: Appendicitis – Investigations: Imaging
content: Ultrasound is the first-line imaging modality in paediatric appendicitis, showing a non-compressible, enlarged appendix >6 mm diameter. CT scan is reserved for equivocal cases.

title: Appendicitis – Differential diagnosis
content: Differential diagnoses in children include mesenteric adenitis, gastroenteritis, Meckel’s diverticulitis, intussusception, urinary tract infection, and ovarian torsion in females.

title: Appendicitis – Management: Initial treatment
content: Initial management includes nil by mouth, intravenous fluids, analgesia with paracetamol and/or ibuprofen, and intravenous antibiotics such as co-amoxiclav 30 mg/kg every 8 hours.

title: Appendicitis – Management: Surgical treatment
content: Definitive treatment is appendicectomy, preferably laparoscopic, performed urgently to prevent perforation and complications.

title: Appendicitis – Complications
content: Complications include perforation, peritonitis, abscess formation, sepsis, and bowel obstruction. Perforation risk is higher in children under 5 years.

title: Appendicitis – Prognosis
content: With prompt diagnosis and treatment, prognosis is excellent; mortality is rare in the UK. Delayed treatment increases risk of complications and longer hospital stay.

title: Atopic dermatitis and eczema – Definition
content: Atopic dermatitis and eczema is a chronic, relapsing inflammatory skin condition characterised by dry, itchy, and inflamed skin, commonly affecting children and often associated with other atopic diseases such as asthma and allergic rhinitis.

title: Atopic dermatitis and eczema – Epidemiology
content: Atopic dermatitis affects approximately 15-20% of children in the UK, with onset commonly before 5 years of age; prevalence has increased over recent decades.

title: Atopic dermatitis and eczema – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Risk factors include family history of atopy, filaggrin gene mutations, environmental triggers such as allergens and irritants, and impaired skin barrier function.

title: Atopic dermatitis and eczema – Pathophysiology
content: Atopic dermatitis involves a defective skin barrier with reduced ceramide levels and filaggrin deficiency, leading to increased transepidermal water loss and enhanced allergen penetration, triggering a Th2-mediated immune response.

title: Atopic dermatitis and eczema – Clinical features: Acute rash
content: Acute flares present with intensely pruritic, erythematous, weeping, and crusted plaques commonly on the face, scalp, and extensor surfaces in infants, and flexural areas in older children.

title: Atopic dermatitis and eczema – Clinical features: Chronic rash
content: Chronic eczema is characterised by lichenification, scaling, and thickened skin due to repeated scratching, often affecting flexural areas such as the antecubital and popliteal fossae.

title: Atopic dermatitis and eczema – Investigations
content: Diagnosis is clinical; skin swabs may be taken if secondary bacterial infection is suspected, commonly Staphylococcus aureus. Patch testing may be used in chronic or refractory cases to identify contact allergens.

title: Atopic dermatitis and eczema – Management
content: Management includes regular use of emollients (e.g., aqueous cream or emulsifying ointment applied liberally at least twice daily), topical corticosteroids (e.g., hydrocortisone 1% cream for mild flares, potent steroids like betamethasone valerate 0.1% for severe flares) applied once or twice daily for 1-2 weeks, and avoidance of triggers. Antihistamines may be used for severe pruritus. Infected eczema requires topical or oral antibiotics (e.g., flucloxacillin 25-50 mg/kg/day divided into 3-4 doses for 7 days).

title: Atopic dermatitis and eczema – Complications
content: Complications include secondary bacterial infection (commonly Staphylococcus aureus), eczema herpeticum caused by herpes simplex virus, and chronic skin changes such as lichenification and pigmentary changes.

title: Atopic dermatitis and eczema – Prognosis
content: Most children experience improvement or resolution by late childhood or adolescence; however, some may have persistent or relapsing disease into adulthood.

title: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder – Definition
content: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by a persistent pattern of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity that interferes with functioning or development, typically diagnosed in childhood.

title: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder – Epidemiology
content: ADHD affects approximately 5% of children in the UK, with a higher prevalence in boys (male to female ratio of about 3:1). Symptoms typically present before the age of 12 years.

title: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder – Aetiology and risk factors
content: ADHD is multifactorial with genetic factors accounting for up to 75% of risk. Environmental risk factors include prenatal exposure to tobacco smoke, alcohol, low birth weight, and psychosocial adversity.

title: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder – Pathophysiology
content: ADHD is associated with dysregulation of dopaminergic and noradrenergic neurotransmission in the prefrontal cortex, leading to impaired attention, executive function, and behavioural control.

title: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder – Clinical features: Inattention
content: Children with ADHD often show inattention characterised by difficulty sustaining focus, careless mistakes, poor organisational skills, and forgetfulness in daily activities.

title: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder – Clinical features: Hyperactivity and impulsivity
content: Hyperactivity presents as excessive fidgeting, inability to remain seated, running or climbing in inappropriate situations, and impulsivity includes interrupting others, difficulty waiting turn, and acting without thinking.

title: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder – Investigations
content: Diagnosis of ADHD is clinical based on DSM-5 or ICD-10 criteria; no specific laboratory or imaging tests are required. Assessment includes detailed history, behaviour rating scales (e.g., Conners’), and exclusion of other causes.

title: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder – Management: Pharmacological treatment
content: First-line pharmacological treatment in the UK for children over 5 years with moderate to severe ADHD is methylphenidate, starting at 5 mg once or twice daily, titrated up to a maximum of 60 mg daily. Alternatives include lisdexamfetamine and atomoxetine.

title: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder – Management: Non-pharmacological treatment
content: Non-pharmacological management includes behavioural therapy, parent training programmes, educational support, and school-based interventions to improve attention and reduce disruptive behaviour.

title: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder – Complications
content: Complications of untreated ADHD include poor academic performance, low self-esteem, increased risk of substance misuse, conduct disorders, and higher rates of accidental injury.

title: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder – Prognosis
content: ADHD symptoms persist into adulthood in approximately 60% of cases. Early diagnosis and treatment improve long-term outcomes including academic achievement and social functioning.

title: Autism spectrum disorder – Definition
content: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition characterised by persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction across multiple contexts, alongside restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests, or activities.

title: Autism spectrum disorder – Epidemiology
content: The prevalence of autism spectrum disorder in the UK is approximately 1 in 100 children, with a male to female ratio of around 4:1. Diagnosis typically occurs in early childhood, often by age 3 years.

title: Autism spectrum disorder – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: ASD has a multifactorial aetiology including genetic factors such as mutations in genes like SHANK3 and environmental risk factors including advanced parental age, prenatal exposure to valproate, and low birth weight.

title: Autism spectrum disorder – Pathophysiology
content: ASD is associated with atypical brain development including altered synaptic connectivity and neurotransmitter imbalances, particularly involving glutamate and GABA pathways, leading to impaired social cognition and repetitive behaviours.

title: Autism spectrum disorder – Clinical features: Social communication deficits
content: Children with ASD often present with impaired social interaction including poor eye contact, difficulty understanding social cues, lack of shared enjoyment, and delayed or absent speech development.

title: Autism spectrum disorder – Clinical features: Restricted and repetitive behaviours
content: ASD is characterised by repetitive motor movements, insistence on sameness, inflexible adherence to routines, and highly restricted, fixated interests that are abnormal in intensity or focus.

title: Autism spectrum disorder – Clinical features: Associated conditions
content: Common comorbidities in ASD include intellectual disability (present in approximately 30-50% of cases), epilepsy (20-30%), attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and anxiety disorders.

title: Autism spectrum disorder – Investigations
content: Diagnosis of ASD is clinical based on DSM-5 or ICD-11 criteria; investigations include developmental assessments, Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS), and Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised (ADI-R). Genetic testing and metabolic screening may be considered in selected cases.

title: Autism spectrum disorder – Management
content: Management of ASD involves early intensive behavioural interventions such as Applied Behaviour Analysis (ABA), speech and language therapy, occupational therapy, and educational support. Pharmacological treatment with risperidone or aripiprazole may be used for irritability or behavioural problems at doses of 0.5-3 mg/day and 2-15 mg/day respectively.

title: Autism spectrum disorder – Complications
content: Complications of ASD include social isolation, increased risk of anxiety and depression, self-injurious behaviours, and increased risk of premature mortality due to accidents or comorbid epilepsy.

title: Autism spectrum disorder – Prognosis
content: Prognosis varies widely; early diagnosis and intervention improve outcomes. Many individuals achieve varying degrees of independence, though some require lifelong support. Intellectual disability and comorbidities worsen prognosis.

title: Bronchiectasis – Definition
content: Bronchiectasis is a chronic paediatric respiratory condition characterised by permanent dilatation and destruction of the bronchial walls, leading to impaired mucociliary clearance and recurrent respiratory infections.

title: Bronchiectasis – Epidemiology
content: Bronchiectasis is an uncommon but important cause of chronic respiratory morbidity in UK paediatric populations, with higher prevalence in children with underlying conditions such as cystic fibrosis or immunodeficiency.

title: Bronchiectasis – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Common aetiological factors for paediatric bronchiectasis in the UK include post-infectious causes (e.g. severe or recurrent pneumonia), cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia, immunodeficiency, and aspiration syndromes.

title: Bronchiectasis – Pathophysiology
content: Bronchiectasis results from a cycle of airway inflammation, infection, and impaired mucociliary clearance causing permanent bronchial wall damage and dilation, which predisposes to further infection and inflammation.

title: Bronchiectasis – Clinical features: Chronic productive cough
content: The most common presentation of paediatric bronchiectasis is a chronic productive cough lasting more than 8 weeks, often with purulent sputum.

title: Bronchiectasis – Clinical features: Recurrent chest infections
content: Children with bronchiectasis frequently experience recurrent chest infections characterised by increased cough, sputum production, fever, and malaise.

title: Bronchiectasis – Clinical features: Digital clubbing
content: Digital clubbing is a common physical sign in children with bronchiectasis, indicating chronic hypoxia and lung disease.

title: Bronchiectasis – Investigations: Chest X-ray
content: Chest X-ray in bronchiectasis may show tram-track lines, ring shadows, and areas of lung hyperinflation but has limited sensitivity compared to CT.

title: Bronchiectasis – Investigations: High-resolution CT chest
content: High-resolution CT (HRCT) chest is the gold standard investigation for bronchiectasis, showing bronchial wall thickening, bronchial dilation (signet ring sign), and lack of bronchial tapering.

title: Bronchiectasis – Investigations: Microbiological sputum analysis
content: Sputum culture in bronchiectasis often grows pathogens such as Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Moraxella catarrhalis, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, guiding antibiotic therapy.

title: Bronchiectasis – Management: Airway clearance physiotherapy
content: Regular airway clearance physiotherapy is essential in managing paediatric bronchiectasis to improve mucus clearance and reduce infection risk; techniques include active cycle of breathing and postural drainage.

title: Bronchiectasis – Management: Antibiotic therapy
content: Acute exacerbations of bronchiectasis are treated with targeted antibiotics based on sputum culture; common choices include amoxicillin 25-50 mg/kg/day orally in three divided doses or co-amoxiclav 25-45 mg/kg/day, with intravenous therapy for severe cases.

title: Bronchiectasis – Management: Immunisations
content: Children with bronchiectasis should receive routine UK immunisations including annual influenza vaccine and pneumococcal conjugate vaccine to reduce respiratory infection risk.

title: Bronchiectasis – Complications
content: Potential complications of paediatric bronchiectasis include recurrent respiratory infections, haemoptysis, respiratory failure, and cor pulmonale due to chronic hypoxia.

title: Bronchiectasis – Prognosis
content: With early diagnosis and appropriate management including airway clearance and infection control, many children with bronchiectasis can maintain good lung function and quality of life; however, untreated disease may progress to irreversible lung damage.

title: Candidiasis – Definition
content: Candidiasis is a fungal infection caused by Candida species, most commonly Candida albicans, affecting mucosal surfaces, skin, and occasionally systemic sites in paediatric patients.

title: Candidiasis – Epidemiology
content: Candidiasis is a common fungal infection in paediatric populations, particularly in neonates and immunocompromised children; Candida albicans accounts for over 70% of cases in the UK.

title: Candidiasis – Aetiology and Risk Factors
content: Risk factors for paediatric candidiasis include prematurity, broad-spectrum antibiotic use, immunosuppression, indwelling catheters, and prolonged hospitalisation.

title: Candidiasis – Pathophysiology
content: Candida species colonise mucosal surfaces and can invade epithelial tissues when host immunity is compromised, leading to superficial or systemic infection in children.

title: Candidiasis – Clinical features: Oral thrush
content: Oral thrush presents with white, curd-like plaques on the buccal mucosa, tongue, and palate in infants, which can be wiped off to reveal erythematous mucosa; associated with difficulty with breast feeding.

title: Candidiasis – Clinical features: Diaper dermatitis
content: Candidal diaper dermatitis presents as a bright red rash with satellite pustules and papules in the diaper area, typically in infants with prolonged exposure to moisture.

title: Candidiasis – Clinical features: Oesophageal candidiasis
content: Oesophageal candidiasis in children presents with odynophagia, dysphagia, and retrosternal pain, often in immunocompromised patients.

title: Candidiasis – Investigations
content: Diagnosis of candidiasis is confirmed by microscopic examination and culture of samples from affected sites; blood cultures are required for suspected systemic infection.

title: Candidiasis – Management: Oral thrush
content: Oral thrush in paediatric patients is treated with topical antifungals such as nystatin oral suspension 100,000 units/mL, 1 mL four times daily for 7–14 days.

title: Candidiasis – Management: Systemic infection
content: Systemic candidiasis in children requires intravenous antifungal therapy with agents such as liposomal amphotericin B 3–5 mg/kg/day or intravenous fluconazole 6–12 mg/kg/day, adjusted according to clinical response.

title: Candidiasis – Complications
content: Complications of paediatric candidiasis include systemic dissemination causing candidemia, endocarditis, meningitis, and chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis in immunodeficient children.

title: Candidiasis – Prognosis
content: The prognosis of paediatric candidiasis is generally good with prompt antifungal treatment; however, systemic infection in immunocompromised children carries a higher risk of morbidity and mortality.

title: Cardiac arrest – Definition
content: Cardiac arrest in paediatrics is defined as the sudden cessation of effective cardiac mechanical activity, resulting in the absence of a palpable central pulse, unresponsiveness, and apnea or agonal breathing.

title: Cardiac arrest – Epidemiology
content: Paediatric cardiac arrest has an incidence of approximately 8 per 100,000 children per year in the UK, with higher rates in infants under 1 year. Survival to hospital discharge is around 10-20%, varying by cause and setting.

title: Cardiac arrest – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Common causes of paediatric cardiac arrest include respiratory failure, shock, congenital heart disease, arrhythmias, trauma, sepsis, and drowning. Risk factors include prematurity, chronic illness, and sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS).

title: Cardiac arrest – Pathophysiology
content: Paediatric cardiac arrest typically results from hypoxia-induced bradycardia progressing to asystole or pulseless electrical activity, unlike adults where ventricular fibrillation is more common.

title: Cardiac arrest – Clinical features: Decreased/loss of consciousness
content: Paediatric cardiac arrest presents with sudden loss of consciousness and unresponsiveness, with absence of normal breathing or presence of agonal gasping.

title: Cardiac arrest – Clinical features: Shock
content: Signs of shock such as pallor, cool extremities, weak pulses, and delayed capillary refill may precede or accompany paediatric cardiac arrest.

title: Cardiac arrest – Investigations
content: Initial investigations include ECG monitoring to identify rhythm, pulse oximetry, capnography with end-tidal CO2 monitoring during resuscitation, blood gases, glucose, electrolytes, and chest X-ray post-resuscitation.

title: Cardiac arrest – Management
content: Management follows the UK Resuscitation Council paediatric advanced life support guidelines: immediate recognition, call for help, high-quality chest compressions at 100-120/min with depth of one-third chest diameter, 15:2 compression-to-ventilation ratio for two rescuers, airway management, ventilation with 100% oxygen, and administration of adrenaline 10 mcg/kg IV/IO every 3-5 minutes during resuscitation.

title: Cardiac arrest – Complications
content: Potential complications include hypoxic brain injury, multi-organ failure, rib fractures from chest compressions, and post-resuscitation myocardial dysfunction.

title: Cardiac arrest – Prognosis
content: Prognosis depends on cause, duration of arrest, and quality of resuscitation; survival to hospital discharge is approximately 10-20% with many survivors suffering neurological impairment.

title: Cellulitis – Definition
content: Cellulitis is a common bacterial skin infection characterised by inflammation of the dermis and subcutaneous tissues, typically caused by Streptococcus pyogenes or Staphylococcus aureus.

title: Cellulitis – Epidemiology
content: Cellulitis is a common paediatric infection, with an incidence of approximately 1.5 to 4 cases per 1000 children annually in the UK, more frequent in children under 5 years old.

title: Cellulitis – Aetiology and Risk Factors
content: Cellulitis in children is most commonly caused by Group A Streptococcus and Staphylococcus aureus; risk factors include skin barrier disruption (e.g., eczema, insect bites, trauma), immunodeficiency, and lymphatic obstruction.

title: Cellulitis – Pathophysiology
content: Cellulitis results from bacterial invasion of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, leading to localised inflammation, oedema, erythema, and pain due to host immune response and bacterial toxins.

title: Cellulitis – Clinical Features: Local Signs
content: Typical local signs of cellulitis include erythema, warmth, swelling, tenderness, and poorly demarcated borders; affected skin may be shiny and stretched.

title: Cellulitis – Clinical Features: Systemic Signs
content: Systemic features may include fever, malaise, and regional lymphadenopathy; in severe cases, children may appear unwell with tachycardia and hypotension.

title: Cellulitis – Investigations
content: Diagnosis of cellulitis is primarily clinical; blood tests such as full blood count and C-reactive protein may show raised inflammatory markers; blood cultures are reserved for severe or systemic cases.

title: Cellulitis – Differential Diagnosis
content: Differential diagnoses include erysipelas, abscess, necrotising fasciitis, insect bite reactions, and deep vein thrombosis; necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency and must be excluded.

title: Cellulitis – Management: Antibiotic Therapy
content: First-line treatment for uncomplicated paediatric cellulitis in the UK is oral flucloxacillin 25-50 mg/kg/day divided into 4 doses (max 2 g/day) for 5 days; for penicillin allergy, clarithromycin 7.5 mg/kg/dose twice daily is used.

title: Cellulitis – Management: Supportive Care
content: Supportive care includes elevation of the affected limb to reduce swelling, analgesia with paracetamol or ibuprofen, and ensuring adequate hydration and nutrition.

title: Cellulitis – Complications
content: Potential complications include abscess formation, lymphangitis, sepsis, necrotising fasciitis, and chronic lymphoedema; early recognition and treatment reduce risk.

title: Cellulitis – Prognosis
content: With prompt antibiotic treatment, the prognosis of paediatric cellulitis is excellent, with most children recovering fully within 7 to 10 days without sequelae.

title: Cerebral palsy and hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy – Definition
content: Cerebral palsy (CP) is a group of permanent disorders of the development of movement and posture, causing activity limitation, attributed to non-progressive disturbances in the developing fetal or infant brain. Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy (HIE) is brain dysfunction caused by a reduction in oxygen (hypoxia) and blood flow (ischaemia) to the brain around the time of birth.

title: Cerebral palsy and hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy – Epidemiology
content: Cerebral palsy affects approximately 2 per 1000 live births in the UK. Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy occurs in 1 to 3 per 1000 live births and is a leading cause of neonatal encephalopathy and subsequent cerebral palsy.

title: Cerebral palsy and hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Risk factors for HIE include perinatal asphyxia, placental abruption, umbilical cord prolapse, maternal hypotension, and prolonged labour. Prematurity and low birth weight increase risk of cerebral palsy.

title: Cerebral palsy and hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy – Pathophysiology
content: HIE results from impaired cerebral blood flow and oxygen delivery leading to energy failure, excitotoxicity, oxidative stress, and neuronal death. This brain injury during the perinatal period causes the motor and cognitive impairments seen in cerebral palsy.

title: Cerebral palsy and hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy – Clinical features: Neonatal seizures
content: Neonatal seizures are a common presentation of HIE, occurring within the first 24 to 48 hours of life. Seizures may be subtle (e.g., lip smacking, eye deviation) or tonic-clonic.

title: Cerebral palsy and hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy – Clinical features: Abnormal muscle tone
content: Children with cerebral palsy typically present with abnormal muscle tone, which may be spasticity (increased tone), dystonia, or hypotonia, often evident in the first year of life.

title: Cerebral palsy and hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy – Clinical features: Developmental delay
content: Developmental delay, including delayed motor milestones and speech and language problems, is common in children with cerebral palsy secondary to HIE.

title: Cerebral palsy and hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy – Investigations: Neuroimaging
content: MRI brain is the investigation of choice for assessing HIE and cerebral palsy, typically performed between days 4 and 14 of life. It shows patterns of injury such as watershed infarcts or basal ganglia/thalamic lesions.

title: Cerebral palsy and hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy – Management: Therapeutic hypothermia
content: Therapeutic hypothermia (cooling to 33.5°C for 72 hours) initiated within 6 hours of birth reduces death and disability in term infants with moderate to severe HIE and is standard care in UK neonatal units.

title: Cerebral palsy and hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy – Management: Supportive care
content: Supportive care includes maintaining adequate ventilation and oxygenation, managing seizures with phenobarbital (loading dose 20 mg/kg IV, maintenance 3-5 mg/kg/day), and ensuring normoglycaemia and normothermia.

title: Cerebral palsy and hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy – Complications
content: Complications of HIE and cerebral palsy include epilepsy, intellectual disability, feeding difficulties, musculoskeletal deformities such as hip dislocation and scoliosis, and respiratory problems.

title: Cerebral palsy and hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy – Prognosis
content: Prognosis depends on severity of initial brain injury; mild HIE may have normal outcomes, while severe HIE has high mortality and risk of severe cerebral palsy and neurodevelopmental impairment. Early therapeutic hypothermia improves outcomes.

title: Coeliac disease – Definition
content: Coeliac disease is an immune-mediated systemic disorder elicited by gluten and related prolamines in genetically susceptible individuals, characterised by a variable combination of gluten-dependent clinical manifestations, specific antibodies, HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8 haplotypes, and enteropathy.

title: Coeliac disease – Epidemiology
content: Coeliac disease affects approximately 1% of the paediatric population in the UK, with a higher prevalence in females and individuals with a first-degree relative affected by the condition.

title: Coeliac disease – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Risk factors for coeliac disease include carrying HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8 haplotypes, having a first-degree relative with coeliac disease, type 1 diabetes mellitus, autoimmune thyroid disease, and Down syndrome.

title: Coeliac disease – Pathophysiology
content: In coeliac disease, ingestion of gluten leads to an inappropriate T-cell mediated immune response causing villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and intraepithelial lymphocytosis in the small intestine, resulting in malabsorption.

title: Coeliac disease – Clinical features: Diarrhoea
content: Chronic diarrhoea is a common presenting feature in paediatric coeliac disease, often accompanied by steatorrhoea due to malabsorption.

title: Coeliac disease – Clinical features: Abdominal pain
content: Children with coeliac disease may present with chronic abdominal pain, often colicky in nature, related to intestinal inflammation and malabsorption.

title: Coeliac disease – Clinical features: Failure to thrive
content: Failure to thrive and poor weight gain are common in infants and young children with untreated coeliac disease due to malabsorption and nutritional deficiencies.

title: Coeliac disease – Clinical features: Anaemia
content: Iron deficiency anaemia refractory to oral iron therapy is a frequent feature in paediatric coeliac disease due to impaired iron absorption in the proximal small intestine.

title: Coeliac disease – Investigations: Serology
content: Initial screening for coeliac disease includes serological tests such as tissue transglutaminase IgA (tTG-IgA) and total serum IgA to exclude IgA deficiency; tTG-IgA has a sensitivity and specificity >90%.

title: Coeliac disease – Investigations: Small bowel biopsy
content: Definitive diagnosis of coeliac disease is confirmed by duodenal biopsy showing villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes (Marsh classification), performed while the child is on a gluten-containing diet.

title: Coeliac disease – Management
content: The mainstay of treatment for paediatric coeliac disease is a strict lifelong gluten-free diet, eliminating all sources of wheat, barley, and rye, with dietetic support to ensure nutritional adequacy.

title: Coeliac disease – Complications
content: Untreated coeliac disease in children can lead to complications including growth failure, osteoporosis, iron deficiency anaemia, and rarely, enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma.

title: Coeliac disease – Prognosis
content: With adherence to a strict gluten-free diet, children with coeliac disease typically have an excellent prognosis with resolution of symptoms, mucosal healing within 6-12 months, and normal growth and development.

title: Conjunctivitis – Definition
content: Conjunctivitis is inflammation of the conjunctiva, the mucous membrane covering the white part of the eye and the inner surface of the eyelids, commonly presenting with redness, discharge, and irritation in paediatric patients.

title: Conjunctivitis – Epidemiology
content: Conjunctivitis is a common paediatric condition, accounting for approximately 1-2% of general practice consultations in the UK, with viral causes being the most frequent, especially in children under 5 years old.

title: Conjunctivitis – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Common causes of paediatric conjunctivitis include viral infections (adenovirus), bacterial infections (Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae), allergic reactions, and irritants such as smoke or chlorine.

title: Conjunctivitis – Pathophysiology
content: Conjunctivitis results from inflammation of the conjunctival epithelium due to infection, allergy, or irritation, leading to vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, and mucous or purulent discharge.

title: Conjunctivitis – Clinical features: Redness and irritation
content: Children with conjunctivitis typically present with redness of the conjunctiva, a gritty or burning sensation, and mild eye discomfort without significant pain.

title: Conjunctivitis – Clinical features: Discharge type
content: Viral conjunctivitis usually produces a watery discharge, whereas bacterial conjunctivitis causes purulent, sticky discharge often leading to eyelids sticking together, especially in the morning.

title: Conjunctivitis – Clinical features: Associated symptoms
content: Other symptoms may include eyelid swelling, mild photophobia, and regional preauricular lymphadenopathy, particularly in viral conjunctivitis.

title: Conjunctivitis – Investigations
content: Diagnosis is primarily clinical; however, conjunctival swabs for bacterial culture may be considered in severe, recurrent, or non-resolving cases to guide antibiotic therapy.

title: Conjunctivitis – Management: Viral conjunctivitis
content: Management of viral conjunctivitis is supportive, including maintaining eye hygiene, using cold compresses, and lubricating eye drops; antibiotics are not indicated.

title: Conjunctivitis – Management: Bacterial conjunctivitis
content: Topical antibiotics such as chloramphenicol 1% eye drops, 1 drop every 2 hours while awake for the first 2 days, then 4 times daily for 5 days, are recommended for bacterial conjunctivitis in children.

title: Conjunctivitis – Management: Allergic conjunctivitis
content: Treatment includes avoidance of allergens and use of topical antihistamines or mast cell stabilisers such as olopatadine eye drops, 1 drop twice daily, to reduce symptoms.

title: Conjunctivitis – Complications
content: Complications are rare but can include keratitis, corneal ulceration, and rarely, chronic conjunctivitis leading to scarring or visual impairment if untreated.

title: Conjunctivitis – Prognosis
content: The prognosis for paediatric conjunctivitis is excellent, with most cases resolving within 1-2 weeks without long-term sequelae when appropriately managed.

title: Constipation – Definition
content: Constipation in paediatrics is defined as infrequent, hard, painful stools or difficulty passing stools, typically fewer than three bowel movements per week.

title: Constipation – Epidemiology
content: Constipation affects approximately 3% of children worldwide and is one of the most common paediatric gastrointestinal complaints presenting in primary care in the UK.

title: Constipation – Aetiology and Risk factors
content: Common causes of paediatric constipation include low dietary fibre intake, inadequate fluid intake, withholding behaviour, toilet training issues, and secondary causes such as hypothyroidism, Hirschsprung disease, and medication side effects (e.g., anticholinergics).

title: Constipation – Pathophysiology
content: Constipation results from slowed colonic transit or outlet obstruction due to voluntary withholding of stool, leading to faecal impaction and decreased rectal sensation.

title: Constipation – Clinical features: Infrequent and hard stools
content: Children with constipation typically present with fewer than three bowel movements per week and pass hard, pellet-like or large stools that may be painful to pass.

title: Constipation – Clinical features: Abdominal pain and distension
content: Constipated children may complain of intermittent or chronic abdominal pain and visible abdominal distension due to faecal loading.

title: Constipation – Clinical features: Faecal incontinence
content: Overflow soiling or faecal incontinence occurs in up to 30% of children with chronic constipation due to leakage around impacted stool.

title: Constipation – Investigations
content: Diagnosis is clinical; investigations such as abdominal X-ray may be used to assess faecal loading in complex cases. Thyroid function tests and calcium levels may be checked if secondary causes are suspected.

title: Constipation – Management: Lifestyle and dietary advice
content: Initial management includes increasing dietary fibre intake to 10-15 g/day for toddlers and 20-30 g/day for older children, ensuring adequate hydration, and encouraging regular toilet habits with positive reinforcement.

title: Constipation – Management: Pharmacological treatment
content: Oral osmotic laxatives such as polyethylene glycol (PEG) are first-line pharmacological treatment. The typical dose is 0.4-0.8 g/kg/day, adjusted according to response, with treatment duration of at least 2 months to prevent relapse.

title: Constipation – Complications
content: Complications include faecal impaction, anal fissures, rectal prolapse, urinary tract infections due to bladder compression, and psychological distress.

title: Constipation – Prognosis
content: With appropriate management, most children with constipation improve within weeks to months. However, relapse is common, and some children may require prolonged treatment and follow-up.

title: Dehydration – Definition
content: Dehydration in paediatrics is a clinical condition characterised by a deficit of total body water, leading to impaired cellular and organ function. It is commonly classified by severity based on percentage of body weight lost: mild (<5%), moderate (5-10%), and severe (>10%).

title: Dehydration – Epidemiology
content: Dehydration is a common paediatric condition, particularly in children under 5 years old. It is a leading cause of hospital admission and mortality worldwide, especially in low-income settings. In the UK, viral gastroenteritis is the most frequent cause.

title: Dehydration – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Common causes of dehydration in children include acute gastroenteritis (viral or bacterial), inadequate fluid intake, excessive sweating, diabetic ketoacidosis, and heat exposure. Risk factors include young age (<2 years), prematurity, and underlying chronic illnesses.

title: Dehydration – Pathophysiology
content: Dehydration results from a net loss of water exceeding intake, causing hypovolaemia and hyperosmolarity. This leads to reduced tissue perfusion and cellular dysfunction. In children, extracellular fluid volume depletion occurs rapidly due to higher body water content and metabolic rate.

title: Dehydration – Clinical features: General signs
content: Signs of dehydration in children include dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes, decreased skin turgor, delayed capillary refill (>2 seconds), tachycardia, hypotension in severe cases, and reduced urine output (oliguria).

title: Dehydration – Clinical features: Severity classification
content: Mild dehydration presents with thirst and dry mouth; moderate dehydration includes additional signs such as sunken eyes, reduced urine output, and lethargy; severe dehydration is characterised by signs of shock including tachycardia, hypotension, cold extremities, and decreased consciousness.

title: Dehydration – Investigations
content: Investigations include blood tests (serum electrolytes, urea, creatinine, blood glucose), blood gas analysis to assess acid-base status, urine analysis, and assessment of weight loss compared to baseline. In severe cases, capillary blood lactate may be measured.

title: Dehydration – Management: Oral rehydration therapy
content: Mild to moderate dehydration is managed with oral rehydration therapy (ORT) using oral rehydration salts (ORS) solution containing 75 mmol/L sodium, 75 mmol/L glucose, 20 mmol/L potassium, and 10 mmol/L citrate. The WHO recommends 50-100 ml/kg over 3-4 hours.

title: Dehydration – Management: Intravenous fluid therapy
content: Severe dehydration or shock requires intravenous fluid resuscitation with isotonic fluids such as 0.9% sodium chloride or Hartmann's solution. Initial bolus dose is 20 ml/kg over 15-30 minutes, repeated as needed. Subsequent maintenance fluids are calculated using Holliday-Segar method.

title: Dehydration – Complications
content: Complications of dehydration include hypovolaemic shock, acute kidney injury, electrolyte imbalances (hyponatraemia, hypernatraemia, hypokalaemia), seizures, and in severe cases, death.

title: Dehydration – Prognosis
content: With prompt recognition and appropriate management, the prognosis of dehydration in children is excellent. Delayed treatment or severe dehydration increases risk of morbidity and mortality, particularly in infants and children with comorbidities.

title: Developmental delay – Definition
content: Developmental delay is defined as a significant lag in one or more areas of development including gross/fine motor skills, speech and language, cognitive, social, and adaptive skills, compared to normative age expectations in paediatric patients.

title: Developmental delay – Epidemiology
content: Developmental delay affects approximately 5-10% of children in the UK, with higher prevalence in those born prematurely or with low birth weight.

title: Developmental delay – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Common causes of developmental delay include genetic disorders (e.g., Down syndrome), perinatal insults (e.g., hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy), infections (e.g., congenital CMV), metabolic conditions, and environmental factors such as neglect or deprivation.

title: Developmental delay – Pathophysiology
content: Developmental delay results from disruptions in normal brain development or function affecting neuronal migration, synaptogenesis, or myelination, leading to impaired acquisition of developmental milestones.

title: Developmental delay – Clinical features: Gross and fine motor delay
content: Children with developmental delay may present with delayed milestones such as sitting unsupported beyond 9 months, walking independently beyond 18 months, or poor hand-eye coordination.

title: Developmental delay – Clinical features: Speech and language problems
content: Speech delay is common, with children failing to babble by 12 months or speak single words by 18 months, often accompanied by difficulties in language comprehension.

title: Developmental delay – Clinical features: Behavioural difficulties
content: Some children with developmental delay exhibit behavioural difficulties including hyperactivity, inattention, or autistic features.

title: Developmental delay – Investigations
content: Initial investigations include developmental screening tools (e.g., Ages and Stages Questionnaire), hearing and vision assessments, and targeted blood tests such as thyroid function, metabolic screen, and genetic testing as indicated.

title: Developmental delay – Management
content: Management includes early intervention with multidisciplinary input from speech and language therapists, occupational therapists, physiotherapists, and educational support; addressing underlying causes where possible.

title: Developmental delay – Complications
content: Complications include increased risk of learning disabilities, social isolation, behavioural problems, and reduced independence in adulthood.

title: Developmental delay – Prognosis
content: Prognosis varies widely depending on the underlying cause and severity; early intervention improves outcomes, but some children may have persistent disabilities requiring lifelong support.

title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Definition
content: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is a serious acute complication of diabetes mellitus characterised by hyperglycaemia (blood glucose >11 mmol/L), metabolic acidosis (pH <7.3 or bicarbonate <15 mmol/L), and ketonaemia or ketonuria.

title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Epidemiology
content: DKA is the most common presentation of new-onset type 1 diabetes in children in the UK, occurring in approximately 25-30% of cases at diagnosis. It also occurs in children with known diabetes due to insulin omission or intercurrent illness.

title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Aetiology and risk factors
content: DKA is caused by absolute or relative insulin deficiency combined with increased counter-regulatory hormones (glucagon, cortisol, catecholamines). Risk factors include new diagnosis of type 1 diabetes, infection, missed insulin doses, and physiological stress.

title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Pathophysiology
content: Insulin deficiency leads to decreased glucose utilisation and increased lipolysis, resulting in free fatty acid release and hepatic ketogenesis. Accumulation of ketone bodies causes metabolic acidosis. Hyperglycaemia induces osmotic diuresis causing dehydration and electrolyte imbalances.

title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Clinical features: Dehydration
content: Children with DKA commonly present with signs of dehydration including dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, tachycardia, and hypotension in severe cases.

title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Clinical features: Vomiting
content: Vomiting is a common presenting symptom in paediatric DKA due to metabolic acidosis and gastric irritation.

title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Clinical features: Abdominal pain
content: Abdominal pain occurs frequently in children with DKA, often mimicking an acute abdomen but typically resolving with treatment of ketoacidosis.

title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Clinical features: Kussmaul breathing
content: Kussmaul breathing, a deep and laboured respiratory pattern, is a compensatory mechanism for metabolic acidosis seen in DKA.

title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Clinical features: Altered consciousness
content: Severe DKA may present with decreased or loss of consciousness due to cerebral oedema or severe acidosis.

title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Investigations: Blood glucose and ketones
content: Diagnosis requires blood glucose >11 mmol/L and presence of ketones in blood (>3 mmol/L) or urine (ketonuria).

title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Investigations: Blood gas analysis
content: Arterial or venous blood gas shows metabolic acidosis with pH <7.3 and bicarbonate <15 mmol/L in DKA.

title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Investigations: Electrolytes and renal function
content: Serum electrolytes typically show hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia (masked by acidosis), and elevated urea and creatinine due to dehydration.

title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Management: Fluid resuscitation
content: Initial management includes cautious intravenous fluid resuscitation with 0.9% sodium chloride at 10-20 mL/kg over 1-2 hours to restore circulatory volume, avoiding rapid correction to prevent cerebral oedema.

title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Management: Insulin therapy
content: Start intravenous insulin infusion at 0.05-0.1 units/kg/hour after initial fluid resuscitation; do not give insulin as bolus. Continue until acidosis resolves (pH >7.3, bicarbonate >15 mmol/L).

title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Management: Electrolyte monitoring and replacement
content: Monitor serum potassium closely; replace potassium once urine output is confirmed and serum potassium <5.5 mmol/L, typically adding 40 mmol potassium chloride per litre of IV fluids.

title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Management: Avoidance of cerebral oedema
content: Prevent cerebral oedema by avoiding rapid fluid administration and rapid correction of hyperglycaemia; monitor neurological status closely during treatment.

title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Complications
content: Potential complications include cerebral oedema (most common cause of mortality), hypokalaemia, hypoglycaemia, thrombosis, and acute kidney injury.

title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Prognosis
content: With prompt recognition and appropriate management, mortality from paediatric DKA in the UK is low (<1%). Neurological sequelae may occur if cerebral oedema develops.

title: Diabetes mellitus type 1 and 2 – Definition
