content: Diabetes mellitus type 1 is an autoimmune condition characterised by destruction of pancreatic beta cells leading to absolute insulin deficiency. Type 2 diabetes mellitus involves insulin resistance and relative insulin deficiency.

title: Diabetes mellitus type 1 and 2 – Epidemiology
content: Type 1 diabetes is the most common form of diabetes in children in the UK, with an incidence of approximately 25 per 100,000 children per year. Type 2 diabetes is increasing in prevalence among adolescents, particularly in those with obesity and ethnic minority backgrounds.

title: Diabetes mellitus type 1 and 2 – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Type 1 diabetes is associated with genetic susceptibility (HLA-DR3 and DR4) and environmental triggers such as viral infections. Type 2 diabetes risk factors include obesity, family history, sedentary lifestyle, and certain ethnicities (South Asian, African-Caribbean).

title: Diabetes mellitus type 1 and 2 – Pathophysiology
content: In type 1 diabetes, autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells causes absolute insulin deficiency. In type 2 diabetes, peripheral insulin resistance leads to compensatory hyperinsulinaemia and eventual beta cell dysfunction.

title: Diabetes mellitus type 1 and 2 – Clinical features: Polydipsia
content: Polydipsia (excessive thirst) is a common presenting symptom in both type 1 and type 2 diabetes due to osmotic diuresis caused by hyperglycaemia.

title: Diabetes mellitus type 1 and 2 – Clinical features: Polyuria and enuresis
content: Polyuria and secondary nocturnal enuresis occur due to osmotic diuresis from hyperglycaemia in children with diabetes mellitus.

title: Diabetes mellitus type 1 and 2 – Clinical features: Weight loss
content: Unintentional weight loss is a common feature in type 1 diabetes due to catabolism from insulin deficiency.

title: Diabetes mellitus type 1 and 2 – Clinical features: Fatigue
content: Fatigue is commonly reported in children with uncontrolled diabetes due to hyperglycaemia and metabolic derangements.

title: Diabetes mellitus type 1 and 2 – Clinical features: Diabetic ketoacidosis presentation
content: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) presents with dehydration, vomiting, abdominal pain, Kussmaul breathing, and decreased consciousness in children with type 1 diabetes.

title: Diabetes mellitus type 1 and 2 – Investigations: Blood glucose
content: Diagnosis is confirmed by a fasting plasma glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L or random plasma glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L with symptoms. HbA1c ≥48 mmol/mol (6.5%) supports diagnosis.

title: Diabetes mellitus type 1 and 2 – Investigations: Autoantibodies
content: Type 1 diabetes is associated with positive pancreatic autoantibodies including anti-GAD, anti-IA2, and islet cell antibodies.

title: Diabetes mellitus type 1 and 2 – Management: Insulin therapy
content: Type 1 diabetes requires lifelong insulin therapy. Basal-bolus regimens use long-acting insulin (e.g., insulin detemir) once or twice daily and rapid-acting insulin (e.g., insulin aspart) before meals. Doses are individualised based on blood glucose monitoring.

title: Diabetes mellitus type 1 and 2 – Management: Lifestyle and oral therapy in type 2
content: Type 2 diabetes management in children includes lifestyle modification (diet and exercise) and metformin as first-line oral therapy, starting at 500 mg once daily, titrated to 1 g twice daily as tolerated.

title: Diabetes mellitus type 1 and 2 – Complications: Acute diabetic ketoacidosis
content: DKA is a life-threatening complication characterised by hyperglycaemia, metabolic acidosis (pH <7.3), ketonaemia (>3 mmol/L), dehydration, and electrolyte disturbances requiring urgent treatment.

title: Diabetes mellitus type 1 and 2 – Complications: Long-term microvascular complications
content: Long-term complications include retinopathy, nephropathy, and neuropathy. Annual screening for microalbuminuria and retinal examination is recommended from age 12 or 5 years after diagnosis.

title: Diabetes mellitus type 1 and 2 – Prognosis
content: With optimal glycaemic control, children with diabetes can have a normal lifespan; however, poor control increases risk of acute and chronic complications reducing life expectancy by up to 10 years.

title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation – Definition
content: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is a pathological process characterised by systemic activation of coagulation pathways leading to widespread microvascular thrombosis and consumption of platelets and coagulation factors, resulting in bleeding and organ dysfunction.

title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation – Epidemiology
content: DIC occurs in paediatric patients as a complication of various underlying conditions such as sepsis, trauma, malignancy, and severe burns. The incidence varies depending on the underlying cause, with neonatal DIC being more common in premature infants and those with perinatal asphyxia.

title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Common causes of DIC in paediatric patients include severe bacterial sepsis (especially meningococcal septicaemia), viral infections, malignancies such as acute promyelocytic leukaemia, severe trauma, burns, and complications of prematurity.

title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation – Pathophysiology
content: DIC results from excessive thrombin generation causing fibrin deposition in microvasculature, consumption of platelets and clotting factors, activation of fibrinolysis, and secondary bleeding. This leads to microvascular thrombosis, multi-organ ischaemia, and haemorrhagic manifestations.

title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation – Clinical features: Bruising
content: Paediatric patients with DIC commonly present with bruising due to thrombocytopenia and consumption of clotting factors.

title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation – Clinical features: Shock
content: Shock may develop in paediatric patients with DIC secondary to underlying sepsis or massive bleeding.

title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation – Clinical features: The sick child
content: Children with DIC often appear acutely unwell with signs of systemic illness including fever, pallor, tachycardia, and altered consciousness.

title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation – Investigations
content: Laboratory findings in DIC include prolonged prothrombin time (PT) and activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT), low fibrinogen (<1.0 g/L), thrombocytopenia (platelets <100 x10^9/L), elevated D-dimer and fibrin degradation products, and evidence of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia on blood film.

title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation – Management
content: Management of paediatric DIC focuses on treating the underlying cause, supportive care including blood product replacement (platelets if <50 x10^9/L with bleeding, fresh frozen plasma 15-20 mL/kg to replace clotting factors, cryoprecipitate if fibrinogen <1.0 g/L), and maintaining organ perfusion. Heparin is rarely used and only considered in chronic DIC with predominant thrombosis.

title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation – Complications
content: Complications of DIC in children include multi-organ failure due to microvascular thrombosis, severe bleeding, shock, and death if untreated or underlying cause is not controlled.

title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation – Prognosis
content: Prognosis depends on the underlying cause and severity of DIC. Early recognition and treatment improve outcomes; however, mortality remains high in severe cases, especially in neonates and children with sepsis.

title: Drug overdose – Definition
content: Drug overdose in paediatrics refers to the ingestion or administration of a medication in quantities greater than recommended, leading to toxic effects or poisoning.

title: Drug overdose – Epidemiology
content: Paediatric drug overdose is a common cause of emergency hospital admissions in the UK, with accidental ingestions most frequent in children under 5 years and intentional overdoses more common in adolescents.

title: Drug overdose – Aetiology and risk factors
content: Common causes of paediatric drug overdose include accidental ingestion of adult medications such as paracetamol, ibuprofen, and opioids, as well as intentional overdose in adolescents often associated with self-harm or substance misuse.

title: Drug overdose – Pathophysiology
content: Toxic effects in paediatric drug overdose occur due to excessive plasma concentrations of the drug leading to cellular toxicity, organ dysfunction, and metabolic disturbances depending on the drug involved.

title: Drug overdose – Clinical features: Decreased/loss of consciousness
content: Paediatric patients with drug overdose may present with decreased level of consciousness or coma, depending on the drug and dose ingested.

title: Drug overdose – Clinical features: Fits/seizures
content: Seizures may occur in paediatric drug overdose, particularly with agents such as tricyclic antidepressants, theophylline, or isoniazid.

title: Drug overdose – Clinical features: Vomiting
content: Vomiting is a common early symptom in paediatric drug overdose and may be induced by the toxic effects of the drug or as a protective response.

title: Drug overdose – Clinical features: Overdose
content: Clinical signs of overdose vary by drug but may include altered mental status, respiratory depression, hypotension, arrhythmias, and metabolic abnormalities.

title: Drug overdose – Investigations
content: Initial investigations include blood glucose, electrolytes, renal and liver function tests, blood gas analysis, ECG, and specific drug levels such as paracetamol and salicylate concentrations.

title: Drug overdose – Management
content: Management includes stabilisation of airway, breathing, and circulation, administration of activated charcoal if within 1 hour of ingestion, specific antidotes such as N-acetylcysteine for paracetamol overdose, and supportive care in a paediatric intensive care setting if required.

title: Drug overdose – Complications
content: Potential complications include respiratory failure, cardiac arrhythmias, hepatic failure (notably with paracetamol overdose), renal failure, and neurological damage.

title: Drug overdose – Prognosis
content: Prognosis depends on the drug involved, dose, time to treatment, and presence of complications; early recognition and treatment generally result in good outcomes in paediatric patients.

title: Eating disorders – Definition
content: Eating disorders in paediatrics are a group of mental health conditions characterised by abnormal eating behaviours and preoccupation with body weight or shape, including anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, and binge-eating disorder.

title: Eating disorders – Epidemiology
content: Eating disorders affect approximately 1-3% of adolescents in the UK, with a higher prevalence in females (up to 10 times more common) and peak incidence between ages 12 and 18 years.

title: Eating disorders – Aetiology and risk factors
content: Risk factors for paediatric eating disorders include genetic predisposition, female sex, adolescence, family history of psychiatric illness, societal pressure for thinness, low self-esteem, and comorbid mental health disorders such as anxiety and depression.

title: Eating disorders – Pathophysiology
content: Eating disorders involve complex interactions between neurobiological, psychological, and environmental factors leading to dysregulation of appetite, reward pathways, and cognitive distortions about body image and food.

title: Eating disorders – Clinical features: Behavioural difficulties in childhood
content: Children with eating disorders often present with behavioural difficulties including food restriction, excessive exercise, secretive eating, and social withdrawal.

title: Eating disorders – Clinical features: Dehydration
content: Dehydration may occur in paediatric eating disorders due to vomiting, laxative abuse, or inadequate fluid intake.

title: Eating disorders – Clinical features: Self-harm
content: Self-harm and suicidal thoughts are common in paediatric patients with eating disorders, occurring in up to 30% of cases, necessitating careful mental health assessment.

title: Eating disorders – Clinical features: Decreased/loss of consciousness
content: Severe malnutrition in eating disorders can lead to hypoglycaemia and electrolyte imbalances causing decreased consciousness or coma.

title: Eating disorders – Investigations
content: Initial investigations include full blood count, electrolytes, liver function tests, thyroid function, glucose, ECG to assess bradycardia or QT prolongation, and bone density scans if indicated.

title: Eating disorders – Management
content: Management includes a multidisciplinary approach with medical stabilisation, nutritional rehabilitation aiming for gradual weight gain of 0.5-1 kg/week, psychological therapies such as family-based treatment, and pharmacotherapy only for comorbid conditions.

title: Eating disorders – Complications
content: Complications include cardiac arrhythmias, electrolyte disturbances (hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia), osteoporosis, growth retardation, amenorrhoea, and increased risk of suicide.

title: Eating disorders – Prognosis
content: Prognosis varies; approximately 50% of paediatric patients recover fully with treatment, 30% have a chronic course, and mortality rates are around 5-10%, mainly due to medical complications or suicide.

title: Epididymitis and orchitis – Definition
content: Epididymitis and orchitis refer to inflammation of the epididymis and testis respectively, commonly presenting with scrotal pain and swelling in paediatric patients.

title: Epididymitis and orchitis – Epidemiology
content: Epididymitis and orchitis are uncommon in prepubertal boys but more frequent in adolescents, with a peak incidence in boys aged 15-19 years. Viral orchitis, particularly mumps orchitis, is a notable cause in the paediatric population.

title: Epididymitis and orchitis – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Common causes of epididymitis and orchitis in children include viral infections such as mumps virus, bacterial infections often associated with urinary tract infections or sexually transmitted infections in adolescents, and trauma. Risk factors include recent urinary tract instrumentation, congenital urinary tract abnormalities, and unprotected sexual activity in adolescents.

title: Epididymitis and orchitis – Pathophysiology
content: Inflammation of the epididymis and/or testis occurs due to infection or immune response, leading to increased blood flow, oedema, and infiltration of inflammatory cells. This results in scrotal pain, swelling, and sometimes systemic symptoms such as fever.

title: Epididymitis and orchitis – Clinical features: Scrotal/testicular pain and swelling
content: The most common presentation is acute onset of unilateral scrotal or testicular pain and swelling, often accompanied by erythema and tenderness on examination.

title: Epididymitis and orchitis – Clinical features: Fever
content: Fever is commonly present in paediatric patients with epididymitis and orchitis, reflecting systemic inflammatory response.

title: Epididymitis and orchitis – Clinical features: Urinary symptoms
content: Some children may present with urinary symptoms such as dysuria, frequency, or urgency, especially if bacterial infection is the underlying cause.

title: Epididymitis and orchitis – Investigations
content: Investigations include urine dipstick and microscopy to detect infection, urethral swabs for sexually transmitted infections in adolescents, scrotal ultrasound with Doppler to differentiate from testicular torsion, and blood tests including full blood count and inflammatory markers.

title: Epididymitis and orchitis – Management
content: Management includes analgesia with paracetamol and NSAIDs, scrotal support, and antibiotics if bacterial infection is suspected. Empirical antibiotic therapy in children over 15 years includes ceftriaxone 250 mg IM single dose plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 10 days, adjusted for age and weight. Viral orchitis requires supportive care only.

title: Epididymitis and orchitis – Complications
content: Potential complications include abscess formation, testicular infarction, infertility due to impaired spermatogenesis, and chronic epididymitis.

title: Epididymitis and orchitis – Prognosis
content: With prompt diagnosis and appropriate treatment, prognosis is generally good with resolution of symptoms. Delayed treatment increases risk of complications including infertility.

title: Epilepsy – Definition
content: Epilepsy is a neurological disorder characterised by a predisposition to generate epileptic seizures, defined by at least two unprovoked seizures occurring more than 24 hours apart.

title: Epilepsy – Epidemiology
content: Epilepsy affects approximately 5 per 1000 children in the UK, with the highest incidence in the first year of life and during adolescence.

title: Epilepsy – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Common causes of epilepsy in children include genetic factors, structural brain abnormalities (e.g. cortical dysplasia), perinatal brain injury, central nervous system infections, and metabolic disorders.

title: Epilepsy – Pathophysiology
content: Epileptic seizures result from abnormal, excessive, and synchronous neuronal activity in the brain, often due to an imbalance between excitatory glutamate and inhibitory GABA neurotransmission.

title: Epilepsy – Clinical features: Fits/seizures
content: Seizures in paediatric epilepsy can present as focal (with or without impaired awareness) or generalised seizures, including tonic-clonic, absence, myoclonic, or atonic seizures.

title: Epilepsy – Clinical features: Decreased/loss of consciousness
content: Generalised tonic-clonic seizures typically present with sudden loss of consciousness, tonic stiffening followed by clonic jerking, lasting 1-2 minutes, often followed by post-ictal drowsiness.

title: Epilepsy – Investigations
content: Initial investigations include EEG to detect epileptiform activity, brain MRI to identify structural abnormalities, and metabolic and genetic testing if indicated by clinical features.

title: Epilepsy – Management
content: First-line treatment for paediatric epilepsy is monotherapy with antiepileptic drugs such as sodium valproate (initial dose 10-15 mg/kg/day) or carbamazepine (5 mg/kg/day), titrated to seizure control and tolerability.

title: Epilepsy – Complications
content: Complications include status epilepticus, cognitive impairment, psychosocial difficulties, and increased risk of sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP), which occurs in approximately 1 in 1000 children per year.

title: Epilepsy – Prognosis
content: Approximately 70% of children with epilepsy achieve seizure remission with appropriate treatment; prognosis is poorer in those with symptomatic epilepsy or developmental delay.

title: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease – Definition
content: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD) in paediatrics is the pathological retrograde flow of gastric contents into the oesophagus causing troublesome symptoms or complications.

title: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease – Epidemiology
content: GORD affects up to 50% of infants under 3 months, with most cases resolving by 12-18 months; prevalence decreases with age.

title: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Risk factors for paediatric GORD include prematurity, neurological impairment, congenital oesophageal abnormalities (e.g., oesophageal atresia), and obesity.

title: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease – Pathophysiology
content: GORD results from transient lower oesophageal sphincter relaxations, impaired oesophageal clearance, delayed gastric emptying, or anatomical abnormalities leading to reflux of acidic gastric contents.

title: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease – Clinical features: Vomiting
content: Frequent regurgitation or vomiting of feeds, often non-projectile and occurring after meals, is a common presentation in infants with GORD.

title: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease – Clinical features: Infant feeding problems
content: Infants with GORD may exhibit feeding difficulties including refusal to feed, irritability during feeds, and poor weight gain.

title: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease – Clinical features: Chronic cough and wheeze
content: Chronic cough and wheeze may occur due to aspiration of refluxed gastric contents causing airway irritation or reactive airway disease.

title: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease – Investigations
content: Investigations are not routinely required but may include 24-hour oesophageal pH monitoring, oesophageal impedance, and upper GI contrast studies in complicated or atypical cases.

title: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease – Management: Conservative measures
content: Initial management includes positional therapy (elevating the head of the cot), smaller frequent feeds, and thickening feeds with infant formula thickeners.

title: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease – Management: Pharmacological treatment
content: If conservative measures fail, acid suppression with proton pump inhibitors (e.g., omeprazole 1 mg/kg once daily) or H2 receptor antagonists may be used, typically for 4-8 weeks.

title: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease – Management: Surgical treatment
content: Surgical intervention (e.g., Nissen fundoplication) is reserved for severe, refractory cases with complications such as failure to thrive or recurrent aspiration pneumonia.

title: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease – Complications
content: Complications include oesophagitis, strictures, Barrett's oesophagus (rare in children), aspiration pneumonia, and failure to thrive.

title: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease – Prognosis
content: Most infants with GORD improve spontaneously by 12-18 months; long-term prognosis is excellent with appropriate management.

title: Henoch-Schonlein purpura – Definition
content: Henoch-Schonlein purpura (HSP) is a small vessel vasculitis characterised by IgA immune complex deposition, primarily affecting children and causing palpable purpura, arthritis, abdominal pain, and renal involvement.

title: Henoch-Schonlein purpura – Epidemiology
content: Henoch-Schonlein purpura is the most common vasculitis in children, with an incidence of approximately 20 per 100,000 children per year, typically affecting those aged 3 to 15 years, with a slight male predominance.

title: Henoch-Schonlein purpura – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Henoch-Schonlein purpura is often preceded by an upper respiratory tract infection, commonly streptococcal or viral, which triggers IgA immune complex deposition; other risk factors include recent vaccinations and certain medications.

title: Henoch-Schonlein purpura – Pathophysiology
content: Henoch-Schonlein purpura results from IgA1-dominant immune complex deposition in small vessels, leading to leukocytoclastic vasculitis with inflammation and damage to vessel walls, causing purpura, arthritis, and renal involvement.

title: Henoch-Schonlein purpura – Clinical features: Acute rash
content: The characteristic rash of Henoch-Schonlein purpura is palpable purpura predominantly on the lower limbs and buttocks, occurring in nearly 100% of cases.

title: Henoch-Schonlein purpura – Clinical features: Acute joint pain/swelling
content: Arthritis or arthralgia occurs in approximately 80% of children with Henoch-Schonlein purpura, typically affecting knees and ankles with transient, non-erosive joint swelling and pain.

title: Henoch-Schonlein purpura – Clinical features: Acute abdominal pain
content: Abdominal pain occurs in up to 50% of children with Henoch-Schonlein purpura and may be colicky due to bowel vasculitis; it can be accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and gastrointestinal bleeding.

title: Henoch-Schonlein purpura – Clinical features: Haematuria
content: Renal involvement in Henoch-Schonlein purpura occurs in 20-50% of cases, presenting as haematuria and/or proteinuria; microscopic haematuria is common, and nephritic syndrome may develop in severe cases.

title: Henoch-Schonlein purpura – Investigations
content: Diagnosis of Henoch-Schonlein purpura is clinical; investigations include urinalysis for haematuria and proteinuria, full blood count, renal function tests, and skin biopsy showing leukocytoclastic vasculitis with IgA deposition if diagnosis is uncertain.

title: Henoch-Schonlein purpura – Management
content: Management of Henoch-Schonlein purpura is mainly supportive including analgesia with paracetamol or NSAIDs; corticosteroids such as oral prednisolone 1-2 mg/kg/day may be used for severe abdominal pain or renal involvement; monitoring of renal function is essential.

title: Henoch-Schonlein purpura – Complications
content: Complications of Henoch-Schonlein purpura include chronic kidney disease from persistent nephritis, intussusception due to bowel vasculitis, and rare severe gastrointestinal haemorrhage or perforation.

title: Henoch-Schonlein purpura – Prognosis
content: The prognosis of Henoch-Schonlein purpura in children is generally excellent, with over 90% achieving full recovery; however, 1-2% may develop chronic renal impairment requiring long-term follow-up.

title: Hepatitis – Definition
content: Hepatitis is inflammation of the liver, which in paediatric patients can be caused by infectious agents, autoimmune conditions, metabolic diseases, or toxins.

title: Hepatitis – Epidemiology
content: In the UK, paediatric hepatitis is most commonly caused by viral infections, with hepatitis A and B vaccination programmes reducing incidence; hepatitis C remains rare but significant in children born to infected mothers.

title: Hepatitis – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Common causes of paediatric hepatitis in the UK include viral infections (hepatitis A, B, C, E, and rarely D), autoimmune hepatitis, metabolic disorders such as Wilson’s disease, and drug-induced liver injury from paracetamol overdose.

title: Hepatitis – Pathophysiology
content: Hepatitis causes liver inflammation due to immune-mediated hepatocyte injury triggered by viral infection, autoimmune attack, or toxic/metabolic insults, leading to hepatocyte necrosis and impaired liver function.

title: Hepatitis – Clinical features: Jaundice
content: Paediatric hepatitis commonly presents with jaundice characterised by yellowing of the skin and sclera due to elevated serum bilirubin levels, often >34 µmol/L (2 mg/dL).

title: Hepatitis – Clinical features: Fever
content: Children with acute viral hepatitis may present with fever, often low-grade, reflecting systemic viral infection.

title: Hepatitis – Clinical features: Abdominal pain
content: Right upper quadrant or epigastric abdominal pain is a common symptom in paediatric hepatitis due to liver capsule inflammation.

title: Hepatitis – Clinical features: Fatigue and malaise
content: Children with hepatitis often experience fatigue and malaise due to systemic illness and impaired liver function.

title: Hepatitis – Investigations: Liver function tests
content: Liver function tests in paediatric hepatitis typically show elevated alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST), often >500 IU/L in acute viral hepatitis, with raised bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase.

title: Hepatitis – Investigations: Viral serology
content: Diagnosis of viral hepatitis in children involves serological testing for hepatitis A IgM, hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), hepatitis B core IgM antibody, and hepatitis C antibody with PCR for viral RNA if positive.

title: Hepatitis – Management: Supportive care
content: Management of paediatric hepatitis is primarily supportive including adequate hydration, nutrition, and avoidance of hepatotoxic drugs; hospital admission is required for severe cases or acute liver failure.

title: Hepatitis – Management: Antiviral therapy
content: In chronic hepatitis B infection in children, antiviral treatment with entecavir (0.015 mg/kg once daily, max 0.5 mg) or tenofovir may be indicated to reduce viral replication and liver damage.

title: Hepatitis – Complications
content: Complications of paediatric hepatitis include acute liver failure, chronic liver disease with fibrosis and cirrhosis, portal hypertension, and increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma particularly in chronic hepatitis B and C.

title: Hepatitis – Prognosis
content: The prognosis of paediatric hepatitis varies by cause; acute viral hepatitis A usually resolves completely with full recovery, while chronic hepatitis B or C may lead to long-term liver damage requiring specialist follow-up.

title: Hernias – Definition
content: A hernia is the protrusion of an organ or tissue through an abnormal opening in the surrounding muscle or connective tissue, commonly occurring in the abdominal wall in paediatric patients.

title: Hernias – Epidemiology
content: In the UK, paediatric inguinal hernias occur in approximately 1-5% of full-term infants and up to 30% of premature infants, with a male to female ratio of about 6:1.

title: Hernias – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Risk factors for paediatric hernias include prematurity, low birth weight, male sex, family history of hernias, and conditions increasing intra-abdominal pressure such as chronic cough or constipation.

title: Hernias – Pathophysiology
content: Paediatric hernias commonly result from a persistent processus vaginalis, allowing abdominal contents to protrude through the inguinal canal, or from weakness in the abdominal wall muscles.

title: Hernias – Clinical features: Abdominal mass
content: Paediatric hernias typically present as a painless, reducible swelling in the groin or scrotum, which may become more prominent on crying or straining.

title: Hernias – Clinical features: Acute abdominal pain
content: Incarcerated or strangulated hernias present with acute, severe pain, tenderness, erythema over the swelling, and systemic signs such as vomiting and irritability.

title: Hernias – Investigations
content: Diagnosis of paediatric hernias is primarily clinical; ultrasound may be used to confirm diagnosis or assess complications like incarceration, especially in atypical cases.

title: Hernias – Management
content: Elective surgical repair is recommended for paediatric inguinal hernias to prevent incarceration; timing depends on age and symptoms, with emergency surgery indicated for incarcerated hernias.

title: Hernias – Complications
content: Complications include incarceration, strangulation leading to bowel ischaemia, testicular ischaemia in males, and recurrence after surgical repair.

title: Hernias – Prognosis
content: With timely surgical repair, the prognosis for paediatric hernias is excellent, with low rates of recurrence and minimal long-term morbidity.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Definition
content: Herpes simplex virus (HSV) is a double-stranded DNA virus causing infections primarily of the skin, mucous membranes, and central nervous system in paediatric patients. There are two types: HSV-1, commonly causing orolabial infections, and HSV-2, typically associated with genital infections.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Epidemiology
content: HSV infection is common in the UK paediatric population, with HSV-1 seroprevalence reaching 60-70% by adolescence. Neonatal herpes occurs in approximately 1 in 10,000 live births, often due to maternal primary infection near delivery.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Primary risk factors for paediatric HSV infection include close contact with infected individuals, maternal primary HSV infection during pregnancy, prematurity, and immunosuppression. Neonatal infection risk is highest with maternal primary genital HSV infection near delivery.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Pathophysiology
content: HSV infects epithelial cells causing cytolysis and vesicular lesions; it establishes latency in sensory nerve ganglia with potential for reactivation. In neonates, HSV can disseminate causing severe systemic illness including encephalitis.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Clinical features: Fever
content: Paediatric HSV infection often presents with fever, which may be high-grade and persistent, especially in neonatal herpes and HSV encephalitis.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Clinical features: Acute rash
content: HSV causes painful grouped vesicular lesions on an erythematous base, commonly affecting the orolabial area in children (cold sores) and occasionally genital regions.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Clinical features: Decreased/loss of consciousness
content: HSV encephalitis in paediatric patients can present with altered mental status, decreased level of consciousness, seizures, and focal neurological signs.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Investigations
content: Diagnosis is confirmed by PCR testing of vesicle fluid, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), or blood. CSF analysis in HSV encephalitis shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein, and normal glucose. MRI brain may show temporal lobe abnormalities.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Management
content: First-line treatment for paediatric HSV infection is intravenous aciclovir 20 mg/kg every 8 hours for 14-21 days in neonatal or CNS disease. Oral aciclovir or valaciclovir may be used for mucocutaneous disease. Supportive care includes hydration and analgesia.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Complications
content: Complications of paediatric HSV infection include neonatal disseminated disease, HSV encephalitis causing long-term neurological impairment, keratitis leading to vision loss, and secondary bacterial infection of skin lesions.

title: Herpes simplex virus – Prognosis
content: Prognosis depends on disease severity; neonatal HSV and HSV encephalitis have high morbidity and mortality despite treatment. Early aciclovir therapy improves outcomes, but neurological sequelae occur in up to 50% of encephalitis cases.

title: Human papilloma virus infection – Definition
content: Human papilloma virus (HPV) infection is a viral infection caused by human papillomaviruses, a group of DNA viruses that infect epithelial cells, leading to warts and potentially malignant lesions.

title: Human papilloma virus infection – Epidemiology
content: HPV infection is one of the most common sexually transmitted infections in the UK, with peak prevalence in adolescents and young adults. The UK HPV vaccination programme targets children aged 12-13 years to reduce infection rates.

title: Human papilloma virus infection – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Risk factors for HPV infection in paediatric populations include early onset of sexual activity, multiple sexual partners, immunosuppression, and vertical transmission during childbirth.

title: Human papilloma virus infection – Pathophysiology
content: HPV infects basal epithelial cells through micro-abrasions, integrating viral DNA into host cells, causing epithelial proliferation and potential dysplasia, which may progress to malignancy in high-risk HPV types.

title: Human papilloma virus infection – Clinical features: Cutaneous warts
content: Cutaneous warts present as hyperkeratotic papules commonly on hands and feet in children, caused by HPV types 1, 2, and 4, often asymptomatic but may cause discomfort or cosmetic concern.

title: Human papilloma virus infection – Clinical features: Anogenital warts
content: Anogenital warts in paediatric patients may present as soft, flesh-coloured papules or cauliflower-like lesions around the genital or perianal area, caused mainly by HPV types 6 and 11.

title: Human papilloma virus infection – Investigations
content: Diagnosis is primarily clinical; HPV DNA testing via PCR is used in specialised settings. Biopsy may be required for atypical lesions or suspected malignancy. Cytology screening is part of cervical screening in older adolescents.

title: Human papilloma virus infection – Management
content: Management includes watchful waiting for spontaneous resolution, topical treatments such as salicylic acid for cutaneous warts, cryotherapy, and surgical removal for persistent or symptomatic lesions. The UK HPV vaccination programme uses the quadrivalent or nonavalent vaccine at 12-13 years to prevent infection.

title: Human papilloma virus infection – Complications
content: Complications include persistent warts causing discomfort, psychological distress, and in rare cases, progression to malignancies such as cervical, vulvar, penile, or oropharyngeal cancers, especially with high-risk HPV types 16 and 18.

title: Human papilloma virus infection – Prognosis
content: Most HPV infections in children resolve spontaneously within 1-2 years without intervention. Vaccination significantly reduces the risk of persistent infection and HPV-related malignancies, improving long-term prognosis.

title: Hypoglycaemia – Definition
content: Hypoglycaemia in paediatrics is defined as a plasma glucose concentration less than 2.6 mmol/L (47 mg/dL).

title: Hypoglycaemia – Epidemiology
content: Neonatal hypoglycaemia affects approximately 1 to 5 per 1000 live births in the UK, with higher incidence in preterm infants and those with low birth weight.

title: Hypoglycaemia – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Common causes of hypoglycaemia in children include hyperinsulinism, inborn errors of metabolism, endocrine deficiencies such as hypopituitarism or adrenal insufficiency, and prolonged fasting.

title: Hypoglycaemia – Pathophysiology
content: Hypoglycaemia results from an imbalance between glucose utilisation and production, often due to excessive insulin or impaired gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis.

title: Hypoglycaemia – Clinical features: Neurogenic symptoms
content: Neurogenic symptoms of hypoglycaemia in children include sweating, tremor, pallor, tachycardia, irritability, and hunger.

title: Hypoglycaemia – Clinical features: Neuroglycopenic symptoms
content: Neuroglycopenic symptoms include lethargy, irritability, seizures (fits/seizures), decreased level of consciousness, and coma in severe hypoglycaemia.

title: Hypoglycaemia – Investigations: Blood glucose measurement
content: Confirm hypoglycaemia by measuring plasma glucose; a level below 2.6 mmol/L in symptomatic children requires urgent treatment.

title: Hypoglycaemia – Investigations: Critical sample
content: During hypoglycaemia, obtain a critical sample including insulin, cortisol, growth hormone, beta-hydroxybutyrate, free fatty acids, and lactate to aid diagnosis.

title: Hypoglycaemia – Management: Initial treatment
content: Immediate treatment of hypoglycaemia involves administering 200 mg/kg of oral glucose (equivalent to 2 mL/kg of 10% glucose) if the child is conscious; if unconscious, give intravenous 2 mL/kg of 10% dextrose over 5 minutes.

title: Hypoglycaemia – Management: Maintenance therapy
content: After initial correction, maintain normoglycaemia with intravenous dextrose infusion (e.g., 10% dextrose at 6-8 mg/kg/min) and frequent feeds; monitor blood glucose regularly.

title: Hypoglycaemia – Complications
content: Severe or prolonged hypoglycaemia may cause permanent neurological damage including developmental delay, seizures, and cerebral palsy.

title: Hypoglycaemia – Prognosis
content: The prognosis depends on the cause, severity, and duration of hypoglycaemia; early recognition and treatment improve neurological outcomes.

title: Hyposplenism/splenectomy – Definition
content: Hyposplenism refers to reduced splenic function, while splenectomy is the surgical removal of the spleen. Both conditions result in impaired immune function, particularly affecting the clearance of encapsulated bacteria.

title: Hyposplenism/splenectomy – Epidemiology
content: Hyposplenism and splenectomy are uncommon in the paediatric population but occur in children with conditions such as sickle cell disease, thalassaemia, or following trauma or surgery. The prevalence of hyposplenism in sickle cell disease is high due to autosplenectomy.

title: Hyposplenism/splenectomy – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Common causes of hyposplenism in children include sickle cell disease leading to autosplenectomy, thalassaemia, coeliac disease, and post-splenectomy status following trauma or haematological malignancy.

title: Hyposplenism/splenectomy – Pathophysiology
content: Loss of splenic function impairs clearance of encapsulated bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b, and Neisseria meningitidis, increasing risk of severe infections. There is also reduced opsonisation and impaired antibody production.

title: Hyposplenism/splenectomy – Clinical features: Fever
content: Children with hyposplenism or splenectomy are at increased risk of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI), which commonly presents with sudden onset fever and rapid clinical deterioration.

title: Hyposplenism/splenectomy – Clinical features: Abdominal pain
content: Post-splenectomy children may present with acute abdominal pain due to complications such as splenic remnant infarction or infection.

title: Hyposplenism/splenectomy – Investigations
content: Blood film may show Howell-Jolly bodies, target cells, and thrombocytosis. Immunological tests include pneumococcal antibody titres. Imaging may be used to confirm absence of splenic tissue post-splenectomy.

title: Hyposplenism/splenectomy – Management
content: Management includes lifelong prophylactic oral penicillin V (250 mg twice daily for children aged 5 years and older; 125 mg twice daily for younger children), vaccination against pneumococcus (PCV13 and PPSV23), Haemophilus influenzae type b, meningococcus (MenACWY and MenB), and annual influenza vaccination. Parents should be educated on seeking urgent medical attention for fever.

title: Hyposplenism/splenectomy – Complications
content: The major complication is overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI), a rapidly progressive sepsis with high mortality caused by encapsulated organisms, especially Streptococcus pneumoniae.

title: Hyposplenism/splenectomy – Prognosis
content: With appropriate vaccination, antibiotic prophylaxis, and education, children with hyposplenism or splenectomy have a significantly reduced risk of severe infection and good long-term prognosis.

title: Idiopathic arthritis – Definition
content: Idiopathic arthritis in paediatrics, also known as juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA), is a heterogeneous group of autoimmune disorders characterised by persistent arthritis of unknown cause lasting for at least 6 weeks in children under 16 years of age.

title: Idiopathic arthritis – Epidemiology
content: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis affects approximately 1 in 1,000 children in the UK, with a slight female predominance. The peak age of onset is between 1 and 3 years, but it can present at any age before 16 years.

title: Idiopathic arthritis – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: The exact cause of juvenile idiopathic arthritis is unknown, but it is believed to involve a combination of genetic predisposition (e.g., HLA-DRB1 alleles) and environmental triggers such as infections.

title: Idiopathic arthritis – Pathophysiology
content: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis is characterised by chronic synovial inflammation due to autoimmune mechanisms, leading to synovial hypertrophy, joint effusion, cartilage destruction, and potential joint deformity.

title: Idiopathic arthritis – Clinical features: Acute joint pain/swelling
content: Children with juvenile idiopathic arthritis typically present with persistent joint swelling, pain, and stiffness lasting more than 6 weeks, often affecting the knees, wrists, and ankles; morning stiffness is common.

title: Idiopathic arthritis – Clinical features: Fever
content: Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis may present with quotidian high spiking fevers often exceeding 39°C, accompanied by a salmon-pink macular rash, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and serositis.

title: Idiopathic arthritis – Investigations
content: Investigations include raised inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP), normocytic anaemia, thrombocytosis, and negative rheumatoid factor in most cases; ANA positivity is common in oligoarticular JIA. Joint ultrasound or MRI may show synovitis.

title: Idiopathic arthritis – Differential diagnosis
content: Differential diagnoses include septic arthritis, reactive arthritis, haemarthrosis, malignancy (e.g., leukaemia), and other connective tissue diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus.

title: Idiopathic arthritis – Management
content: Management includes NSAIDs such as naproxen 10-15 mg/kg/day in divided doses, intra-articular corticosteroid injections, and disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) like methotrexate 10-15 mg/m2 weekly. Biologic agents (e.g., etanercept) are used for refractory cases. Regular physiotherapy is essential.

title: Idiopathic arthritis – Complications
content: Complications include joint damage and deformity, growth disturbances, uveitis (especially in ANA-positive oligoarticular JIA), and macrophage activation syndrome in systemic JIA.

title: Idiopathic arthritis – Prognosis
content: Prognosis varies by subtype; oligoarticular JIA often has a good prognosis with remission in 50-70% of cases, whereas polyarticular and systemic forms may have a more chronic course with persistent disability.

title: Impetigo – Definition
content: Impetigo is a common, superficial bacterial skin infection primarily affecting children, characterised by honey-coloured crusted lesions typically around the nose and mouth.

title: Impetigo – Epidemiology
content: Impetigo is most common in children aged 2 to 5 years, with higher incidence in summer months and in areas of overcrowding or poor hygiene.

title: Impetigo – Aetiology and Risk factors
content: Impetigo is caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes infection of superficial skin; risk factors include minor skin trauma, insect bites, eczema, and close contact with infected individuals.

title: Impetigo – Pathophysiology
content: Bacterial colonisation of superficial epidermis leads to localised skin inflammation, vesicle formation, rupture, and characteristic honey-coloured crusting; exfoliative toxins from S. aureus may cause bullous impetigo.

title: Impetigo – Clinical features: Non-bullous impetigo
content: Presents with erythematous macules progressing to vesicles and pustules that rupture to form characteristic thick, honey-coloured crusts, commonly around the nose and mouth.

title: Impetigo – Clinical features: Bullous impetigo
content: Characterised by fragile, fluid-filled bullae that rupture easily leaving a thin brown crust, often caused by exfoliative toxin-producing Staphylococcus aureus.

title: Impetigo – Investigations
content: Diagnosis is clinical; bacterial swab for culture and sensitivity may be taken if lesions are extensive, recurrent, or not responding to treatment.

title: Impetigo – Management: Topical antibiotics
content: Mild cases are treated with topical fusidic acid 2% ointment applied three times daily for 5 days.

title: Impetigo – Management: Systemic antibiotics
content: Extensive or bullous impetigo requires oral antibiotics such as flucloxacillin 25-50 mg/kg/day divided into 4 doses for 7 days; erythromycin 30-50 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses is an alternative if penicillin allergy is present.

title: Impetigo – Management: Supportive care
content: Advise good hygiene, regular handwashing, and keeping nails short to reduce spread; lesions should be gently cleaned with soap and water.

title: Impetigo – Complications
content: Potential complications include cellulitis, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, and rarely, bacteraemia or scarring.

title: Impetigo – Prognosis
content: With appropriate treatment, impetigo usually resolves within 7-10 days without scarring; recurrence is common if hygiene measures are not maintained.

title: Inflammatory bowel disease – Definition
content: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) in paediatrics refers to a group of chronic inflammatory conditions of the gastrointestinal tract, primarily including Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, characterised by relapsing and remitting inflammation leading to symptoms such as diarrhoea, abdominal pain, and growth failure.

title: Inflammatory bowel disease – Epidemiology
content: The incidence of paediatric inflammatory bowel disease in the UK is approximately 5.2 per 100,000 children per year, with a rising trend especially in children under 10 years old. It affects males and females equally and is more common in Caucasian populations.

title: Inflammatory bowel disease – Aetiology and risk factors
content: Paediatric IBD aetiology is multifactorial involving genetic predisposition (e.g., NOD2 mutations), environmental factors such as smoking exposure, diet, and alterations in gut microbiota, as well as immune dysregulation leading to chronic intestinal inflammation.

title: Inflammatory bowel disease – Pathophysiology
content: IBD pathophysiology involves an inappropriate immune response to intestinal microbiota in genetically susceptible children, resulting in chronic mucosal inflammation, epithelial barrier disruption, and tissue damage in the gastrointestinal tract.

title: Inflammatory bowel disease – Clinical features: Diarrhoea
content: Chronic diarrhoea is a common presenting symptom in paediatric IBD, often bloody in ulcerative colitis and may be non-bloody in Crohn's disease, lasting for more than four weeks and associated with urgency and tenesmus.

title: Inflammatory bowel disease – Clinical features: Abdominal pain
content: Children with IBD frequently present with chronic or intermittent abdominal pain, which may be colicky or constant, often localised to the right lower quadrant in Crohn's disease or more diffuse in ulcerative colitis.

title: Inflammatory bowel disease – Clinical features: Growth failure and delayed puberty
content: Growth failure occurs in up to 30% of children with IBD due to chronic inflammation, malnutrition, and corticosteroid use; delayed puberty is also common, requiring regular monitoring of height, weight, and pubertal staging.

title: Inflammatory bowel disease – Clinical features: Extraintestinal manifestations
content: Extraintestinal manifestations in paediatric IBD include arthritis (acute joint pain/swelling), erythema nodosum, uveitis, and primary sclerosing cholangitis, occurring in up to 25% of cases and requiring multidisciplinary management.

title: Inflammatory bowel disease – Investigations: Blood tests
content: Blood tests in paediatric IBD typically show raised inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR), anaemia (often microcytic or normocytic), hypoalbuminaemia, and elevated faecal calprotectin (>250 µg/g) indicating intestinal inflammation.

title: Inflammatory bowel disease – Investigations: Endoscopy and biopsy
content: Definitive diagnosis of paediatric IBD requires ileocolonoscopy with biopsy demonstrating characteristic histological features: transmural inflammation and granulomas in Crohn's disease, and continuous mucosal inflammation in ulcerative colitis.

title: Inflammatory bowel disease – Management: Induction of remission
content: Induction of remission in paediatric IBD commonly involves corticosteroids such as oral prednisolone at 1 mg/kg/day (max 40 mg/day) for 4-6 weeks, with tapering thereafter; exclusive enteral nutrition is an alternative first-line therapy in Crohn's disease.

title: Inflammatory bowel disease – Management: Maintenance therapy
content: Maintenance therapy includes immunomodulators such as azathioprine (2-2.5 mg/kg/day) or methotrexate (15 mg/m2 weekly), and biologics like infliximab (5 mg/kg at 0, 2, and 6 weeks then every 8 weeks) for moderate to severe paediatric IBD.

title: Inflammatory bowel disease – Complications
content: Complications of paediatric IBD include strictures, fistulae, growth retardation, colorectal cancer (rare in children), toxic megacolon, and increased risk of osteoporosis due to chronic inflammation and corticosteroid use.

title: Inflammatory bowel disease – Prognosis
content: Paediatric IBD is a lifelong condition with variable prognosis; early diagnosis and treatment improve growth outcomes and quality of life. Approximately 20-30% of children require surgery within 10 years of diagnosis, especially in Crohn's disease.

title: Influenza – Definition
content: Influenza is an acute viral respiratory infection caused by influenza viruses A and B, characterised by sudden onset of fever, cough, and systemic symptoms.

title: Influenza – Epidemiology
content: Influenza affects all age groups but is particularly common in children under 5 years in the UK, with seasonal epidemics occurring mainly in winter months (December to March).

title: Influenza – Aetiology and Risk factors
content: Influenza is caused by influenza A and B viruses transmitted via respiratory droplets; risk factors in children include age under 5 years, chronic respiratory disease, immunosuppression, and lack of vaccination.

title: Influenza – Pathophysiology
content: Influenza virus infects respiratory epithelial cells causing cell death and inflammation, leading to airway epithelial damage, increased mucus production, and systemic cytokine release responsible for fever and malaise.

title: Influenza – Clinical features: Fever
content: Children with influenza typically present with sudden onset high fever, often >38.5°C, lasting 3-4 days.

title: Influenza – Clinical features: Cough and respiratory symptoms
content: A dry cough and sore throat are common in paediatric influenza, often accompanied by nasal congestion and rhinorrhoea.

title: Influenza – Clinical features: Systemic symptoms
content: Children often experience myalgia, headache, lethargy, and anorexia during influenza infection.

title: Influenza – Investigations
content: Diagnosis is primarily clinical; nasopharyngeal swab PCR testing confirms influenza virus; blood tests are usually not required unless complications suspected.

title: Influenza – Management
content: Supportive care includes hydration and antipyretics such as paracetamol (15 mg/kg every 4-6 hours, max 60 mg/kg/day) or ibuprofen (10 mg/kg every 6-8 hours, max 30 mg/kg/day). Oseltamivir is recommended for children at high risk or with severe disease at 3 mg/kg twice daily for 5 days.

title: Influenza – Complications
content: Complications include secondary bacterial pneumonia, otitis media, febrile seizures, and exacerbation of asthma or chronic respiratory disease.

title: Influenza – Prognosis
content: Most children recover fully within 1-2 weeks without sequelae; prognosis is excellent in healthy children but worse in those with comorbidities.

title: Intestinal obstruction and ileus – Definition
content: Intestinal obstruction is a blockage that prevents the normal passage of intestinal contents, while ileus is a functional impairment of intestinal motility without mechanical obstruction, both causing abdominal distension and vomiting in paediatric patients.

title: Intestinal obstruction and ileus – Epidemiology
content: Intestinal obstruction is a common surgical emergency in paediatrics, with causes varying by age; neonatal causes include atresia and malrotation, while older children commonly present with intussusception or adhesions. Ileus is frequently seen postoperatively or with systemic illness.

title: Intestinal obstruction and ileus – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Common causes of paediatric intestinal obstruction include congenital anomalies (e.g. atresia, malrotation with volvulus), intussusception, Hirschsprung disease, and postoperative adhesions; ileus risk factors include abdominal surgery, peritonitis, electrolyte imbalances, and certain medications.

title: Intestinal obstruction and ileus – Pathophysiology
content: Mechanical intestinal obstruction causes proximal bowel dilation, increased intraluminal pressure, and impaired venous return leading to bowel wall oedema and ischaemia; ileus results from disruption of normal enteric nervous system signalling causing decreased peristalsis without physical blockage.

title: Intestinal obstruction and ileus – Clinical features: Vomiting
content: Vomiting is an early and common symptom of intestinal obstruction in children; bilious vomiting suggests distal obstruction and requires urgent assessment.

title: Intestinal obstruction and ileus – Clinical features: Abdominal distension
content: Abdominal distension is a key clinical sign in paediatric intestinal obstruction and ileus, often progressive and associated with tympanic bowel loops on palpation.

title: Intestinal obstruction and ileus – Clinical features: Abdominal pain
content: Acute colicky abdominal pain is typical in mechanical intestinal obstruction due to intermittent peristalsis against the blockage; ileus usually causes less severe, diffuse discomfort.

title: Intestinal obstruction and ileus – Clinical features: Constipation and failure to pass flatus
content: In intestinal obstruction, children often present with constipation and failure to pass flatus, indicating distal bowel blockage.

title: Intestinal obstruction and ileus – Investigations: Abdominal X-ray
content: Abdominal X-ray in paediatric intestinal obstruction typically shows dilated bowel loops with air-fluid levels and absence of gas distal to the obstruction; in ileus, diffuse bowel dilation without a transition point is seen.

title: Intestinal obstruction and ileus – Investigations: Ultrasound
content: Ultrasound is useful in paediatric intestinal obstruction to identify intussusception, assess bowel viability, and detect free fluid; it is non-invasive and preferred in children.

title: Intestinal obstruction and ileus – Management: Initial resuscitation
content: Initial management includes fluid resuscitation with isotonic crystalloid (e.g. 0.9% saline), correction of electrolyte imbalances, nasogastric decompression, and nil by mouth status in paediatric intestinal obstruction and ileus.

title: Intestinal obstruction and ileus – Management: Surgical intervention
content: Surgical intervention is indicated in paediatric intestinal obstruction caused by volvulus, atresia, or failed conservative management; timing depends on clinical stability and risk of bowel ischaemia.

title: Intestinal obstruction and ileus – Complications
content: Complications include bowel ischaemia, perforation, peritonitis, sepsis, electrolyte disturbances, and shock, which can be life-threatening in paediatric intestinal obstruction and ileus.

title: Intestinal obstruction and ileus – Prognosis
content: Prognosis depends on cause, timeliness of diagnosis, and treatment; early intervention in mechanical obstruction generally results in good outcomes, whereas delayed treatment increases morbidity and mortality.

title: Intussusception – Definition
content: Intussusception is a condition where a segment of the intestine telescopes into an adjacent distal segment, causing bowel obstruction and potential ischaemia.

title: Intussusception – Epidemiology
content: Intussusception is the most common cause of intestinal obstruction in children aged 6 months to 3 years, with an incidence of approximately 1 to 4 per 1,000 live births in the UK.

title: Intussusception – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Most cases of intussusception in infants are idiopathic; however, risk factors include viral infections such as adenovirus, Meckel's diverticulum, polyps, and lymphoid hyperplasia.

title: Intussusception – Pathophysiology
content: Telescoping of the proximal bowel segment into the distal bowel causes venous congestion, bowel wall oedema, and can progress to ischaemia, necrosis, and perforation if untreated.

title: Intussusception – Clinical features: Acute abdominal pain
content: Children typically present with sudden onset intermittent severe colicky abdominal pain, often causing the child to draw their knees up and cry inconsolably.

title: Intussusception – Clinical features: Vomiting
content: Vomiting is a common symptom and may initially be non-bilious but can progress to bilious vomiting as obstruction worsens.

title: Intussusception – Clinical features: Red currant jelly stools
content: A classic late sign is the passage of red currant jelly stools, caused by intestinal mucosal sloughing and blood mixing with mucus.

title: Intussusception – Clinical features: Abdominal mass
content: A palpable, sausage-shaped, tender abdominal mass is often felt in the right upper quadrant or epigastrium during physical examination.

title: Intussusception – Investigations: Ultrasound
content: Abdominal ultrasound is the diagnostic investigation of choice, showing the characteristic 'target' or 'doughnut' sign representing the intussuscepted bowel.

title: Intussusception – Investigations: Contrast enema
content: A therapeutic and diagnostic air or contrast (barium) enema can confirm intussusception and may reduce it by hydrostatic pressure; success rates are approximately 75-90%.

title: Intussusception – Management: Initial resuscitation
content: Initial management includes fluid resuscitation with isotonic saline to correct dehydration and electrolyte imbalances, and nasogastric decompression if vomiting is severe.

title: Intussusception – Management: Non-surgical reduction
content: Non-surgical reduction using pneumatic (air) or hydrostatic (contrast) enema under fluoroscopic or ultrasound guidance is first-line treatment in stable patients without signs of perforation.

title: Intussusception – Management: Surgical treatment
content: Surgical intervention is required if non-surgical reduction fails, if there is evidence of bowel perforation or peritonitis, or if the patient is unstable; surgery involves manual reduction or bowel resection.

title: Intussusception – Complications
content: Complications include bowel necrosis, perforation, peritonitis, sepsis, and recurrence of intussusception which occurs in approximately 10% of cases after successful reduction.

title: Intussusception – Prognosis
content: With prompt diagnosis and treatment, prognosis is excellent with low mortality; delayed treatment increases risk of bowel necrosis and mortality.

title: Leukaemia – Definition
content: Leukaemia is a malignant neoplasm of haematopoietic stem cells characterised by uncontrolled proliferation of abnormal white blood cells in the bone marrow and peripheral blood.

title: Leukaemia – Epidemiology
content: Leukaemia is the most common childhood cancer in the UK, accounting for approximately 30% of all paediatric malignancies, with an incidence of around 4 per 100,000 children per year.

title: Leukaemia – Aetiology and Risk Factors
content: Risk factors for paediatric leukaemia include genetic conditions such as Down syndrome, exposure to ionising radiation, previous chemotherapy, and certain inherited bone marrow failure syndromes.

title: Leukaemia – Pathophysiology
content: Leukaemia arises from clonal proliferation of immature lymphoid or myeloid precursors in the bone marrow, leading to marrow failure and infiltration of other organs.

title: Leukaemia – Clinical features: Pallor
content: Pallor is a common presenting feature due to anaemia caused by marrow infiltration and reduced red cell production.

title: Leukaemia – Clinical features: Bruising
content: Bruising and petechiae occur due to thrombocytopenia from bone marrow failure.

title: Leukaemia – Clinical features: Fever
content: Fever is frequently present due to neutropenia and increased susceptibility to infection.

title: Leukaemia – Clinical features: Lymphadenopathy
content: Lymphadenopathy may be present due to infiltration of lymph nodes by leukaemic cells.

title: Leukaemia – Clinical features: Abdominal mass
content: An abdominal mass may be palpable due to hepatosplenomegaly from leukaemic infiltration.

title: Leukaemia – Investigations: Full blood count
content: Full blood count typically shows anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and variable white cell count with presence of blasts in peripheral blood.

title: Leukaemia – Investigations: Bone marrow biopsy
content: Bone marrow biopsy confirms diagnosis by demonstrating >20% blasts in marrow aspirate or biopsy sample.

title: Leukaemia – Management: Chemotherapy
content: Treatment involves multi-agent chemotherapy protocols such as the UKALL regimen, including induction with vincristine, corticosteroids (prednisolone 60 mg/m2/day), and asparaginase, followed by consolidation and maintenance phases.

title: Leukaemia – Management: Supportive care
content: Supportive care includes transfusions for anaemia and thrombocytopenia, antimicrobial prophylaxis, and management of tumour lysis syndrome with hydration and allopurinol.

title: Leukaemia – Complications: Infection
content: Neutropenia during treatment increases risk of severe infections including sepsis, requiring prompt antibiotic therapy.

title: Leukaemia – Complications: Tumour lysis syndrome
content: Tumour lysis syndrome can cause hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hypocalcaemia, and acute kidney injury, typically within 48 hours of chemotherapy initiation.

title: Leukaemia – Prognosis
content: The 5-year survival rate for paediatric acute lymphoblastic leukaemia in the UK exceeds 90% with current treatment protocols.

title: Lymphoma – Definition
content: Lymphoma is a malignant neoplasm of lymphoid tissue characterised by the clonal proliferation of lymphocytes. It is broadly classified into Hodgkin lymphoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma, both of which can occur in paediatric patients.

title: Lymphoma – Epidemiology
content: Lymphoma is the third most common paediatric malignancy after leukaemia and brain tumours, accounting for approximately 10-15% of childhood cancers in the UK. Hodgkin lymphoma peaks in adolescence, while non-Hodgkin lymphoma is more common in younger children.

title: Lymphoma – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Risk factors for paediatric lymphoma include immunodeficiency states (e.g. HIV infection, post-transplant immunosuppression), Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection, family history of lymphoma, and certain genetic syndromes such as ataxia-telangiectasia.

title: Lymphoma – Pathophysiology
content: Lymphoma arises from malignant transformation of lymphocytes, leading to uncontrolled proliferation and accumulation in lymph nodes and extranodal sites. Hodgkin lymphoma is characterised by Reed-Sternberg cells, while non-Hodgkin lymphoma includes diverse subtypes such as Burkitt lymphoma and lymphoblastic lymphoma.

title: Lymphoma – Clinical features: Lymphadenopathy
content: The most common presentation of paediatric lymphoma is painless, firm lymphadenopathy, often cervical or supraclavicular. Nodes may be rubbery and non-tender, and persist for more than 2 weeks.

title: Lymphoma – Clinical features: Fever
content: B symptoms including unexplained fever >38°C lasting more than 1 week are common in paediatric lymphoma and indicate systemic involvement.

title: Lymphoma – Clinical features: Abdominal mass
content: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma in children often presents with an abdominal mass due to involvement of mesenteric or retroperitoneal lymph nodes or extranodal sites such as the bowel.

title: Lymphoma – Clinical features: Breathlessness
content: Mediastinal lymphadenopathy in paediatric lymphoma can cause compression of airways or large vessels, leading to breathlessness and superior vena cava syndrome.

title: Lymphoma – Investigations
content: Diagnosis of paediatric lymphoma involves excisional lymph node biopsy for histopathology and immunophenotyping. Staging includes chest X-ray, CT scan of chest, abdomen and pelvis, and bone marrow biopsy. LDH is often elevated and can be used as a tumour marker.

title: Lymphoma – Management
content: Treatment of paediatric lymphoma depends on subtype and stage. Hodgkin lymphoma is treated with combination chemotherapy (e.g. ABVD regimen: doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine, dacarbazine) and sometimes radiotherapy. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma requires intensive multi-agent chemotherapy protocols such as the UK Children's Cancer Study Group regimens.

title: Lymphoma – Complications
content: Complications of paediatric lymphoma and its treatment include tumour lysis syndrome, infection due to immunosuppression, secondary malignancies, and long-term effects such as cardiotoxicity from anthracyclines and infertility.

title: Lymphoma – Prognosis
content: Paediatric lymphoma generally has a favourable prognosis with current treatment, with 5-year survival rates exceeding 85% for Hodgkin lymphoma and 70-90% for non-Hodgkin lymphoma depending on subtype and stage.

title: Malaria – Definition
content: Malaria is a parasitic infection caused by Plasmodium species, transmitted by the bite of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes, leading to cyclical febrile illness primarily affecting red blood cells.

title: Malaria – Epidemiology
content: Malaria is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions, with the highest burden in sub-Saharan Africa; children under 5 years are most at risk of severe disease and mortality.

title: Malaria – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Risk factors for paediatric malaria include living in or travelling to endemic areas, lack of insecticide-treated bed nets, poor socioeconomic status, and absence of prior immunity.

title: Malaria – Pathophysiology
content: Plasmodium parasites invade hepatocytes and then erythrocytes, causing haemolysis and microvascular obstruction, leading to anaemia, hypoxia, and organ dysfunction.

title: Malaria – Clinical features: Fever
content: Children with malaria typically present with intermittent fever, often with a cyclical pattern every 48–72 hours depending on Plasmodium species.

title: Malaria – Clinical features: Anaemia and pallor
content: Haemolysis of infected red blood cells causes anaemia, presenting as pallor and fatigue in paediatric patients with malaria.

title: Malaria – Clinical features: Jaundice
content: Severe malaria may cause jaundice due to haemolysis and hepatic dysfunction, evident as yellowing of the sclera and skin.

title: Malaria – Clinical features: Fits/seizures
content: Cerebral malaria can present with neurological symptoms including seizures, altered consciousness, and coma in children.

title: Malaria – Investigations: Blood film microscopy
content: Definitive diagnosis is by thick and thin blood film microscopy demonstrating Plasmodium parasites; species identification guides treatment.

title: Malaria – Investigations: Rapid diagnostic tests
content: Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) detect Plasmodium antigens and provide quick diagnosis when microscopy is unavailable.

title: Malaria – Management: Uncomplicated malaria
content: First-line treatment for uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria in children is artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT), e.g., artemether-lumefantrine dosed by weight for 3 days.

title: Malaria – Management: Severe malaria
content: Severe malaria requires intravenous artesunate 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, and 24 hours, then daily until oral therapy is possible; supportive care includes fluid management and treatment of complications.

title: Malaria – Complications
content: Complications of paediatric malaria include cerebral malaria, severe anaemia, hypoglycaemia, metabolic acidosis, acute kidney injury, and respiratory distress.

title: Malaria – Prognosis
content: With prompt diagnosis and treatment, prognosis is good; however, cerebral malaria and severe anaemia carry significant mortality risk, especially in children under 5 years.

title: Measles – Definition
content: Measles is a highly contagious viral infection caused by the measles virus, characterised by fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, and a characteristic maculopapular rash.

title: Measles – Epidemiology
content: Measles primarily affects children under 5 years old in the UK, with outbreaks occurring mainly in unvaccinated populations. The incidence has decreased significantly due to the MMR vaccine, but sporadic cases and outbreaks still occur.

title: Measles – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Measles is caused by the measles virus, transmitted via respiratory droplets. Risk factors include lack of vaccination with MMR, immunodeficiency, and close contact with infected individuals.

title: Measles – Pathophysiology
content: The measles virus infects respiratory epithelial cells, then spreads via lymphatics causing viremia. It leads to immune suppression and characteristic epithelial damage causing rash and Koplik spots.

title: Measles – Clinical features: Fever
content: High fever typically begins 3-5 days after exposure, often exceeding 39°C and lasting 4-7 days.

title: Measles – Clinical features: Cough
content: A dry, hacking cough is common during the prodromal phase and may persist throughout the illness.

title: Measles – Clinical features: Coryza
content: Nasal congestion and runny nose (coryza) occur early in the illness, contributing to respiratory symptoms.

title: Measles – Clinical features: Conjunctivitis
content: Bilateral conjunctivitis with photophobia and watery eyes is common during the prodromal phase.

title: Measles – Clinical features: Koplik spots
content: Koplik spots are small, white lesions on the buccal mucosa opposite the molars, appearing 1-2 days before rash onset and lasting 1-3 days.

title: Measles – Clinical features: Rash
content: A maculopapular rash appears 3-5 days after prodrome onset, starting at the hairline and spreading cephalocaudally and centrifugally, lasting 5-6 days.

title: Measles – Investigations
content: Diagnosis is clinical but can be confirmed by detection of measles-specific IgM antibodies in serum or by PCR testing of throat swabs or urine.

title: Measles – Management
content: Management is supportive: ensure adequate hydration, antipyretics such as paracetamol or ibuprofen for fever and discomfort. Vitamin A supplementation (200,000 IU orally on diagnosis and the next day for children >12 months) reduces morbidity and mortality.

title: Measles – Complications
content: Complications include otitis media (7-9%), pneumonia (1-6%), diarrhoea, encephalitis (1 in 1000 cases), and subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (rare, delayed).

title: Measles – Prognosis
content: Prognosis is generally good in immunocompetent children with supportive care; mortality is rare in the UK but higher in malnourished or immunocompromised children.

title: Migraine – Definition
content: Migraine in paediatrics is a primary headache disorder characterised by recurrent episodes of moderate to severe headache, often unilateral, pulsating in nature, lasting 1 to 72 hours, and associated with nausea, vomiting, photophobia, and phonophobia.

title: Migraine – Epidemiology
content: Migraine affects approximately 10% of children and adolescents in the UK, with prevalence increasing with age; it is more common in females after puberty.

title: Migraine – Aetiology and Risk factors
content: Common triggers for paediatric migraine include stress, sleep deprivation, certain foods (e.g. chocolate, caffeine), dehydration, and hormonal changes; family history is a significant risk factor.

title: Migraine – Pathophysiology
content: Paediatric migraine pathophysiology involves neuronal hyperexcitability, cortical spreading depression, and activation of the trigeminovascular system causing release of vasoactive neuropeptides leading to inflammation and pain.

title: Migraine – Clinical features: Headache
content: Paediatric migraine headache is typically moderate to severe, unilateral or bilateral, pulsating, worsened by physical activity, lasting 1 to 72 hours.

title: Migraine – Clinical features: Associated symptoms
content: Associated symptoms in paediatric migraine include nausea (up to 80%), vomiting (up to 50%), photophobia, phonophobia, and occasionally aura such as visual disturbances lasting less than 60 minutes.

title: Migraine – Investigations
content: Diagnosis of paediatric migraine is clinical; neuroimaging (MRI) is reserved for atypical features such as abnormal neurological signs, sudden onset, or progressive symptoms.

title: Migraine – Management: Acute treatment
content: First-line acute treatment for paediatric migraine includes weight-based dosing of ibuprofen (10 mg/kg per dose) or paracetamol (15 mg/kg per dose) given early in the headache; antiemetics such as domperidone may be used if vomiting occurs.

title: Migraine – Management: Preventive treatment
content: Preventive treatment is considered if migraines occur more than 4 times per month or significantly impair quality of life; options include propranolol starting at 0.5 mg/kg/day up to 2 mg/kg/day, or topiramate 1–3 mg/kg/day, under specialist supervision.

title: Migraine – Complications
content: Complications of paediatric migraine include chronic migraine (headache on 15 or more days per month for over 3 months) and medication overuse headache from frequent analgesic use.

title: Migraine – Prognosis
content: Paediatric migraine often improves with age; approximately 50% of children experience significant reduction or resolution of symptoms by late adolescence.

title: Mumps – Definition
content: Mumps is an acute viral infection caused by the mumps virus, a paramyxovirus, primarily affecting the salivary glands, especially the parotid glands, leading to painful swelling.

title: Mumps – Epidemiology
content: Mumps incidence has declined significantly in the UK due to the MMR vaccine; however, outbreaks still occur, particularly in unvaccinated children and adolescents.

title: Mumps – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Mumps is caused by the mumps virus transmitted via respiratory droplets or direct contact with saliva; risk factors include lack of MMR vaccination and close contact in school or household settings.

title: Mumps – Pathophysiology
content: The mumps virus infects the respiratory epithelium, then spreads via the bloodstream to the salivary glands causing inflammation and swelling, predominantly affecting the parotid glands.

title: Mumps – Clinical features: Fever
content: Fever is a common early symptom in mumps, typically low-grade to moderate, occurring 1-2 days before parotid swelling.

title: Mumps – Clinical features: Parotid gland swelling
content: Painful unilateral or bilateral parotid gland swelling occurs 16-18 days after exposure, lasting 7-10 days, causing characteristic facial swelling below and in front of the ears.

title: Mumps – Clinical features: Lymphadenopathy
content: Tender regional lymphadenopathy, particularly of the submandibular and cervical nodes, may accompany parotid swelling.

title: Mumps – Clinical features: Orchitis
content: Orchitis occurs in approximately 20-30% of post-pubertal males with mumps, presenting with unilateral testicular pain and swelling typically 4-8 days after parotitis onset.

title: Mumps – Clinical features: Meningitis
content: Aseptic meningitis occurs in up to 10% of mumps cases, presenting with headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, and vomiting, usually within the first week of illness.

title: Mumps – Investigations
content: Diagnosis is clinical but can be confirmed by detecting mumps-specific IgM antibodies in serum or mumps RNA by PCR from saliva or cerebrospinal fluid; full blood count may show lymphocytosis.

title: Mumps – Management
content: Management of mumps is supportive: analgesia with paracetamol or ibuprofen, adequate hydration, and isolation for 5 days after parotid swelling onset to reduce transmission; no specific antiviral treatment is available.

title: Mumps – Complications
