content: Complications include orchitis, oophoritis, aseptic meningitis, pancreatitis, hearing loss, and rarely encephalitis; orchitis can lead to testicular atrophy and infertility in post-pubertal males.

title: Mumps – Prognosis
content: The prognosis for mumps in children is generally excellent with full recovery; complications are uncommon, and mortality is rare in the UK with appropriate supportive care.

title: Obstructive sleep apnoea – Definition
content: Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) in paediatrics is characterised by repeated episodes of partial or complete upper airway obstruction during sleep, leading to disrupted sleep patterns and intermittent hypoxia.

title: Obstructive sleep apnoea – Epidemiology
content: Paediatric obstructive sleep apnoea affects approximately 1-5% of children aged 2 to 8 years, with peak incidence between 2 and 6 years, often related to adenotonsillar hypertrophy.

title: Obstructive sleep apnoea – Aetiology and risk factors
content: Common risk factors for paediatric OSA include adenotonsillar hypertrophy, obesity, craniofacial abnormalities (e.g., micrognathia), neuromuscular disorders, and Down syndrome.

title: Obstructive sleep apnoea – Pathophysiology
content: In paediatric OSA, upper airway obstruction during sleep results from adenotonsillar hypertrophy causing airway narrowing, leading to intermittent hypoxia, hypercapnia, and sleep fragmentation.

title: Obstructive sleep apnoea – Clinical features: nocturnal symptoms
content: Children with OSA commonly present with habitual loud snoring (≥3 nights/week), witnessed apnoeas, restless sleep, and nocturnal sweating.

title: Obstructive sleep apnoea – Clinical features: daytime symptoms
content: Daytime features of paediatric OSA include behavioural difficulties, hyperactivity, poor concentration, and excessive daytime sleepiness.

title: Obstructive sleep apnoea – Investigations
content: The gold standard investigation for paediatric OSA is overnight polysomnography, which measures apnoea-hypopnoea index (AHI); an AHI >1 event/hour is diagnostic in children.

title: Obstructive sleep apnoea – Management: first-line treatment
content: First-line treatment for paediatric OSA is adenotonsillectomy, especially in children with adenotonsillar hypertrophy; surgery improves symptoms in approximately 80% of cases.

title: Obstructive sleep apnoea – Management: medical therapy
content: Intranasal corticosteroids (e.g., mometasone 100 mcg once daily) and montelukast may be used in mild paediatric OSA or when surgery is contraindicated.

title: Obstructive sleep apnoea – Management: continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP)
content: CPAP therapy is indicated for children with persistent OSA after adenotonsillectomy or those unsuitable for surgery; pressure settings are titrated during sleep studies.

title: Obstructive sleep apnoea – Complications
content: Untreated paediatric OSA can lead to cardiovascular complications (e.g., pulmonary hypertension), growth failure, behavioural problems, and neurocognitive impairment.

title: Obstructive sleep apnoea – Prognosis
content: With appropriate treatment, most children with OSA have an excellent prognosis; however, residual symptoms may persist in obese children or those with craniofacial anomalies.

title: Otitis media – Definition
content: Otitis media is an inflammation or infection of the middle ear, commonly occurring in children aged 6 months to 3 years, characterised by ear pain, fever, and sometimes hearing loss.

title: Otitis media – Epidemiology
content: Otitis media affects up to 80% of children by the age of 3 years in the UK, making it one of the most common paediatric infections.

title: Otitis media – Aetiology and risk factors
content: Common causative organisms include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis; risk factors include young age, attendance at daycare, exposure to tobacco smoke, and recent upper respiratory tract infection.

title: Otitis media – Pathophysiology
content: Eustachian tube dysfunction leads to fluid accumulation in the middle ear, creating an environment for bacterial or viral infection and inflammation.

title: Otitis media – Clinical features: Fever
content: Children with otitis media commonly present with a fever, often ranging from 38°C to 39°C.

title: Otitis media – Clinical features: Ear pain
content: Otalgia is a hallmark symptom of otitis media, often described as moderate to severe ear pain, which may cause irritability or crying in young children.

title: Otitis media – Clinical features: Hearing loss
content: Temporary conductive hearing loss may occur due to middle ear effusion in otitis media, potentially affecting speech development if recurrent or persistent.

title: Otitis media – Investigations
content: Diagnosis is primarily clinical; otoscopy reveals a bulging, erythematous tympanic membrane with loss of normal landmarks; tympanometry and audiometry may be used in recurrent or chronic cases.

title: Otitis media – Management: Analgesia
content: First-line management includes analgesia with paracetamol (15 mg/kg every 4-6 hours, max 60 mg/kg/day) or ibuprofen (5-10 mg/kg every 6-8 hours, max 40 mg/kg/day) to relieve pain and fever.

title: Otitis media – Management: Antibiotic use
content: Antibiotics are recommended for children under 2 years with bilateral otitis media or those with severe symptoms (moderate/severe otalgia or fever ≥39°C); first-line is amoxicillin 25 mg/kg orally every 8 hours for 5 days.

title: Otitis media – Management: Watchful waiting
content: In children over 2 years with mild symptoms, a watchful waiting approach for 48-72 hours is advised before starting antibiotics, as many cases resolve spontaneously.

title: Otitis media – Complications
content: Potential complications include tympanic membrane perforation, mastoiditis, hearing loss, and rarely intracranial infections such as meningitis or brain abscess.

title: Otitis media – Prognosis
content: Most children recover fully within 3 days with appropriate management; recurrent otitis media may affect hearing and speech development but usually resolves by school age.

title: Pancytopenia – Definition
content: Pancytopenia is defined as a reduction in all three blood cell lines: haemoglobin <11 g/dL, white blood cells <4 x10^9/L, and platelets <150 x10^9/L in paediatric patients.

title: Pancytopenia – Epidemiology
content: Pancytopenia is a rare haematological condition in paediatrics, with an incidence of approximately 2-5 cases per 100,000 children per year in the UK.

title: Pancytopenia – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Common causes of pancytopenia in paediatric patients include aplastic anaemia, leukaemia, myelodysplastic syndromes, infections such as parvovirus B19, and nutritional deficiencies like vitamin B12 or folate deficiency.

title: Pancytopenia – Pathophysiology
content: Pancytopenia results from bone marrow failure or infiltration leading to decreased production of red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets in paediatric patients.

title: Pancytopenia – Clinical features: Pallor
content: Pallor due to anaemia is a common clinical feature in paediatric pancytopenia, often presenting with fatigue and lethargy.

title: Pancytopenia – Clinical features: Bruising
content: Bruising and petechiae occur in paediatric pancytopenia due to thrombocytopenia, with platelet counts often below 50 x10^9/L.

title: Pancytopenia – Clinical features: Fever
content: Fever in paediatric pancytopenia may indicate neutropenia-related infection, with neutrophil counts often <0.5 x10^9/L.

title: Pancytopenia – Investigations
content: Initial investigations for paediatric pancytopenia include a full blood count showing reductions in haemoglobin, white blood cells, and platelets, blood film, reticulocyte count, and bone marrow aspiration and biopsy for definitive diagnosis.

title: Pancytopenia – Management
content: Management of paediatric pancytopenia depends on the underlying cause; supportive care includes transfusions of red cells and platelets, infection prophylaxis with antibiotics, and immunosuppressive therapy such as ciclosporin 3-5 mg/kg/day or bone marrow transplantation in aplastic anaemia.

title: Pancytopenia – Complications
content: Complications of paediatric pancytopenia include severe infections due to neutropenia, bleeding from thrombocytopenia, and heart failure secondary to severe anaemia.

title: Pancytopenia – Prognosis
content: The prognosis of paediatric pancytopenia varies with cause; aplastic anaemia has a 5-year survival of approximately 70% with bone marrow transplantation, while untreated leukaemia has a poor prognosis.

title: Peptic ulcer disease and gastritis – Definition
content: Peptic ulcer disease (PUD) in paediatrics refers to mucosal erosions equal to or greater than 5 mm in the stomach or duodenum, caused by an imbalance between mucosal protective factors and aggressive factors such as gastric acid. Gastritis is inflammation of the gastric mucosa, which may be acute or chronic.

title: Peptic ulcer disease and gastritis – Epidemiology
content: Peptic ulcer disease affects approximately 1-2% of children, with duodenal ulcers more common than gastric ulcers. Helicobacter pylori infection prevalence in UK children is estimated at 5-10%, higher in socioeconomically deprived populations.

title: Peptic ulcer disease and gastritis – Aetiology/Risk factors: Helicobacter pylori infection
content: Helicobacter pylori infection is the leading cause of peptic ulcer disease and chronic gastritis in children, transmitted via oral-oral or faecal-oral routes. Infection prevalence is higher in children from lower socioeconomic backgrounds.

title: Peptic ulcer disease and gastritis – Aetiology/Risk factors: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)
content: Use of NSAIDs such as ibuprofen can cause mucosal injury leading to gastritis and peptic ulcer disease in children by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis, reducing mucosal protection.

title: Peptic ulcer disease and gastritis – Aetiology/Risk factors: Other causes
content: Other causes include stress-related mucosal damage in critically ill children, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (gastrinoma), Crohn’s disease, and rare infections such as cytomegalovirus or fungal gastritis.

title: Peptic ulcer disease and gastritis – Pathophysiology
content: Peptic ulcer disease results from an imbalance between aggressive factors (gastric acid, pepsin, H. pylori, NSAIDs) and mucosal defence mechanisms (mucus, bicarbonate, prostaglandins, mucosal blood flow). Gastritis involves inflammation of the gastric mucosa, which may progress to mucosal erosion and ulceration.

title: Peptic ulcer disease and gastritis – Clinical features: Abdominal pain
content: Children with peptic ulcer disease typically present with epigastric or upper abdominal pain, often described as burning or gnawing, which may be relieved by food or antacids. Pain may be nocturnal or occur several hours after meals.

title: Peptic ulcer disease and gastritis – Clinical features: Vomiting
content: Vomiting may occur in children with peptic ulcer disease or gastritis, sometimes containing blood (haematemesis) if there is mucosal bleeding.

title: Peptic ulcer disease and gastritis – Clinical features: Gastrointestinal bleeding
content: Upper gastrointestinal bleeding may present as haematemesis or melaena in children with peptic ulcer disease, indicating mucosal ulceration and erosion into blood vessels.

title: Peptic ulcer disease and gastritis – Investigations: Helicobacter pylori testing
content: Non-invasive tests for H. pylori include the urea breath test and stool antigen test, both with sensitivity and specificity >90%. Serology is less useful in children due to poor specificity. Endoscopic biopsy with rapid urease test or histology is the gold standard.

title: Peptic ulcer disease and gastritis – Investigations: Endoscopy
content: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy is indicated in children with suspected peptic ulcer disease to visualise ulcers, obtain biopsies for H. pylori, and exclude malignancy or other causes. It allows direct assessment of mucosal damage.

title: Peptic ulcer disease and gastritis – Management: Helicobacter pylori eradication therapy
content: First-line eradication therapy in children includes a 14-day triple therapy regimen: amoxicillin 50 mg/kg/day divided twice daily (max 1 g twice daily), clarithromycin 15 mg/kg/day divided twice daily (max 500 mg twice daily), and a proton pump inhibitor (e.g., omeprazole 1 mg/kg/day divided twice daily, max 40 mg/day).

title: Peptic ulcer disease and gastritis – Management: Acid suppression therapy
content: Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) such as omeprazole (1 mg/kg/day in two divided doses, max 40 mg/day) or H2 receptor antagonists like ranitidine (4-8 mg/kg/day divided twice daily) are used to reduce gastric acid secretion and promote ulcer healing.

title: Peptic ulcer disease and gastritis – Management: Avoidance of NSAIDs and supportive care
content: Discontinuation of NSAIDs and avoidance of irritant foods (spicy, acidic) are advised. Supportive care includes adequate hydration and nutritional support.

title: Peptic ulcer disease and gastritis – Complications
content: Complications include upper gastrointestinal bleeding, perforation, gastric outlet obstruction, and rarely gastric malignancy. In children, bleeding is the most common serious complication requiring urgent management.

title: Peptic ulcer disease and gastritis – Prognosis
content: With appropriate treatment including H. pylori eradication and acid suppression, most children achieve complete healing with low recurrence rates. Untreated ulcers may lead to chronic symptoms and complications.

title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Definition
content: Periorbital cellulitis is an infection of the eyelid and surrounding skin anterior to the orbital septum, whereas orbital cellulitis involves infection of the tissues posterior to the orbital septum, including the fat and muscles within the orbit.

title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Epidemiology
content: Periorbital cellulitis is more common in children under 5 years old, with orbital cellulitis being less common but more severe. The incidence of orbital cellulitis is approximately 3.5 cases per 100,000 children per year in the UK.

title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Common causative organisms include Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA), Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Haemophilus influenzae type b (rare since vaccination). Risk factors include recent upper respiratory tract infection, sinusitis (especially ethmoid), trauma, insect bites, and dacryocystitis.

title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Pathophysiology
content: Infection spreads via contiguous spread from adjacent structures such as the paranasal sinuses or through local trauma. Periorbital cellulitis is limited anterior to the orbital septum, while orbital cellulitis involves the orbit posteriorly, risking complications such as abscess formation and intracranial spread.

title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Clinical features: Fever
content: Children with periorbital or orbital cellulitis commonly present with fever, often above 38°C, indicating systemic infection.

title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Clinical features: Eyelid swelling and erythema
content: Periorbital cellulitis presents with unilateral eyelid swelling, erythema, and tenderness without proptosis or ophthalmoplegia.

title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Clinical features: Proptosis and ophthalmoplegia
content: Orbital cellulitis is characterised by proptosis, painful and restricted eye movements (ophthalmoplegia), decreased visual acuity, and chemosis, indicating involvement of orbital tissues.

title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Investigations: Blood tests
content: Blood tests typically show raised inflammatory markers including C-reactive protein (CRP) and white cell count (WCC). Blood cultures may be positive in severe cases.

title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Investigations: Imaging
content: Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the orbits and sinuses is the imaging modality of choice to differentiate periorbital from orbital cellulitis and to identify abscess formation or sinusitis.

title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Differential diagnosis
content: Differential diagnoses include allergic reaction, insect bite, dacryocystitis, trauma with haematoma, and neoplasms such as rhabdomyosarcoma.

title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Management: Antibiotic therapy
content: Initial management includes intravenous antibiotics targeting common pathogens: intravenous flucloxacillin 50 mg/kg every 6 hours plus ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg once daily. If MRSA is suspected, add intravenous vancomycin dosed according to weight and renal function. Switch to oral antibiotics when clinically improved, typically for a total of 10-14 days.

title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Management: Surgical intervention
content: Surgical drainage is indicated for orbital abscesses, subperiosteal abscesses, or if there is no improvement after 48 hours of intravenous antibiotics. Sinus surgery may be required if sinusitis is the source.

title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Complications
content: Potential complications include subperiosteal or orbital abscess, vision loss, cavernous sinus thrombosis, meningitis, brain abscess, and sepsis.

title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Prognosis
content: With prompt diagnosis and appropriate antibiotic treatment, prognosis is excellent with full recovery. Delayed treatment increases risk of serious complications and permanent visual impairment.

title: Peripheral nerve injuries/palsies – Definition
content: Peripheral nerve injuries or palsies in paediatrics refer to damage or dysfunction of the peripheral nerves resulting in motor, sensory, or autonomic deficits. These injuries can be caused by trauma, compression, or iatrogenic factors affecting nerves outside the central nervous system.

title: Peripheral nerve injuries/palsies – Epidemiology
content: Peripheral nerve injuries in children are relatively uncommon but important causes of motor and sensory deficits. Neonatal brachial plexus palsy occurs in approximately 1-2 per 1000 live births in the UK, often associated with difficult deliveries.

title: Peripheral nerve injuries/palsies – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Common causes of peripheral nerve injuries in paediatrics include birth trauma (e.g., shoulder dystocia causing brachial plexus injury), fractures, penetrating injuries, iatrogenic nerve damage during surgery, and compression neuropathies such as carpal tunnel syndrome.

title: Peripheral nerve injuries/palsies – Pathophysiology
content: Peripheral nerve injury results in disruption of axonal conduction and Wallerian degeneration distal to the site of injury. The degree of injury ranges from neurapraxia (temporary conduction block) to axonotmesis and neurotmesis (complete nerve transection), affecting motor and sensory function.

title: Peripheral nerve injuries/palsies – Clinical features: Motor deficits
content: Peripheral nerve injuries in children commonly present with weakness or paralysis of muscles supplied by the affected nerve. For example, Erb's palsy (upper brachial plexus injury) causes weakness of shoulder abduction, external rotation, and elbow flexion.

title: Peripheral nerve injuries/palsies – Clinical features: Sensory deficits
content: Sensory loss or altered sensation such as numbness or paraesthesia may be present in the distribution of the injured peripheral nerve. For example, median nerve injury can cause sensory loss over the palmar aspect of the thumb, index, middle, and lateral half of the ring finger.

title: Peripheral nerve injuries/palsies – Investigations
content: Diagnosis is primarily clinical but can be supported by nerve conduction studies and electromyography (EMG) to assess the extent and location of nerve injury. Ultrasound or MRI may be used to visualise nerve continuity or compression.

title: Peripheral nerve injuries/palsies – Management
content: Initial management includes physiotherapy to maintain joint mobility and muscle strength. Analgesia with paracetamol or ibuprofen is used for pain. Surgical nerve repair or grafting may be indicated in severe cases or if no recovery occurs after 3-6 months.

title: Peripheral nerve injuries/palsies – Complications
content: Complications include permanent motor and sensory deficits, muscle atrophy, joint contractures, and chronic pain syndromes such as neuropathic pain. Early intervention reduces the risk of long-term disability.

title: Peripheral nerve injuries/palsies – Prognosis
content: Prognosis depends on the severity and type of nerve injury. Neurapraxia often recovers fully within weeks to months. More severe injuries may have incomplete recovery despite surgical intervention. Early diagnosis and rehabilitation improve outcomes.

title: Peritonitis – Definition
content: Peritonitis is inflammation of the peritoneum, the serous membrane lining the abdominal cavity and covering the viscera, often due to infection or chemical irritation.

title: Peritonitis – Epidemiology
content: Peritonitis in paediatrics is most commonly secondary to appendicitis, bowel perforation, or peritoneal dialysis, with higher incidence in neonates and infants due to immature immune response.

title: Peritonitis – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Common causes of paediatric peritonitis include perforated appendicitis, intestinal perforation (e.g. necrotising enterocolitis in neonates), trauma, peritoneal dialysis infection, and intra-abdominal abscess rupture.

title: Peritonitis – Pathophysiology
content: Peritonitis results from bacterial invasion or chemical irritation of the peritoneum causing an inflammatory response with exudate formation, increased vascular permeability, and recruitment of neutrophils leading to pain and systemic illness.

title: Peritonitis – Clinical features: Acute abdominal pain
content: Children with peritonitis typically present with severe, constant abdominal pain that worsens with movement and coughing, often localised initially then becoming generalised.

title: Peritonitis – Clinical features: Fever
content: Fever is a common presenting feature in paediatric peritonitis, often exceeding 38°C, reflecting systemic inflammatory response to infection.

title: Peritonitis – Clinical features: Vomiting
content: Vomiting is frequently observed in paediatric peritonitis due to bowel irritation and ileus.

title: Peritonitis – Clinical features: Dehydration
content: Dehydration may develop secondary to vomiting, fever, and reduced oral intake in children with peritonitis.

title: Peritonitis – Investigations
content: Investigations include blood tests (FBC showing raised WCC, CRP elevated), blood cultures, abdominal ultrasound to detect fluid collections or abscess, and abdominal X-ray to identify free air under diaphragm indicating perforation.

title: Peritonitis – Management
content: Initial management includes fluid resuscitation with isotonic crystalloid (e.g. 20 mL/kg boluses), correction of electrolyte imbalances, analgesia with paracetamol and opioids if required, and empiric intravenous antibiotics such as cefotaxime 50 mg/kg every 8 hours plus metronidazole 7.5 mg/kg every 8 hours. Surgical intervention is often required for source control.

title: Peritonitis – Complications
content: Complications include sepsis, septic shock, abscess formation, adhesions causing bowel obstruction, and multi-organ failure.

title: Peritonitis – Prognosis
content: Prognosis depends on prompt diagnosis and treatment; with early intervention, mortality is low in children, but delayed treatment increases risk of morbidity and mortality.

title: Pyloric stenosis – Definition
content: Pyloric stenosis is a condition characterised by hypertrophy and hyperplasia of the pyloric muscle, leading to gastric outlet obstruction in infants, typically presenting within the first 2 to 8 weeks of life.

title: Pyloric stenosis – Epidemiology
content: Pyloric stenosis occurs in approximately 2 to 4 per 1000 live births in the UK, with a higher incidence in first-born male infants and a male-to-female ratio of about 4:1.

title: Pyloric stenosis – Aetiology and risk factors
content: Risk factors for pyloric stenosis include male sex, first-born status, family history of the condition, exposure to erythromycin in the first two weeks of life, and bottle feeding.

title: Pyloric stenosis – Pathophysiology
content: Hypertrophy and hyperplasia of the circular muscle of the pylorus cause progressive narrowing of the pyloric canal, resulting in gastric outlet obstruction and subsequent projectile non-bilious vomiting.

title: Pyloric stenosis – Clinical features: Vomiting
content: Infants with pyloric stenosis typically present with progressive, projectile, non-bilious vomiting occurring after feeds, usually starting between 2 and 8 weeks of age.

title: Pyloric stenosis – Clinical features: Palpable abdominal mass
content: A palpable, firm, mobile 'olive-shaped' mass is often felt in the right upper quadrant or epigastrium during abdominal examination in infants with pyloric stenosis.

title: Pyloric stenosis – Clinical features: Dehydration
content: Due to persistent vomiting, infants may develop signs of dehydration including dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes, reduced skin turgor, and tachycardia.

title: Pyloric stenosis – Investigations: Ultrasound
content: Abdominal ultrasound is the diagnostic investigation of choice, showing an elongated pyloric canal >17 mm in length and a pyloric muscle thickness >3 mm.

title: Pyloric stenosis – Investigations: Blood tests
content: Blood tests typically reveal hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis due to loss of gastric acid from vomiting.

title: Pyloric stenosis – Differential diagnosis
content: Differential diagnoses include gastro-oesophageal reflux, gastroenteritis, milk protein allergy, intestinal malrotation with volvulus, and other causes of vomiting in infants.

title: Pyloric stenosis – Management: Preoperative care
content: Initial management involves correcting dehydration and electrolyte imbalances with intravenous fluids, typically 0.9% sodium chloride with potassium chloride added once urine output is adequate.

title: Pyloric stenosis – Management: Surgical treatment
content: Definitive treatment is a Ramstedt pyloromyotomy, a surgical procedure that splits the hypertrophied pyloric muscle to relieve obstruction, usually performed once the infant is stable.

title: Pyloric stenosis – Complications
content: Potential complications include persistent vomiting postoperatively, wound infection, mucosal perforation during surgery, and metabolic disturbances if untreated.

title: Pyloric stenosis – Prognosis
content: With timely diagnosis and surgical treatment, prognosis is excellent; most infants recover fully with normal feeding and growth.

title: Reactive arthritis – Definition
content: Reactive arthritis is an aseptic inflammatory arthritis that occurs following an infection, typically affecting children and young adults. It is characterised by the triad of arthritis, conjunctivitis, and urethritis, although not all features are always present.

title: Reactive arthritis – Epidemiology
content: Reactive arthritis is uncommon in the paediatric population but can occur at any age, with a peak incidence in late childhood and adolescence. It is more common in males and is associated with HLA-B27 positivity in approximately 60-80% of cases.

title: Reactive arthritis – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Reactive arthritis in children is typically triggered by a preceding gastrointestinal infection (e.g., Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia, Campylobacter) or genitourinary infection (e.g., Chlamydia trachomatis). The interval between infection and arthritis onset is usually 1-4 weeks.

title: Reactive arthritis – Pathophysiology
content: Reactive arthritis is an autoimmune response triggered by bacterial antigens from a distant infection site. It involves immune complex deposition and T-cell mediated inflammation in joints, entheses, and other tissues, often in genetically predisposed individuals (HLA-B27 positive).

title: Reactive arthritis – Clinical features: Acute joint pain/swelling
content: Children with reactive arthritis typically present with acute onset of asymmetric oligoarthritis, predominantly affecting the lower limb large joints such as knees and ankles. Joint swelling, pain, and limited range of movement are common.

title: Reactive arthritis – Clinical features: Acute rash
content: Some children develop keratoderma blennorrhagicum, a hyperkeratotic rash on the palms and soles, or circinate balanitis, a painless erythematous rash on the glans penis, as part of reactive arthritis.

title: Reactive arthritis – Clinical features: Fever
content: Low-grade fever is common in children with reactive arthritis, often accompanying joint inflammation and systemic symptoms.

title: Reactive arthritis – Clinical features: Conjunctivitis
content: Conjunctivitis occurs in approximately 30-50% of paediatric reactive arthritis cases, presenting as a mild, bilateral, non-purulent inflammation of the conjunctiva.

title: Reactive arthritis – Investigations
content: Investigations include raised inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR), sterile joint aspirate with elevated white cells, negative bacterial cultures, HLA-B27 testing, and evidence of preceding infection via stool cultures or urethral swabs. Imaging may show joint effusion and enthesitis.

title: Reactive arthritis – Management
content: Management includes NSAIDs such as ibuprofen 20-30 mg/kg/day divided into 3-4 doses for symptom relief. Intra-articular corticosteroids may be used for persistent monoarthritis. Antibiotics are indicated only if active infection is present. Physical therapy supports joint function.

title: Reactive arthritis – Complications
content: Chronic arthritis may develop in a minority of children, leading to joint damage and functional impairment. Rare complications include uveitis and secondary amyloidosis.

title: Reactive arthritis – Prognosis
content: The prognosis in paediatric reactive arthritis is generally good, with most children experiencing resolution within 6 months. Approximately 15-20% may develop chronic symptoms requiring long-term management.

title: Respiratory arrest – Definition
content: Respiratory arrest in paediatrics is the complete cessation of effective breathing, resulting in inadequate oxygenation and ventilation, requiring immediate intervention to prevent hypoxic injury and death.

title: Respiratory arrest – Epidemiology
content: Respiratory arrest is a rare but life-threatening event in paediatrics, often occurring secondary to respiratory failure, airway obstruction, or severe neurological impairment; it is a leading cause of paediatric cardiac arrest in the UK.

title: Respiratory arrest – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Common causes of respiratory arrest in paediatric patients include severe asthma exacerbation, bronchiolitis, foreign body airway obstruction, neuromuscular disorders, trauma, central nervous system infections, and drug overdose.

title: Respiratory arrest – Pathophysiology
content: Respiratory arrest results from failure of the respiratory centre or airway obstruction leading to cessation of effective ventilation, causing hypoxia, hypercapnia, and subsequent respiratory acidosis, which can rapidly progress to cardiac arrest if untreated.

title: Respiratory arrest – Clinical features: Decreased/loss of consciousness
content: Paediatric patients in respiratory arrest typically present with decreased or complete loss of consciousness due to hypoxia and hypercapnia affecting cerebral function.

title: Respiratory arrest – Clinical features: Cyanosis
content: Central cyanosis is a key clinical feature in paediatric respiratory arrest, indicating significant hypoxaemia due to inadequate oxygenation of haemoglobin.

title: Respiratory arrest – Clinical features: Absence of respiratory effort
content: In respiratory arrest, there is a complete absence of spontaneous respiratory effort, with no chest wall movement or airflow detected on auscultation or observation.

title: Respiratory arrest – Investigations
content: Initial investigations in paediatric respiratory arrest include pulse oximetry, arterial blood gas analysis showing hypoxaemia and hypercapnia, chest X-ray to identify underlying causes, and capnography during resuscitation to confirm airway placement.

title: Respiratory arrest – Management
content: Management of paediatric respiratory arrest involves immediate airway opening using head tilt-chin lift or jaw thrust, bag-valve-mask ventilation with 100% oxygen, advanced airway placement if necessary, and adherence to paediatric advanced life support (PALS) guidelines; adrenaline (epinephrine) 10 mcg/kg IV/IO may be administered during resuscitation.

title: Respiratory arrest – Complications
content: Complications of paediatric respiratory arrest include hypoxic brain injury, cardiac arrest, multi-organ failure, and death if not promptly recognised and treated.

title: Respiratory arrest – Prognosis
content: Prognosis following paediatric respiratory arrest depends on the duration of hypoxia and timeliness of resuscitation; early intervention can result in full recovery, whereas prolonged arrest often leads to permanent neurological impairment or death.

title: Rubella – Definition
content: Rubella is a contagious viral infection caused by the rubella virus, characterised by a mild febrile illness and a maculopapular rash, primarily affecting children and young adults.

title: Rubella – Epidemiology
content: Rubella incidence has significantly declined in the UK due to the MMR vaccination programme; however, outbreaks can still occur, particularly in unvaccinated populations and susceptible pregnant women.

title: Rubella – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Rubella is caused by the rubella virus, transmitted via respiratory droplets; risk factors include lack of immunisation, close contact with infected individuals, and pregnancy due to risk of congenital rubella syndrome.

title: Rubella – Pathophysiology
content: Rubella virus infects the upper respiratory tract, replicates in nasopharyngeal mucosa and regional lymph nodes, causing viraemia and dissemination leading to characteristic rash and systemic symptoms.

title: Rubella – Clinical features: Fever
content: Low-grade fever is typically present for 1–5 days before rash onset in paediatric rubella cases.

title: Rubella – Clinical features: Rash
content: A pink maculopapular rash typically appears 14–21 days after exposure, starting on the face and spreading to the trunk and limbs, lasting approximately 3 days.

title: Rubella – Clinical features: Lymphadenopathy
content: Tender, bilateral postauricular, occipital, and posterior cervical lymphadenopathy is common in paediatric rubella.

title: Rubella – Clinical features: Arthralgia
content: Arthralgia or arthritis, especially in adolescent females, may occur and typically affects small joints such as wrists, fingers, and knees.

title: Rubella – Investigations
content: Diagnosis is confirmed by rubella-specific IgM antibodies in serum or by rubella RNA detection using RT-PCR from throat swabs or urine; serology is the mainstay in the UK.

title: Rubella – Management
content: Management is supportive with antipyretics such as paracetamol (dose 10–15 mg/kg every 4–6 hours, max 60 mg/kg/day) and isolation to prevent spread; no specific antiviral treatment exists.

title: Rubella – Complications
content: Congenital rubella syndrome occurs if maternal infection happens during the first trimester, causing sensorineural deafness, cataracts, cardiac defects (e.g., patent ductus arteriosus), and developmental delay.

title: Rubella – Prognosis
content: Prognosis in immunocompetent children is excellent with full recovery; however, congenital rubella syndrome has significant morbidity and mortality.

title: Self-harm – Definition
content: Self-harm is defined as the intentional self-poisoning or self-injury irrespective of the apparent purpose of the act, commonly seen in paediatric populations as a coping mechanism for emotional distress.

title: Self-harm – Epidemiology
content: Self-harm affects approximately 10-15% of adolescents in the UK, with higher prevalence in females and peak incidence between ages 12 and 16 years.

title: Self-harm – Aetiology and risk factors
content: Risk factors for self-harm in paediatric patients include a history of mental health disorders (e.g., depression, anxiety), family dysfunction, bullying, abuse, substance misuse, and social isolation.

title: Self-harm – Pathophysiology
content: Self-harm is thought to result from complex interactions between psychological distress, impaired emotional regulation, and neurobiological factors including altered serotonin pathways.

title: Self-harm – Clinical features: Presentation with self-inflicted cuts or lacerations
content: Paediatric patients may present with superficial or deep cuts, often on the forearms, wrists, thighs, or abdomen, sometimes concealed by clothing; scars from previous episodes may also be evident.

title: Self-harm – Clinical features: Presentation with self-poisoning or overdose
content: Presentation may include ingestion of medications such as paracetamol, ibuprofen, or prescribed psychotropic drugs, with symptoms ranging from nausea and vomiting to altered consciousness and metabolic disturbances.

title: Self-harm – Investigations
content: Investigations include blood tests such as full blood count, liver function tests, coagulation profile, and toxicology screening; ECG is indicated if cardiotoxic drug overdose is suspected.

title: Self-harm – Differential diagnosis
content: Differential diagnoses include accidental injury, dermatological conditions causing skin lesions, factitious disorder, and suicidal attempts requiring psychiatric assessment.

title: Self-harm – Management: Immediate care
content: Immediate management includes assessment of airway, breathing, and circulation; wound care with cleaning and dressing; administration of antidotes such as N-acetylcysteine for paracetamol overdose as per UK guidelines (150 mg/kg over 15 minutes, then 50 mg/kg over 4 hours, then 100 mg/kg over 16 hours).

title: Self-harm – Management: Psychiatric assessment and follow-up
content: All paediatric patients presenting with self-harm require urgent mental health assessment, risk stratification for suicide, and referral to child and adolescent mental health services (CAMHS) for ongoing support and therapy.

title: Self-harm – Complications
content: Complications include infection, scarring, permanent tissue damage, accidental severe overdose leading to organ failure, and increased risk of completed suicide.

title: Self-harm – Prognosis
content: Prognosis varies; many adolescents recover with appropriate psychological intervention, but there is a significant risk of recurrence and increased suicide risk, necessitating long-term follow-up.

title: Sickle cell disease – Definition
content: Sickle cell disease is an inherited autosomal recessive haematological disorder characterised by the presence of abnormal haemoglobin S, leading to chronic haemolytic anaemia and vaso-occlusive phenomena.

title: Sickle cell disease – Epidemiology
content: Sickle cell disease affects approximately 1 in 2000 live births in the UK, predominantly in children of African, Caribbean, Middle Eastern, and South Asian descent.

title: Sickle cell disease – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Sickle cell disease is caused by a point mutation in the beta-globin gene resulting in haemoglobin S; risk factors include having two copies of the mutated gene (homozygous HbSS) or compound heterozygous states such as HbSC or HbSβ-thalassaemia.

title: Sickle cell disease – Pathophysiology
content: Polymerisation of deoxygenated haemoglobin S causes red blood cells to sickle, leading to vaso-occlusion, chronic haemolysis, endothelial damage, and increased risk of thrombosis.

title: Sickle cell disease – Clinical features: Anaemia and pallor
content: Children with sickle cell disease often present with chronic haemolytic anaemia causing pallor and fatigue; haemoglobin levels typically range from 6 to 9 g/dL.

title: Sickle cell disease – Clinical features: Acute painful crises
content: Vaso-occlusive crises present as acute joint pain and swelling, commonly affecting long bones, ribs, and back; pain episodes may require opioid analgesia for management.

title: Sickle cell disease – Clinical features: Acute chest syndrome
content: Acute chest syndrome is characterised by new pulmonary infiltrates on chest X-ray, fever, chest pain, cough, and hypoxia; it is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in paediatric sickle cell patients.

title: Sickle cell disease – Clinical features: Splenic sequestration
content: Splenic sequestration presents with sudden enlargement of the spleen, severe anaemia, pallor, and hypovolaemic shock; it is a paediatric emergency requiring urgent blood transfusion.

title: Sickle cell disease – Investigations: Haemoglobin electrophoresis
content: Haemoglobin electrophoresis is the diagnostic test of choice, demonstrating predominantly haemoglobin S in homozygous sickle cell disease; newborn screening is standard in the UK.

title: Sickle cell disease – Investigations: Blood tests
content: Blood tests typically show normocytic anaemia, reticulocytosis, raised bilirubin, and elevated lactate dehydrogenase reflecting haemolysis.

title: Sickle cell disease – Management: Penicillin prophylaxis
content: Oral penicillin V prophylaxis (125 mg twice daily for children under 3 years, 250 mg twice daily for children over 3 years) is recommended from diagnosis until at least 5 years old to prevent pneumococcal infections.

title: Sickle cell disease – Management: Hydroxycarbamide therapy
content: Hydroxycarbamide (hydroxyurea) is used in children with frequent vaso-occlusive crises or severe disease; typical dosing starts at 15 mg/kg/day orally, titrated up to a maximum of 35 mg/kg/day under haematology supervision.

title: Sickle cell disease – Management: Acute pain crisis treatment
content: Management of acute pain crises includes adequate hydration, analgesia with paracetamol and NSAIDs, and opioids such as oral morphine starting at 0.3-0.5 mg/kg every 4 hours as needed, with careful monitoring.

title: Sickle cell disease – Management: Blood transfusion
content: Blood transfusions are indicated for severe anaemia, acute chest syndrome, stroke, and splenic sequestration; exchange transfusion may be required in severe cases to reduce HbS levels below 30%.

title: Sickle cell disease – Complications: Stroke
content: Children with sickle cell disease are at increased risk of ischaemic stroke, especially between ages 2 and 16; transcranial Doppler screening is recommended to identify high-risk patients for regular transfusion therapy.

title: Sickle cell disease – Complications: Infection
content: Functional asplenia increases susceptibility to encapsulated organisms such as Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae; prompt treatment of fever with empirical intravenous antibiotics is essential.

title: Sickle cell disease – Prognosis
content: With early diagnosis, penicillin prophylaxis, vaccination, and specialist care, children with sickle cell disease in the UK have improved life expectancy, with many surviving into adulthood; however, complications may reduce quality of life.

title: Subarachnoid haemorrhage – Definition
content: Subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) is bleeding into the subarachnoid space, the area between the arachnoid membrane and the pia mater surrounding the brain, leading to increased intracranial pressure and potential brain injury.

title: Subarachnoid haemorrhage – Epidemiology
content: Subarachnoid haemorrhage is rare in paediatric populations, accounting for less than 5% of all strokes in children. The incidence is approximately 0.5 to 1 per 100,000 children per year in the UK.

title: Subarachnoid haemorrhage – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: In children, common causes of subarachnoid haemorrhage include arteriovenous malformations (AVMs), cerebral aneurysms, trauma, bleeding disorders such as haemophilia, and less commonly, infections or vasculitis.

title: Subarachnoid haemorrhage – Pathophysiology
content: Bleeding into the subarachnoid space causes increased intracranial pressure, cerebral vasospasm, and irritation of meninges, leading to headache, neurological deficits, and risk of secondary brain injury.

title: Subarachnoid haemorrhage – Clinical features: Headache
content: The most common presenting symptom in paediatric subarachnoid haemorrhage is a sudden, severe headache often described as 'the worst headache of life'.

title: Subarachnoid haemorrhage – Clinical features: Decreased/loss of consciousness
content: Children with subarachnoid haemorrhage may present with decreased level of consciousness or coma due to raised intracranial pressure or brain injury.

title: Subarachnoid haemorrhage – Clinical features: Fits/seizures
content: Seizures may occur in paediatric patients with subarachnoid haemorrhage due to cortical irritation from blood in the subarachnoid space.

title: Subarachnoid haemorrhage – Investigations
content: Initial investigation includes non-contrast CT head which detects acute blood in over 95% of cases within 24 hours. If CT is negative but suspicion remains, lumbar puncture is performed to detect xanthochromia. MRI and cerebral angiography are used to identify underlying vascular abnormalities.

title: Subarachnoid haemorrhage – Management
content: Management includes stabilisation with airway, breathing, and circulation support. Nimodipine 1 mg/kg orally every 4 hours is used to reduce cerebral vasospasm in children. Neurosurgical intervention such as clipping or endovascular coiling of aneurysms or AVMs is indicated. Supportive care includes analgesia, seizure control with anticonvulsants like levetiracetam, and monitoring in a paediatric intensive care unit.

title: Subarachnoid haemorrhage – Complications
content: Complications include cerebral vasospasm leading to ischaemic stroke, hydrocephalus, rebleeding, seizures, and long-term neurological deficits.

title: Subarachnoid haemorrhage – Prognosis
content: Prognosis depends on the severity of haemorrhage and promptness of treatment. Mortality in paediatric SAH is lower than adults but significant morbidity including cognitive impairment and neurological deficits occurs in up to 30% of survivors.

title: Subdural haemorrhage – Definition
content: Subdural haemorrhage (SDH) is a collection of blood between the dura mater and the arachnoid membrane of the brain, often resulting from tearing of bridging veins.

title: Subdural haemorrhage – Epidemiology
content: Subdural haemorrhage is more common in infants and young children, particularly under 2 years of age, and is a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in paediatric head trauma.

title: Subdural haemorrhage – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Common causes of paediatric subdural haemorrhage include non-accidental injury (child abuse), accidental head trauma such as falls or road traffic accidents, and bleeding disorders like haemophilia.

title: Subdural haemorrhage – Pathophysiology
content: Subdural haemorrhage occurs due to rupture of bridging veins between the cerebral cortex and dural sinuses, leading to blood accumulation that increases intracranial pressure and causes brain compression.

title: Subdural haemorrhage – Clinical features: Decreased/loss of consciousness
content: Children with subdural haemorrhage often present with decreased level of consciousness or coma depending on the severity of brain injury.

title: Subdural haemorrhage – Clinical features: Fits/seizures
content: Seizures are a common presentation in paediatric subdural haemorrhage and may be focal or generalised.

title: Subdural haemorrhage – Clinical features: Trauma
content: A history of head trauma, including falls or suspected non-accidental injury, is often present in children with subdural haemorrhage.

title: Subdural haemorrhage – Investigations
content: Diagnosis is confirmed by neuroimaging; non-contrast CT head is the first-line investigation showing crescent-shaped hyperdense collection over the cerebral hemisphere. MRI may be used for further characterisation.

title: Subdural haemorrhage – Management
content: Management depends on severity; mild cases may be observed with supportive care, while significant haemorrhages require neurosurgical intervention such as burr hole drainage. Intracranial pressure monitoring and seizure control with anticonvulsants like levetiracetam may be necessary.

title: Subdural haemorrhage – Complications
content: Complications include raised intracranial pressure, brain herniation, persistent neurological deficits, developmental delay, and death.

title: Subdural haemorrhage – Prognosis
content: Prognosis depends on severity and promptness of treatment; mild cases have good outcomes, but severe haemorrhages, especially those associated with non-accidental injury, have higher rates of mortality and long-term neurological impairment.

title: Substance use disorder – Definition
content: Substance use disorder in paediatrics is characterised by a pattern of harmful use of substances such as alcohol, cannabis, opioids, or stimulants leading to clinically significant impairment or distress, as defined by DSM-5 criteria.

title: Substance use disorder – Epidemiology
content: In the UK, approximately 14% of 11-15 year olds report having used an illicit drug at least once, with cannabis being the most commonly used substance among adolescents.

title: Substance use disorder – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Risk factors for paediatric substance use disorder include family history of substance misuse, peer pressure, mental health disorders such as depression or ADHD, social deprivation, and early exposure to substances.

title: Substance use disorder – Pathophysiology
content: Substance use disorder involves neuroadaptations in the brain's reward pathways, particularly affecting dopaminergic circuits in the mesolimbic system, leading to tolerance, dependence, and compulsive drug-seeking behaviour.

title: Substance use disorder – Clinical features: Behavioural difficulties in childhood
content: Children and adolescents with substance use disorder often present with behavioural difficulties including irritability, aggression, truancy, and decline in academic performance.

title: Substance use disorder – Clinical features: Substance misuse
content: Presentation may include signs of intoxication or withdrawal from substances such as alcohol, cannabis, opioids, or stimulants, with symptoms like slurred speech, impaired coordination, or agitation.

title: Substance use disorder – Clinical features: Overdose
content: Overdose presentations in paediatric substance use disorder can include respiratory depression, altered consciousness, seizures, or cardiac arrhythmias depending on the substance involved.

title: Substance use disorder – Investigations
content: Investigations include urine drug screening, blood tests for liver function and full blood count, and assessment for coexisting mental health disorders; no single test confirms diagnosis.

title: Substance use disorder – Management
content: Management includes psychosocial interventions such as cognitive behavioural therapy and family therapy; pharmacological treatments like methadone or buprenorphine are used for opioid dependence under specialist supervision.

title: Substance use disorder – Complications
content: Complications include increased risk of accidents, mental health disorders such as depression and anxiety, social problems, and long-term cognitive impairment.

title: Substance use disorder – Prognosis
content: Prognosis varies; early intervention improves outcomes, but untreated substance use disorder in paediatric patients is associated with chronic substance dependence and increased morbidity into adulthood.

title: Tension headache – Definition
content: Tension headache is a common primary headache disorder characterised by bilateral, pressing or tightening pain of mild to moderate intensity, not aggravated by routine physical activity, and without nausea or vomiting. It is the most frequent type of headache in children and adolescents.

title: Tension headache – Epidemiology
content: Tension headache affects up to 30% of school-aged children in the UK, with prevalence increasing during adolescence. It is slightly more common in females than males after puberty.

title: Tension headache – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Risk factors for tension headache in children include psychological stress, poor posture, sleep disturbances, and family history of headache disorders. Environmental triggers such as screen time and dehydration may also contribute.

title: Tension headache – Pathophysiology
content: Tension headache pathophysiology involves increased pericranial muscle tenderness and heightened sensitivity of pain pathways in the central nervous system, resulting in a sensitised response to normal stimuli.

title: Tension headache – Clinical features: Headache characteristics
content: Tension headache presents with bilateral, pressing or tightening headache of mild to moderate intensity, lasting from 30 minutes to several hours, typically without associated nausea or vomiting.

title: Tension headache – Clinical features: Associated symptoms
content: Unlike migraine, tension headache in children usually lacks photophobia, phonophobia, nausea, or vomiting, and is not worsened by routine physical activity.

title: Tension headache – Investigations
content: Diagnosis of tension headache is clinical; neuroimaging is not routinely indicated unless red flags such as neurological deficits, altered consciousness, or signs of raised intracranial pressure are present.

title: Tension headache – Management: Acute treatment
content: First-line acute treatment for paediatric tension headache includes paracetamol (15 mg/kg per dose, maximum 60 mg/kg/day) or ibuprofen (10 mg/kg per dose, maximum 40 mg/kg/day), administered at onset of headache.

title: Tension headache – Management: Preventative strategies
content: Preventative management includes addressing triggers such as stress reduction, improving sleep hygiene, regular physical activity, and ergonomic posture correction. Cognitive behavioural therapy may be considered for recurrent headaches.

title: Tension headache – Complications
content: Chronic tension-type headache may develop if acute headaches become frequent and persistent, potentially impacting school attendance and quality of life.

title: Tension headache – Prognosis
content: The prognosis for paediatric tension headache is generally good with appropriate management; many children experience resolution or significant improvement during adolescence.

title: Testicular torsion – Definition
content: Testicular torsion is a urological emergency characterised by the twisting of the spermatic cord leading to ischaemia of the testis.

title: Testicular torsion – Epidemiology
content: Testicular torsion most commonly occurs in males aged 12-18 years, with an incidence of approximately 4.5 per 100,000 males under 25 years annually in the UK.

title: Testicular torsion – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Risk factors for testicular torsion include a congenital 'bell clapper' deformity, previous torsion episodes, trauma, and rapid testicular growth during puberty.

title: Testicular torsion – Pathophysiology
content: Testicular torsion occurs when the spermatic cord twists, obstructing venous outflow and arterial inflow, causing ischaemia and potential infarction of the testis.

title: Testicular torsion – Clinical features: Scrotal/testicular pain and/or lump/swelling
content: Acute onset of severe unilateral scrotal pain and swelling is the hallmark presentation of testicular torsion in paediatric patients.

title: Testicular torsion – Clinical features: Absent cremasteric reflex
content: An absent cremasteric reflex on the affected side is a key clinical sign suggestive of testicular torsion.

title: Testicular torsion – Clinical features: Nausea and vomiting
content: Nausea and vomiting may accompany the acute scrotal pain in paediatric patients with testicular torsion.

title: Testicular torsion – Investigations: Doppler ultrasound
content: Doppler ultrasound is the imaging modality of choice to confirm testicular torsion, demonstrating reduced or absent blood flow to the affected testis.

title: Testicular torsion – Management: Emergency surgical detorsion and orchidopexy
content: Immediate surgical exploration with detorsion and bilateral orchidopexy is the definitive treatment for testicular torsion and should be performed ideally within 6 hours of symptom onset to optimise testicular salvage.

title: Testicular torsion – Management: Analgesia
content: Paracetamol 15 mg/kg orally or intravenously every 4-6 hours (maximum 60 mg/kg/day) is recommended for pain relief in paediatric patients with testicular torsion.

title: Testicular torsion – Complications
content: Delayed treatment of testicular torsion can result in testicular infarction, atrophy, infertility, and rarely, sepsis.

title: Testicular torsion – Prognosis
content: Testicular salvage rates are approximately 90-100% if surgery occurs within 6 hours of symptom onset, decreasing to less than 50% after 12 hours.

title: Thyrotoxicosis – Definition
content: Thyrotoxicosis in paediatrics is a clinical syndrome caused by excess circulating thyroid hormones, resulting in a hypermetabolic state. It is most commonly due to Graves' disease in children.

title: Thyrotoxicosis – Epidemiology
content: Paediatric thyrotoxicosis is rare, with an incidence of approximately 0.9 per 100,000 children per year in the UK. It is more common in girls, with a peak incidence in adolescence.

title: Thyrotoxicosis – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: The most common cause of paediatric thyrotoxicosis is Graves' disease, an autoimmune disorder characterised by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins. Other causes include toxic multinodular goitre, thyroiditis, and iodine excess.

title: Thyrotoxicosis – Pathophysiology
content: In paediatric thyrotoxicosis, excess thyroid hormones (T3 and T4) increase basal metabolic rate, enhance beta-adrenergic receptor sensitivity, and cause multisystem effects including increased cardiac output and heat intolerance.

title: Thyrotoxicosis – Clinical features: Weight loss
content: Children with thyrotoxicosis often present with unexplained weight loss despite an increased appetite.

title: Thyrotoxicosis – Clinical features: Tachycardia and palpitations
content: Tachycardia is common in paediatric thyrotoxicosis, often exceeding 100 beats per minute at rest, and may be accompanied by palpitations and arrhythmias.

title: Thyrotoxicosis – Clinical features: Heat intolerance and sweating
content: Affected children frequently experience heat intolerance and excessive sweating due to increased metabolic rate.

title: Thyrotoxicosis – Clinical features: Goitre
content: A diffuse, smooth, and sometimes tender goitre is often present in children with Graves' disease causing thyrotoxicosis.

title: Thyrotoxicosis – Clinical features: Eye signs
content: Paediatric Graves' disease may present with ophthalmopathy including lid lag, lid retraction, and proptosis, although less common than in adults.

title: Thyrotoxicosis – Clinical features: Behavioural difficulties
content: Children with thyrotoxicosis may exhibit behavioural difficulties including irritability, hyperactivity, and poor concentration.

title: Thyrotoxicosis – Investigations: Thyroid function tests
content: Diagnosis is confirmed by suppressed thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH <0.01 mU/L) with elevated free thyroxine (FT4) and free triiodothyronine (FT3) levels.

title: Thyrotoxicosis – Investigations: Thyroid autoantibodies
content: Positive thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI) or TSH receptor antibodies support the diagnosis of Graves' disease in paediatric thyrotoxicosis.

title: Thyrotoxicosis – Investigations: Radioactive iodine uptake scan
content: A radioactive iodine uptake scan shows diffusely increased uptake in Graves' disease, but is rarely used in children due to radiation exposure.

title: Thyrotoxicosis – Management: Antithyroid drugs
content: First-line treatment is carbimazole, starting at 0.5 to 0.75 mg/kg/day divided into two doses, adjusted according to thyroid function tests every 4-6 weeks.

title: Thyrotoxicosis – Management: Beta-blockers
content: Propranolol is used to control adrenergic symptoms at 0.5 to 2 mg/kg/day divided into 3-4 doses, particularly in the initial phase of treatment.

title: Thyrotoxicosis – Management: Definitive treatment
content: Definitive treatment options for refractory or relapsing paediatric thyrotoxicosis include thyroidectomy or radioactive iodine ablation, with specialist paediatric endocrinology input.

title: Thyrotoxicosis – Complications: Thyroid storm
content: Thyroid storm is a rare but life-threatening complication characterised by fever, tachycardia, altered consciousness, and heart failure requiring urgent intensive care.

title: Thyrotoxicosis – Complications: Growth and development delay
content: Untreated thyrotoxicosis in children can cause delayed growth and pubertal development due to metabolic disturbances.

title: Thyrotoxicosis – Prognosis
content: With appropriate treatment, most children with thyrotoxicosis achieve remission; however, relapse occurs in up to 50% within 2 years, necessitating long-term follow-up.

title: Tonsillitis – Definition
content: Tonsillitis is inflammation of the palatine tonsils, commonly caused by viral or bacterial infections, leading to sore throat, fever, and difficulty swallowing in paediatric patients.

title: Tonsillitis – Epidemiology
content: Tonsillitis is most common in children aged 5 to 15 years and accounts for a significant proportion of paediatric sore throat presentations in the UK, with viral causes predominating.

title: Tonsillitis – Aetiology and Risk factors
content: Common causes of tonsillitis in children include viral infections such as adenovirus, rhinovirus, and Epstein-Barr virus, and bacterial infections predominantly Group A beta-haemolytic Streptococcus (GABHS). Risk factors include close contact in school settings and immunodeficiency.

title: Tonsillitis – Pathophysiology
content: Tonsillitis results from infection-induced inflammation of the tonsillar lymphoid tissue, leading to oedema, erythema, and exudate formation, which causes pain and difficulty swallowing.

title: Tonsillitis – Clinical features: Sore throat and fever
content: Children with tonsillitis typically present with a sore throat and fever, often above 38°C, which may be accompanied by malaise and headache.

title: Tonsillitis – Clinical features: Tonsillar erythema and exudate
content: On examination, tonsils are enlarged, erythematous, and may have white or yellow exudate; this is more common in bacterial tonsillitis.

title: Tonsillitis – Clinical features: Cervical lymphadenopathy
content: Tender, enlarged anterior cervical lymph nodes are commonly palpable in paediatric tonsillitis.

title: Tonsillitis – Clinical features: Difficulty swallowing and drooling
content: Children may have odynophagia causing difficulty swallowing and in severe cases drooling due to pain.

title: Tonsillitis – Investigations: Throat swab and rapid antigen test
content: A throat swab for bacterial culture or rapid antigen detection test may be performed to identify Group A Streptococcus in children with suspected bacterial tonsillitis.

title: Tonsillitis – Investigations: Blood tests
content: Blood tests such as full blood count may show raised white cell count with neutrophilia in bacterial tonsillitis or lymphocytosis in viral causes like infectious mononucleosis.

title: Tonsillitis – Management: Supportive care
content: Supportive management includes analgesia with paracetamol (15 mg/kg every 4-6 hours, max 60 mg/kg/day) or ibuprofen (5-10 mg/kg every 6-8 hours, max 40 mg/kg/day), adequate hydration, and rest.

title: Tonsillitis – Management: Antibiotic therapy
content: Oral phenoxymethylpenicillin is first-line for bacterial tonsillitis in children: 250 mg twice daily for under 10 years, 500 mg twice daily for over 10 years, for 10 days. Alternatives include erythromycin if penicillin-allergic.

title: Tonsillitis – Management: Indications for tonsillectomy
content: Tonsillectomy may be considered in children with recurrent tonsillitis defined as 7 or more episodes in one year, 5 or more episodes per year for two consecutive years, or 3 or more episodes per year for three consecutive years.

title: Tonsillitis – Complications: Peritonsillar abscess
content: A peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) is a serious complication characterised by severe unilateral throat pain, trismus, muffled voice, and uvular deviation; it requires urgent ENT referral and drainage.

title: Tonsillitis – Complications: Rheumatic fever and glomerulonephritis
content: Untreated Group A Streptococcal tonsillitis can lead to immune-mediated complications such as acute rheumatic fever and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, although these are rare in the UK due to widespread antibiotic use.

title: Tonsillitis – Prognosis
content: Most cases of paediatric tonsillitis resolve within 7 to 10 days with appropriate supportive care; bacterial tonsillitis responds well to antibiotics with low risk of complications.

title: Toxic shock syndrome – Definition
content: Toxic shock syndrome (TSS) is a rare, acute, life-threatening condition caused by toxin-producing strains of Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes, characterised by sudden high fever, rash, hypotension, and multi-organ involvement.

title: Toxic shock syndrome – Epidemiology
content: Toxic shock syndrome is rare in the UK paediatric population, with an incidence estimated at 0.5 to 1.0 cases per 100,000 children annually; it predominantly affects children aged 5 to 15 years.

title: Toxic shock syndrome – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Risk factors for paediatric toxic shock syndrome include recent skin or soft tissue infections, surgical wounds, burns, tampon use in adolescent girls, and varicella infection.

title: Toxic shock syndrome – Pathophysiology
content: Toxic shock syndrome results from superantigen exotoxins (TSST-1 from Staphylococcus aureus or pyrogenic exotoxins from Streptococcus pyogenes) causing massive T-cell activation and cytokine release leading to systemic inflammation and shock.

title: Toxic shock syndrome – Clinical features: Fever
content: Children with toxic shock syndrome typically present with a sudden onset of high fever, often ≥39°C.

title: Toxic shock syndrome – Clinical features: Acute rash
content: A diffuse, erythematous macular rash resembling sunburn is characteristic, often involving the trunk and extremities, which may desquamate after 1-2 weeks.

title: Toxic shock syndrome – Clinical features: Shock
content: Hypotension is a key feature, defined as systolic blood pressure <5th percentile for age or signs of poor perfusion, often progressing to shock requiring fluid resuscitation.

title: Toxic shock syndrome – Clinical features: Multi-organ involvement
content: Clinical signs may include vomiting, diarrhoea, confusion or altered consciousness, conjunctival hyperaemia without exudate, mucous membrane erythema, and elevated liver enzymes or renal impairment.

title: Toxic shock syndrome – Investigations
content: Investigations include blood cultures, wound or mucosal site cultures, full blood count showing leukocytosis or leukopenia, elevated C-reactive protein, renal and liver function tests, coagulation profile, and chest X-ray if respiratory symptoms present.

title: Toxic shock syndrome – Management
content: Management includes urgent supportive care with aggressive fluid resuscitation, vasopressors if needed, empirical intravenous antibiotics such as clindamycin 10 mg/kg every 6-8 hours plus flucloxacillin 50 mg/kg every 6 hours, and surgical debridement of infected foci if present.

title: Toxic shock syndrome – Complications
content: Complications include multi-organ failure, disseminated intravascular coagulation, acute respiratory distress syndrome, and death if untreated or delayed treatment.

title: Toxic shock syndrome – Prognosis
content: With prompt recognition and treatment, paediatric toxic shock syndrome has a mortality rate of less than 5%, but delayed diagnosis significantly increases risk of death and long-term morbidity.

title: Urinary tract infection – Definition
content: A urinary tract infection (UTI) in paediatrics is an infection involving any part of the urinary system, including the urethra, bladder, ureters, and kidneys, caused predominantly by bacteria such as Escherichia coli.

title: Urinary tract infection – Epidemiology
content: UTIs affect approximately 5% of children under 5 years in the UK, with a higher incidence in females and uncircumcised males under 1 year of age.

title: Urinary tract infection – Aetiology and risk factors
content: Common risk factors for paediatric UTI include urinary tract malformations (e.g., vesicoureteric reflux), constipation, poor perineal hygiene, bladder dysfunction, and female sex.

title: Urinary tract infection – Pathophysiology
content: UTIs occur when uropathogenic bacteria colonise the periurethral area and ascend the urethra to infect the bladder (cystitis) or kidneys (pyelonephritis), causing inflammation and tissue damage.

title: Urinary tract infection – Clinical features: Fever
content: Fever is a common presenting feature of UTI in children, often the only symptom in infants and young children.

title: Urinary tract infection – Clinical features: Urinary symptoms
content: Older children with UTI may present with dysuria, frequency, urgency, and urinary incontinence.

title: Urinary tract infection – Clinical features: Vomiting and abdominal pain
content: Vomiting and acute abdominal pain may occur in children with pyelonephritis or severe UTI.

title: Urinary tract infection – Investigations: Urine dipstick and microscopy
content: Urine dipstick testing for leukocyte esterase and nitrites is used for initial UTI screening; microscopy may show pyuria and bacteriuria.

title: Urinary tract infection – Investigations: Urine culture
content: Urine culture is the gold standard for diagnosing UTI; a significant growth is defined as ≥10^5 colony-forming units/mL of a single uropathogen.

title: Urinary tract infection – Management: Antibiotic treatment
content: First-line oral antibiotics for uncomplicated UTI in children include trimethoprim 2 mg/kg once daily or nitrofurantoin 1-2 mg/kg/dose four times daily for 3 days; intravenous antibiotics such as cefotaxime 50 mg/kg every 8 hours are used for severe cases or pyelonephritis.

title: Urinary tract infection – Management: Supportive care
content: Supportive care includes adequate hydration, antipyretics such as paracetamol (15 mg/kg every 4-6 hours, max 60 mg/kg/day), and monitoring for clinical improvement.

title: Urinary tract infection – Complications
content: Complications of paediatric UTI include renal scarring, hypertension, chronic kidney disease, and recurrent infections.

title: Urinary tract infection – Prognosis
content: With prompt diagnosis and appropriate treatment, most children recover fully from UTI without long-term sequelae; however, delayed treatment increases risk of renal damage.

title: Urticaria – Definition
content: Urticaria is a common paediatric condition characterised by transient, pruritic, raised wheals (hives) on the skin, often accompanied by angioedema. Lesions typically last less than 24 hours and resolve without scarring.

title: Urticaria – Epidemiology
content: Urticaria affects up to 15-20% of children at some point in childhood. Acute urticaria is more common than chronic urticaria in paediatric populations, with chronic urticaria affecting approximately 0.5-1% of children.

title: Urticaria – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Common triggers for paediatric urticaria include viral infections, food allergens (e.g. nuts, eggs, milk), medications (e.g. penicillin, NSAIDs), insect stings, and physical stimuli such as cold or pressure. Family history of atopy increases risk.

title: Urticaria – Pathophysiology
content: Urticaria results from mast cell degranulation in the skin, releasing histamine and other mediators causing increased vascular permeability, leading to wheal formation and angioedema.

title: Urticaria – Clinical features: Acute rash
content: Children with urticaria present with sudden onset of pruritic, erythematous wheals that blanch on pressure. Individual lesions last less than 24 hours but new lesions may appear continuously.

title: Urticaria – Clinical features: Angioedema
content: Approximately 40% of children with urticaria also develop angioedema, characterised by deeper swelling of the lips, eyelids, or extremities, which may be painful but is usually non-pruritic.

title: Urticaria – Investigations
content: Diagnosis of urticaria is clinical. Routine blood tests are not required unless chronic urticaria persists beyond 6 weeks. Specific IgE testing or skin prick tests may be considered if an allergic trigger is suspected.

title: Urticaria – Differential diagnosis
content: Differential diagnoses include erythema multiforme, viral exanthems, mastocytosis, and vasculitis such as urticarial vasculitis. Lesion duration over 24 hours and systemic symptoms suggest alternative diagnoses.

title: Urticaria – Management
content: First-line treatment is non-sedating H1-antihistamines such as cetirizine (0.25 mg/kg twice daily, max 10 mg twice daily) or loratadine. Avoid known triggers. Severe cases may require short courses of oral corticosteroids (e.g. prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day for 3-5 days).

title: Urticaria – Complications
content: Complications are rare but may include anaphylaxis, especially if urticaria is part of an allergic reaction. Chronic urticaria can impact quality of life due to persistent itching and sleep disturbance.

title: Urticaria – Prognosis
content: Acute urticaria in children usually resolves within days to weeks with complete recovery. Chronic urticaria may persist for months to years but often improves by adolescence.

title: Viral exanthema – Definition
content: Viral exanthema refers to a widespread rash occurring in children, typically caused by viral infections. It is characterised by erythematous maculopapular lesions that may be accompanied by systemic symptoms such as fever.

title: Viral exanthema – Epidemiology
content: Viral exanthems are common in paediatric populations, particularly in children aged 6 months to 10 years. Incidence peaks in early childhood due to exposure to common viruses such as measles, rubella, and parvovirus B19.

title: Viral exanthema – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Common viral causes of viral exanthema in children include measles virus, rubella virus, parvovirus B19, human herpesvirus 6 (roseola), and enteroviruses. Risk factors include lack of vaccination, recent exposure to infected individuals, and immunocompromised status.

title: Viral exanthema – Pathophysiology
content: Viral exanthems result from immune-mediated responses to viral infections, causing inflammation and damage to dermal blood vessels and skin cells, leading to characteristic erythematous maculopapular rashes.

title: Viral exanthema – Clinical features: Fever
content: Fever is a common presenting feature in viral exanthema, often preceding the rash by 1 to 2 days. Temperatures typically range from 38°C to 40°C in paediatric patients.

title: Viral exanthema – Clinical features: Rash
content: The rash in viral exanthema typically presents as a widespread erythematous maculopapular eruption, starting on the face or trunk and spreading centrifugally. The rash is usually non-pruritic and resolves within 3 to 7 days.

title: Viral exanthema – Clinical features: Lymphadenopathy
content: Cervical and postauricular lymphadenopathy may be present in viral exanthema, particularly in rubella infection, and is usually tender and bilateral.

title: Viral exanthema – Investigations
content: Diagnosis of viral exanthema is primarily clinical. Laboratory investigations may include viral serology (e.g., measles IgM, rubella IgM), PCR testing from throat swabs or blood, and full blood count showing lymphocytosis.

title: Viral exanthema – Management
content: Management of viral exanthema is supportive, including antipyretics such as paracetamol (15 mg/kg every 4-6 hours, max 60 mg/kg/day) and adequate hydration. Isolation is recommended to prevent spread. Specific antiviral treatment is rarely indicated.

title: Viral exanthema – Complications
content: Complications of viral exanthema can include secondary bacterial infection of the skin, post-infectious arthritis (notably with parvovirus B19), and, rarely, encephalitis in measles infection.

title: Viral exanthema – Prognosis
content: The prognosis for viral exanthema in children is generally excellent, with most rashes resolving spontaneously without sequelae within 1 week. Serious complications are uncommon in immunocompetent children.

title: Viral gastroenteritis – Definition
content: Viral gastroenteritis is an inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract caused by viral infection, leading to symptoms such as diarrhoea and vomiting in paediatric patients.

title: Viral gastroenteritis – Epidemiology
content: Viral gastroenteritis is a common cause of acute diarrhoea in children under 5 years old in the UK, with rotavirus being the most frequent pathogen before the introduction of the rotavirus vaccine in 2013.

title: Viral gastroenteritis – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Common viral causes of paediatric viral gastroenteritis in the UK include rotavirus, norovirus, adenovirus (types 40 and 41), and astrovirus; risk factors include poor hand hygiene, close contact in childcare settings, and lack of rotavirus vaccination.

title: Viral gastroenteritis – Pathophysiology
content: Viral gastroenteritis causes inflammation and damage to the small intestinal mucosa, leading to malabsorption and secretory diarrhoea due to disruption of enterocytes and increased intestinal motility.

title: Viral gastroenteritis – Clinical features: Diarrhoea
content: Paediatric viral gastroenteritis typically presents with acute onset of watery diarrhoea, which may be frequent and without blood or mucus.

title: Viral gastroenteritis – Clinical features: Vomiting
content: Vomiting is a common symptom in paediatric viral gastroenteritis, often preceding diarrhoea and lasting 1-3 days.

title: Viral gastroenteritis – Clinical features: Fever
content: Mild to moderate fever (up to 38.5°C) may be present in children with viral gastroenteritis.

title: Viral gastroenteritis – Clinical features: Dehydration
content: Signs of dehydration in paediatric viral gastroenteritis include dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, sunken eyes, lethargy, and decreased urine output.

title: Viral gastroenteritis – Investigations
