content: Diagnosis is usually clinical; stool PCR testing may be used in severe or prolonged cases to identify viral pathogens; blood tests are not routinely required unless dehydration or complications are suspected.

title: Viral gastroenteritis – Management: Oral rehydration therapy
content: First-line management of paediatric viral gastroenteritis is oral rehydration therapy using WHO-recommended oral rehydration solution (ORS) to prevent or treat dehydration.

title: Viral gastroenteritis – Management: Antiemetics
content: Ondansetron may be used in children over 6 months with persistent vomiting to facilitate oral rehydration; typical dose is 0.15 mg/kg orally once.

title: Viral gastroenteritis – Management: Hospital admission criteria
content: Hospital admission is indicated for children with severe dehydration, inability to tolerate oral fluids, shock, or other complications requiring intravenous fluids and monitoring.

title: Viral gastroenteritis – Complications
content: Complications of viral gastroenteritis include severe dehydration, electrolyte imbalances, metabolic acidosis, and in rare cases, intussusception or secondary bacterial infection.

title: Viral gastroenteritis – Prognosis
content: The prognosis of paediatric viral gastroenteritis is generally excellent with appropriate rehydration; symptoms usually resolve within 3-7 days without long-term sequelae.

title: Visual field defects – Definition
content: Visual field defects in paediatrics refer to areas of lost or reduced vision within the visual field, caused by damage or dysfunction along the visual pathway from the retina to the visual cortex.

title: Visual field defects – Epidemiology
content: Visual field defects in children are relatively uncommon but can occur due to congenital, traumatic, neoplastic, or neurological causes. The prevalence varies depending on the underlying aetiology, with congenital causes being more frequent in early childhood.

title: Visual field defects – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Common causes of visual field defects in paediatrics include congenital optic nerve hypoplasia, brain tumours (e.g. craniopharyngioma), trauma, stroke, infections such as meningitis, and demyelinating diseases like multiple sclerosis.

title: Visual field defects – Pathophysiology
content: Visual field defects result from interruption or damage to the visual pathway, which includes the retina, optic nerve, optic chiasm, optic tract, lateral geniculate nucleus, optic radiations, and visual cortex. The location of the lesion determines the pattern of visual field loss.

title: Visual field defects – Clinical features: Presentation
content: Children with visual field defects may present with difficulty seeing objects to one side, bumping into objects, squint, or behavioural difficulties related to impaired vision. Visual field loss may be detected during routine vision screening or following neurological symptoms.

title: Visual field defects – Clinical features: Types of visual field loss
content: Common visual field defects include bitemporal hemianopia (lesion at optic chiasm), homonymous hemianopia (lesion posterior to optic chiasm), quadrantanopia (lesion in optic radiations), and central scotomas (lesion affecting macular fibres).

title: Visual field defects – Investigations
content: Assessment includes formal visual field testing adapted for children (e.g. confrontation testing, automated perimetry if possible), fundoscopic examination, neuroimaging with MRI brain and orbits to identify structural lesions, and visual evoked potentials if optic nerve dysfunction is suspected.

title: Visual field defects – Differential diagnosis
content: Differential diagnoses include ocular causes such as retinal dystrophies, amblyopia, refractive errors, and neurological causes like cortical visual impairment or optic neuritis.

title: Visual field defects – Management
content: Management depends on the underlying cause. For example, brain tumours may require neurosurgical intervention and oncology input. Supportive measures include referral to paediatric ophthalmology and low vision services, and educational support for children with persistent visual impairment.

title: Visual field defects – Complications
content: Complications include permanent visual impairment, increased risk of injury due to impaired peripheral vision, and psychosocial impact including learning difficulties and behavioural problems.

title: Visual field defects – Prognosis
content: Prognosis depends on the cause and extent of visual pathway damage. Some defects may improve with treatment (e.g. inflammation), but many visual field defects are permanent. Early diagnosis and intervention improve functional outcomes and quality of life.

title: Volvulus – Definition
content: Volvulus is a paediatric surgical emergency characterised by twisting of a loop of intestine around its mesenteric attachment, leading to bowel obstruction and potential ischaemia.

title: Volvulus – Epidemiology
content: Volvulus most commonly presents in neonates and infants, particularly within the first month of life, with an incidence of approximately 1 in 6000 live births in the UK.

title: Volvulus – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Risk factors for volvulus in paediatric patients include malrotation of the intestine, Hirschsprung disease, intestinal atresia, and previous abdominal surgery.

title: Volvulus – Pathophysiology
content: Volvulus causes twisting of the bowel around its mesentery, leading to obstruction of the intestinal lumen and vascular compromise, which can result in bowel ischaemia, necrosis, and perforation if untreated.

title: Volvulus – Clinical features: Acute abdominal pain
content: Presentation typically includes sudden onset of severe, colicky abdominal pain in infants or children, often accompanied by irritability and inconsolable crying.

title: Volvulus – Clinical features: Vomiting
content: Bilious vomiting is a key clinical feature in paediatric volvulus and should be considered a surgical emergency until proven otherwise.

title: Volvulus – Clinical features: Abdominal distension
content: Abdominal distension is commonly observed in infants with volvulus due to bowel obstruction and accumulation of gas and fluid proximal to the twist.

title: Volvulus – Clinical features: Shock
content: Signs of shock such as tachycardia, hypotension, pallor, and poor peripheral perfusion may develop rapidly in volvulus due to bowel ischaemia and systemic inflammatory response.

title: Volvulus – Investigations
content: Initial investigations include erect abdominal X-ray showing a 'double bubble' sign or dilated bowel loops; upper gastrointestinal contrast study is the gold standard to diagnose malrotation and volvulus.

title: Volvulus – Differential diagnosis
content: Differential diagnoses include midgut malrotation without volvulus, intussusception, necrotising enterocolitis, Hirschsprung disease, and other causes of neonatal intestinal obstruction.

title: Volvulus – Management
content: Management requires urgent surgical intervention with laparotomy and detorsion of the volvulus; intravenous fluid resuscitation, correction of electrolyte imbalances, and broad-spectrum antibiotics such as intravenous amoxicillin 30 mg/kg every 8 hours plus gentamicin 7.5 mg/kg once daily are administered preoperatively.

title: Volvulus – Complications
content: Complications include bowel ischaemia, necrosis, perforation, peritonitis, sepsis, short bowel syndrome following extensive resection, and death if untreated.

title: Volvulus – Prognosis
content: Prognosis depends on prompt diagnosis and treatment; early surgical intervention leads to good outcomes, but delayed treatment increases mortality rates up to 30% in neonates.
